paper.title: Same Legal Facts, Different Verdicts: Evaluating Cross-Lingual and Dialectal Robustness in LLM Legal Reasoning
paper.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly evaluated on legal reasoning tasks, but most benchmarks remain English-centered and test each legal problem in only one linguistic form. We examine whether LLMs preserve legal reasoning performance when the same legal question is expressed across English, formal Arabic, simplified Arabic, and Egyptian Arabic. We construct a controlled benchmark of 200 bar-exam-style multiple-choice questions, preserving the legal facts, answer choices, and correct answer across all language versions. We evaluate GPT-4o, Gemini 2.5 Pro, Grok, and Qwen against a shared human-verified answer key. All models achieve their highest accuracy in English, but Arabic performance varies substantially. Qwen scores 97.0% in English and 79.0% in each Arabic condition, while GPT-4o is the most stable model, with 90.0% in English and 80.0–82.0% across Arabic variants. Gemini 2.5 Pro drops from 80.5% in English to 17.5–21.0% in Arabic, and Grok drops from 45.0% to 16.5–26.5%. These results show that strong English legal accuracy does not guarantee robust Arabic legal reasoning. We argue that multilingual legal evaluation should measure not only accuracy, but also English–Arabic gaps and cross-language variation across semantically aligned legal questions.

paper.title: Fine-tuning Small Language Models for Cross-Prompt Arabic Essay Scoring: A Benchmarking Study
paper.abstract: Automated Essay Scoring (AES) has been studied since the early days of computational methods. While recent advances incorporating large language models (LLMs) have significantly improved performance, most research has focused on English. In this paper, we present the first benchmark of Arabic cross-prompt AES using Arabic-centric LLMs. We evaluate ALLaM 7B, Jais 8B, and Fanar 9B under zero-shot, few-shot, and fine-tuning settings, and compare them against established AES systems and frontier LLMs. Fine-tuning substantially improves performance across all models, with Fanar achieving state-of-the-art results and outperforming the strongest baseline by 8 points on LAILA dataset. We further show that fine-tuned Arabic-centric LLMs generalize effectively in cross-dataset setting (LAILA \rightarrow ZAEBUC). Finally, we analyze the best-performing model, examining error patterns, trait interactions, and the effects of multi-trait autoregressive scoring.

paper.title: Align-Extract-Score: Graded Relevance of Arabic Essays
paper.abstract: Relevance is a central component of Automated Essay Scoring (AES), as it measures how well a student essay addresses a given writing prompt. In this work, we propose AESER, a novel approach to address the problem of graded relevance scoring in Arabic cross-prompt AES. AESER adapts the given prompt more towards the writing space of essays and computes token-level prompt-essay similarity matrices from contextual embeddings. These matrices are processed by a convolutional neural network to predict the relevance score. Experiments on a large Arabic AES dataset show that AESER outperforms strong baselines, establishing a new state-of-the-art performance.

paper.title: AraDetox: A Multi-Dialect Arabic Detoxification Dataset
paper.abstract: Arabic harmful-language detection has received considerable attention, yet Arabic text detoxification remains underexplored. We introduce AraDetox, a multi-dialect Arabic detoxification dataset comprising 10,500 harmful social-media posts and 84,000 detoxified rewrites generated using GPT-5 and Gemini 2.5 Flash across Modern Standard Arabic, Gulf, Levantine, and Egyptian Arabic. The generated outputs were assessed through human evaluation and automatic analyses of lexical change, semantic preservation, sentiment, and dialectal style. Results show that detoxification is primarily a meaning-preserving rewriting task: substantial lexical and structural reformulation is accompanied by consistently high semantic similarity. Human evaluation confirms successful harmful-language removal while largely preserving the original meaning. Dialectal analyses further indicate that the generated variants exhibit measurable stylistic alignment with reference Arabic dialect corpora. Comparison with existing resources highlights two complementary approaches to detoxification: minimal-edit lexical substitution and meaning-preserving reformulation. Our findings demonstrate that large-scale Arabic detoxification resources can be constructed through LLM-assisted generation and human verification. The dataset is publicly available at https://github.com/ArabicNLP-UK/AraDetox to support future research on Arabic detoxification, safe text generation, and multi-dialect Arabic NLP.

paper.title: Some Dialects are More Equal than Others: Non-Prestigious Arabic Dialectal Bias in LLMs
paper.abstract: Previous work on Egyptian Arabic in NLP has focused largely on the prestigious Cairene Egyptian Arabic (CEA) dialect, resulting in a lack of representation for the less prestigious Sa’idi Egyptian Arabic (SEA) dialect both in LLM and resource development. Does this lack of representation influence an LLM’s view of the acceptability of SEA (upstream), and does an upstream bias against SEA lead to worse performance (downstream)? We investigate the upstream effect of SEA dialectal features on LLM preferences in a Targeted Syntactic Evaluation (TSE) task which reveals a significant bias against SEA across multiple LLMs. We then analyze the effect of these same features on downstream model performance on MMLU benchmarks and show that models frequently experience a degradation in performance when presented with SEA. This work highlights the need for further exploration on how sub-dialectal variation impacts language technologies.

paper.title: DAASI: Arabic Text Simplification Corpus for Israeli Government Documents
paper.abstract: Arabic-speaking citizens in Israel routinely encounter government website documents written in Modern Standard Arabic (MSA), a variety that differs substantially from the Levantine dialect they use daily. This diglossia gap limits access to public services and creates informational inequity, especially for elderly citizens unfamiliar with modern language tools. We address this problem through three contributions. First, we present DAASI (Disglossia-Aware Arabic Simplification for Inclusion): a new parallel corpus of drawn from Israeli National Insurance Institute documents, constructed via GPT-4o draft simplification followed by expert human validation. Second, we conduct a sociolinguistic survey of 50 Arabic-speaking adults in Israel confirming that government documents are harder to comprehend than school-level texts. Third, we benchmark two Arabic transformer models and GPT-4o across multiple fine-tuning strategies and conduct human evaluations to assess simplified text. Our results confirm that existing Arabic NLP benchmarks do not generalize to the Israeli government domain and that DAASI fills a critical resource gap for inclusive Arabic NLP in a diglossic context.

paper.title: Beyond Gender, Number, and Rationality: Modeling Extended Arabic Morpho-Syntactic Agreement with Aggregation

author.affiliation: New York University and State University of New York, Stony Brook

paper.abstract: Arabic gender–number morpho-syntactic agreement exhibits systematic variation beyond functional gender, number, and rationality (GNR) (Alkuhlani and Habash, 2011). We identify and classify agreement patterns involving plural-to-unit and unit-to-members shifts, and introduce _aggregation_ (AGG), a lexeme-level feature and corpus-derived lexical-semantic resource that captures these extended agreement affordances. We extend the GNR agreement framework with aggregation and evaluate it on over one million agreement pairs from ATB1/2/3 and BAREC. AGG improves agreement prediction over a strong baseline by 1.4% absolute on average (38% error reduction). Remaining errors largely reflect analyzer, parser, and treebank limitations. Interpretable agreement assessment of this kind can support the development of pedagogical applications and benchmarking the grammaticality of generative model outputs.[Data and Code are publicly available: https://github.com/CAMeL-Lab/Arabic_GNRA_Lexicon.]

paper.title: SHAMS: An Audio-Grounded Pronunciation Benchmark for Levantine Arabic

author.affiliation: Tel Aviv University, Tel Aviv University

paper.abstract: Levantine Arabic (LA) is spoken by tens of millions of people, creating a pressing need for shared benchmarks to evaluate LA speech-language technologies. Evaluating such technology is particularly challenging given LA’s internal diversity and its opaque and non-standardized orthography. We present SHAMS (SHami Annotated Multi-dialect Speech), a benchmark comprising 1,300 utterances drawn from open audio corpora, balanced across five LA varieties (Urban and Rural Palestinian, and Urban Jordanian, Lebanese, and Syrian). Each utterance is represented across four aligned tiers: audio, unvocalized orthography, diacritized text, and phonetic transcription. This structure supports evaluation of various downstream tasks such as diacritization, grapheme-to-phoneme conversion, automatic speech recognition, and audio-to-phoneme, grounded in audio and stratified by variety. We benchmark open and proprietary models across these tasks to demonstrate the utility of this benchmark for measuring progress across LA. We release SHAMS at https://shams-nlp.github.io.

paper.title: BAREC-TB: A Dependency Treebank and Parsing Benchmark for Arabic Children’s Texts

author.affiliation: Mohamed bin Zayed University of Artificial Intelligence and New York University, Abu Dhabi
Mohamed bin Zayed University of Artificial Intelligence

paper.abstract: We present BAREC-TB, the first dependency treebank of Arabic children’s literature and educational texts. The 156K-word corpus includes texts drawn from eight sources, including curricula, reading materials, children’s stories, poems, and songs. The treebank is annotated according to the Columbia Arabic Treebank (CATiB) dependency representation. We compare BAREC-TB with existing Arabic treebanks, including the Penn Arabic Treebank and Camel Treebank, using corpus statistics, dependency-based measures of syntactic complexity, readability and vocabulary-related features. We also establish parsing benchmarks using both a trainable parser and large language models. The corpus will be made publicly available to support Arabic NLP, educational NLP, and language pedagogy research: https://barec.camel-lab.com/.

paper.title: HalluTruthQA: A Fine-Grained Benchmark for Hallucination Detection, Localization, and Explanation in Arabic Question Answering
paper.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) can generate fluent Arabic answers, yet factual errors remain difficult to detect, localize, explain, and verify. Existing hallucination benchmarks often provide only response-level labels, offering limited support for identifying the exact erroneous content, explaining why it is incorrect, or recovering the correct factual answer. We introduce HalluTruthQA, a fine-grained benchmark for hallucination evaluation in Arabic question answering. HalluTruthQA contains 2,400 expert-curated examples across four knowledge-intensive domains: Islamic knowledge, history, science, and geography. Each example includes an Arabic question, a model-generated answer, a verified reference answer, a binary hallucination label, and six candidate answers for factual verification. For hallucinated answers, the benchmark additionally provides character-level erroneous spans, human-written explanations, and macro- and micro-level hallucination types. We evaluate four open-source LLMs—ALLaM-7B, Falcon-H1R-7B, Qwen3-32B, and SILMA—in a zero-shot setting across four tasks: hallucination detection, span-level localization, factual verification, and explanation evaluation. The results show that these tasks measure complementary capabilities, with no single model achieving the best performance across all of them. The best observed scores are 0.880 Macro-F1 for hallucination detection, 0.516 F1-Sp for span localization, 0.852 LO-Score for factual verification, and 0.644 for explanation evaluation. Our findings highlight the importance of moving beyond binary hallucination detection toward fine-grained evaluation that also localizes, verifies, categorizes, and explains factual errors. Code, data, prompts, and evaluation scripts are available at https://gitlab.com/nlpresearcher/HalluTruthQA

paper.title: MAQAM: A Richly Annotated Corpus for Quranic Arabic Morphological Analysis and Disambiguation
paper.abstract: Quranic Arabic poses important challenges for Arabic NLP due to its distinctive morphology, syntax, and orthography. We present MAQAM, a richly annotated Morphosyntactic Arabic Quranic Analysis and Modeling resource covering the entire Quran, providing 22 lexical, inflectional, and clitic features for every word. The resource is constructed through a semi-automatic pipeline combining feature enrichment, morphological synchronization, and expert manual annotation and validation. We further evaluate Quranic morphosyntactic disambiguation under a realistic setting where the input may be represented in either the Uthmani or Imla’i script, and investigate cross-domain transfer between Quranic Arabic and MSA. Our results show that MSA and Quranic resources are complementary for Quranic disambiguation, with the best performance obtained by combining MSA training data, Quran-specific analyzers, and both script representations, whereas for MSA, only integrating Quranic resources provide modest gains. We make MAQAM publicly available.

paper.title: Using LALMs for Pronunciation Error Detection in Arabic

author.affiliation: University of Edinburgh, University of Edinburgh
Saudi Data and AI Authority, Saudi Data and AI Authority

paper.abstract: This paper presents Qwen-MDD-AR, our system for the Iqra’Eval.2 Interspeech 2026 challenge on Modern Standard Arabic pronunciation assessment. Built on Qwen3-ASR-1.7B, it frames Arabic mispronunciation detection and diagnosis as autoregressive speech-to-phoneme generation. We add the 68-phoneme MSA inventory as special tokens, freeze the audio encoder, and adapt the decoder with LoRA. Using only provided challenge data, our submission ranked 6th of 19 teams on the hidden QuranMB.v2 test set, with 0.6702 F1 and 0.0445 PER. In a controlled comparison on our internal mixed held-out set, a Wav2Vec2-BERT CTC baseline trained on the same data achieved better PER, precision, and F1, while Qwen-MDD-AR obtained the same recall and a small Correct Diagnosis advantage (0.9496 vs. 0.9328). Results suggest LoRA-adapted LALMs are a practical alternative for Arabic MDD, while alignment accuracy and inference cost remain open.

paper.title: Optimizing Inference Cost for Arabic–English Mathematical Reasoning in LLMs

author.affiliation: Jordan University of Science and Technology

paper.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) can solve mathematical problems through prompting, yet not all reasoning is cost-justified when using paid APIs. We study prompt-only methods for overthinking control in the black-box setting across four datasets: Arabic GSM8K, English GSM8K, English SVAMP, and ArMATH, each evaluated on 100-question subsets divided into Easy, Medium, and Hard categories. We test Direct Answer, Chain-of-Thought (CoT), First Answer Anchoring (FAA-lite), Confidence-Triggered Escalation (CTE), Self-Consistency, Verification, Arabic prompt variations, and Language-Optimal Prompt Routing (LOPR). CTE achieves 90% accuracy on Arabic GSM8K at 1.14 calls/query, 96% on English GSM8K at 1.06 calls/query, and 98% on SVAMP at 1.08 calls/query. Self-Consistency leads on ArMATH at 90% but costs 2.00 calls/query. Verification consistently increases token cost without accuracy gains. Format-Controlled CoT is the best single-call Arabic method; Bilingual-Glossary CoT is consistently harmful. CTE calibration reveals that explicit low-confidence outputs are rare (<1%), so CTE succeeds mainly because high-confidence predictions are accurate, not through active uncertainty detection.

paper.title: Shaer: Controlled Arabic Poetry Generation with Meter Subform and Semantic Conditioning

author.affiliation: Arab Center for Research and Policy Studies

paper.abstract: Classical Arabic poetry generation requires simultaneously satisfying semantic, linguistic, and fine-grained prosodic constraints. Existing systems typically control broad poetic attributes but do not jointly model semantic intent, meter subform, and poem length. We present Shaer, a controllable Classical Arabic poetry generation framework jointly conditioned on natural-language descriptions, meter subforms, and target hemistich counts. To support this task, we construct an enriched corpus of 116,032 classical Arabic poems derived from Ashaar, containing normalized meter-subform labels and automatically generated, validated semantic descriptions. We then adapt Yehia-7B using QLoRA-based supervised fine-tuning with a completion-only objective. Our evaluation combines automatic assessment of base-meter conformity, requested-subform adherence, and length control with three LLM judges, blinded human evaluation, and memorization analysis. Shaer achieves 95.17% base-meter accuracy, 91.75% poem-level meter-subform accuracy, and 83.40% exact count accuracy. Relative to its untuned foundation model, these results represent gains of 68.68, 57.77, and 38.93 percentage points, respectively; Shaer also attains the highest base-meter accuracy among all evaluated systems. Multi-LLM evaluation and a blinded human assessment of top-ranked outputs further indicate competitive semantic and literary quality. Finally, analysis of all 3,481 test generations finds no exact copies from the training corpus or paired source poems. Code, models, and datasets are publicly available.

paper.title: Cultural Understanding in Large Language Models: A Comparative Study with Human Judgments
paper.abstract: This paper evaluates whether large language models (LLMs) can demonstrate cultural competence in Egyptian Arabic—not just factual knowledge about culture, but the ability to choose culturally appropriate idiomatic and figurative expressions in everyday social situations. 67 Egyptian participants completed a multiple-choice questionnaire of 90 everyday scenarios to provide human gold labels. Using the same scenarios, each pairing a culturally appropriate Egyptian idiom against a plausible distractor, we evaluated 11 open-source and 3 proprietary models under five prompts and two answer orderings. The results indicated that humans performed near ceiling (98.2%), while LLMs averaged 68.2%. The results also showed that a single accuracy figure conflates three separable behaviors: cultural competence, an answer-position heuristic, and abstention. These behaviors are distributed so unevenly that the model ranking reorders depending on which one is measured. One model’s apparent mid-tier accuracy is almost entirely a “pick the first option” heuristic (a 0.75 normal–reversed gap), and another falls from 51.8% to below chance once refusals to answer are scored as errors. We argue that cultural-competence evaluation should report this decomposition rather than a headline accuracy.

paper.title: Gahwa: A Computational Lexicon for Emirati Arabic

author.affiliation: New York University and State University of New York, Stony Brook
Mohamed bin Zayed University of Artificial Intelligence

paper.abstract: Emirati Arabic remains one of the least-resourced Arabic dialects, with lexical information scattered across corpora, morphological databases, and dictionaries developed under incompatible annotation schemes. We present Gahwa, a machine-readable lexicon constructed by extracting, enriching, and standardizing evidence from an annotated Emirati corpus, a Gulf Arabic verb database, and a Gulf Arabic Wiktionary, unifying their input into one lemma-POS keyed scheme. We evaluate Gahwa through automatic coverage analysis of three Emirati datasets, GumarAE, Mixat, and the Ramsa Corpus, against existing Arabic morphological resources, and through analysis of out-of-vocabulary (OOV) forms. Results show that Gahwa has high word coverage across the three datasets, achieving 89.1-94.2% effective dediacritized lemma-POS token coverage, while the remaining OOV cases primarily reflect lexical gaps, orthographic variations, fused expressions, and morphological gaps.

paper.title: Arabic Safety Alignment as Selective Refusal: An Empirical Study of SFT, DPO, and Guard Calibration
paper.abstract: Arabic large language models must refuse harmful prompts without over-refusing benign or sensitive prompts, yet a single refusal rate hides this trade-off. We evaluate it using benign refusal B and harmful-prompt refusal H, where H measures refusal rather than harmful compliance. Across five Arabic-capable models and 130 runs on the full human-written AraSafe set, refusal-only supervised fine-tuning (SFT) collapses toward blanket refusal, whereas selected mixed-SFT configurations reach H\approx90–93% at B=14–23%; four selected configurations exceed H=90% in all three runs, while Fanar does so in two of three. Direct Preference Optimization (DPO) and inference guards change B and H differently across models rather than acting as uniform upgrades. In a blinded 300-response audit, annotator binary-refusal agreement is 89.0% (\kappa=0.78); Qwen3Guard and Aya Expanse 32B reach 88.7% and 91.0% accuracy, respectively, with no conclusive paired difference. Selected SFT raises H on Arabizi for all five models, but none reaches 90%, showing only partial transfer from Modern Standard Arabic; overall, the results support model-specific operating-point selection: set a deployment target and retain only interventions that improve it.

paper.title: What Makes a Good Fiqh Retriever? Answer Retrieval for Arabic Islamic Jurisprudence
paper.abstract: Retrieval-Augmented Generation is used for Islamic question answering, but most systems are evaluated end-to-end, making retrieval failures difficult to isolate from generation failures. We study answer-bearing retrieval for Arabic fiqh, where a passage is relevant only if it states the ruling required by the question. We build a retrieval test collection for Arabic fiqh and use it to evaluate dense, lexical, hybrid, fine-tuned, and madhhab-aware retrieval strategies. The best retriever achieves 0.524 MRR@5, while fine-tuning improves performance to 0.553. Hybrid retrieval provides limited gains for strong models, whereas madhhab-aware filtering more than doubles MRR@5 on school-specific questions. We further present an error analysis showing that the main challenge is distinguishing answer-bearing passages from topically similar passages that do not contain the requested ruling. The best-performing model and fine-tuning dataset are publicly available at https://huggingface.co/collections/somayaeltanbouly/badr-arabic-fiqh-retrieval

paper.title: From Subwords to Pixels: Evaluating Text Representations for Arabic Machine Translation

author.affiliation: Mohamed bin Zayed University of Artificial Intelligence and Egypt-Japan University of Science and Technology (E-JUST)
Mohamed bin Zayed University of Artificial Intelligence
Mohamed bin Zayed University of Artificial Intelligence

paper.abstract: Subword tokenization underpins modern neural NLP but can be suboptimal for morphologically rich languages with substantial orthographic variation. In this paper, we compare vocabulary-based and vocabulary-free representations for Arabic-to-English machine translation, including subword, byte-level, and pixel-level approaches. Across 35 evaluation sets spanning Modern Standard Arabic (MSA) and 18 dialects, all approaches achieve comparable translation performance with sufficient supervision. While subword models perform best with limited MSA pretraining data, differences diminish with scale and dialect-specific fine-tuning. Pixel-based models further exhibit the greatest robustness to unseen orthographic variation and provide the highest training and inference throughput. We make our code and models publicly available.

paper.title: SAFIR: A Sub-Dialectal Benchmark for Saudi Arabic–English Machine Translation

author.affiliation: King Salman International Academy for the Arabic Language

paper.abstract: Arabic machine translation benchmarks provide limited coverage of variation within Saudi Arabic. We introduce SAFIR, a Saudi-centric benchmark of 610 unique sentence pairs organized into 12 creator specific evaluation splits across five regional groups: Najdi, Hijazi, Southern, Northern, and Eastern. Native speakers authored the Arabic sentences and their English translations; 235 pairs received independent double review for dialect authenticity, translation adequacy, and fluency. We evaluate twelve systems, comprising losed-weight LLMs, open-weight LLMs, and dedicated MT models, in the zero-shot Saudi\rightarrowEnglish setting using reference-based metrics and GPT-4o judgments. Closed-weight LLMs obtain the strongest aggregate results. Gemini 2.5 Pro achieves the highest average BLEU (34.41), while GPT-5 achieves the highest BERTScore (83.60). Rankings vary across splits, and Southern varieties present particular challenges in judged adequacy. Differences between reference overlap, adequacy, and fluency support reporting performance by sampled variety and evaluation dimension. SAFIR and its leaderboard support more detailed assessment of Saudi Arabic translation.

paper.title: QuranicMMLU: A Cognitively-Aware Benchmark for Evaluating Generative AI Solutions on Quranic Linguistic Knowledge
paper.abstract: We introduce QuranicMMLU, a benchmark for evaluating generative AI on Quranic Arabic across multiple dimensions of linguistic complexity. Existing Quranic benchmarks center on general question answering and semantic retrieval, without probing specific linguistic competencies or stratifying by cognitive demand and verse difficulty. We construct a five-pillar Quranic taxonomy spanning Phonology, Morphology, Syntax, Semantics, and Pragmatics, with 31 leaves covering phenomena from tajwid and root-and-pattern morphology to occasions of revelation and inter-surah coherence. For each leaf we generate questions stratified by Bloom’s cognitive level and verse perplexity, then have LLM as a judge to independently answer and score every item and route the annotations to manual review. The resulting dataset comprises 980 human reviewed questions, each issued in both open ended and multiple-choice form. We benchmark 12 systems on these items and find that the Islamic-specialized model leads, yet every system scores higher on multiple-choice accuracy (average 84%) than open-ended answer quality (average 60%): the two rankings agree closely (Kendall’s τ = 0.73), but multiple-choice scoring hides failures that surface only once answer choices are removed. QuranicMMLU thus offers a rigorous, linguistically grounded framework for evaluating Arabic NLP in the Quranic domain.

paper.title: Comparative Study of Classical NLP and Pretrained Language Models for Tunisian Dialect Processing
paper.abstract: Recent transformer-based language models rely on subword tokenization and contextual embeddings, raising questions about the continued effectiveness of traditional preprocessing techniques such as stemming. This issue remains underexplored for low-resource Arabic dialects, particularly Tunisian Dialect (TD). In this paper, we investigate the impact of light and aggressive stemming on two main Tunisian NLP tasks: sentiment analysis and domain classification. We compare classical machine learning methods with transformer-based Arabic language models, including TunBERT. To support this study, we release an open Tunisian stemming resource containing 7,730 words annotated with both light and aggressive stems. Our experiments provide a comprehensive analysis of TD processing and show that the effectiveness of stemming depends on both the task and the model type.

paper.title: AraMIP: Extending MIPVU Towards Metaphor Identification in Arabic

author.affiliation: School of Oriental and African Studies, University of London

paper.abstract: Metaphor research has gained increasing attention due to its relevance to linguistic creativity, language use, cognitive processes, and related areas. While many efforts have been devoted to metaphor identification and annotation in English and other languages, Arabic remains under-resourced in this area. In this work, we propose the Arabic Metaphor Identification Procedure (AraMIP), a novel guideline for Arabic metaphor annotation. AraMIP builds on the widely used Metaphor Identification Procedure Vrije Universiteit (MIPVU) framework, incorporating adaptations that account for the language-specific properties of Arabic. We distinguish three major types of Arabic figurative language: isti‘āra (metaphor), kināya (metonymy/indirect expression), and tashbīh (simile) and annotate a pilot dataset of 300 sentences (5277 words). Our analysis reveals key challenges specific to Arabic, including morphological complexity, inconsistencies in dictionary sense ordering, and the absence of standardized contextual materials for annotators. This work contributes a first step toward standardized Arabic figurative instances and facilitates the development of larger annotated resources, thereby supporting future research on figurative language in Arabic.

paper.title: AraScholar: Calibrating Academic Paraphrasing in Modern Standard Arabic

author.affiliation: Al-Imam Mohamed Ibn Saud Islamic University

paper.abstract: Academic paraphrasing in Modern Standard Arabic must change expression without distorting scientific content. We study this balance through AraScholar, a corpus of 20,002 manually written source–paraphrase pairs with 522 raw domain labels and item-level provenance. On 2,000 held-out sentences, fine-tuned AraT5v2 favors lexical reuse under beam search, while frontier models produce more extensive rewrites. With corrected Arabic punctuation normalization, diverse decoding and preservation-constrained reranking attain 74.25% coverage of a fixed novelty–preservation band, compared with 52.60% for zero-shot GPT-4o. Gold coverage is only 46.65%, showing that this band measures constraint compliance rather than human quality. Post-hoc target matching substantially improves a calibrated GPT-4o control and narrows the gap, although candidate budgets differ. Crucially, an independent 200-instance audit favors frontier models on meaning and paraphrase quality. We document the corpus, decoding controls, negative distillation result, and metric sensitivity, including test-derived calibration and checkpoint-selection limitations. The findings establish operating-point control as a useful capability while demonstrating why calibration must be evaluated alongside independent assessments of writing quality.

paper.title: Arabic-Centric Preference Optimization for Efficient Dialect-Sensitive Machine Translation: A Seq2Seq Approach

author.affiliation: Alexandria University and Applied Innovation Center

paper.abstract: Arabic machine translation remains challenging because Modern Standard Arabic and dialectal varieties such as Egyptian Colloquial Arabic differ substantially in morphology, lexical choice, register, and everyday usage. We introduce a compact Arabic-centric encoder–decoder machine translation model designed to strengthen translation involving Modern Standard Arabic and Egyptian Arabic while preserving multilingual translation ability. We pretrain from scratch with multilingual Seq2Seq training and contrastive cross-lingual alignment, using an Arabic-centered data mixture covering Arabic, English, Egyptian Arabic, and 111 additional languages. We further apply Direct Preference Optimization (DPO) for our Seq2Seq model using grounded preference pairs targeting Arabic-specific translation errors, including literal translation, register mismatch, lexical ambiguity, domain terminology, and dialectal naturalness. We evaluate our model on FLORES, WMT24++, and NTREX using spBLEU. Results show that our model remains competitive with substantially larger LLM baselines and achieves its clearest gains on Arabic-centered directions, especially Egyptian Arabic. DPO improves FLORES translation into English by approximately +2 spBLEU for Egyptian Arabic and +2 spBLEU for Modern Standard Arabic. Our findings support targeted Arabic-centric Seq2Seq modeling as an efficient path for dialect-sensitive machine translation.

paper.title: What WER Hides: A Closer Look at Algerian Code-Switched ASR
paper.abstract: Automatic speech recognition for Algerian social-media speech is hard because of dialectal variation, Arabic-French code-switching, and non-standard orthography, yet these difficulties are usually summarised by a single word error rate that hides where recognition fails and whether gains reach information-bearing content. We evaluate seven systems on roughly 30 minutes of Algerian political social-media speech, annotated by language variety as Algerian dialect, Modern Standard Arabic, code-switched, or French: a Whisper-large-v3 baseline, five Whisper variants fine-tuned on different combinations of broadcast, dialectal, and code-switched speech, and the prompted Qwen3-Omni model. The best system reduces overall WER from 60.1% to 31.3%, but still reaches 44.0% on code-switched speech, and named entities remain harder than ordinary tokens, with fewer than half preserved. These results show that ASR difficulty on Algerian social-media speech cannot be read from overall WER alone; it must be measured separately by language variety and by whether named entities survive.

paper.title: AHA-Memes: A Fine-Grained Multimodal Benchmark for Hate Detection in Arabic Memes
paper.abstract: Hateful memes are a growing form of multimodal online harm, where hostile intent is often conveyed through the joint interpretation of images, text, cultural references, and implicit targets. While hateful meme detection has advanced in high-resource languages, Arabic remains underexplored, with existing meme resources focusing mainly on propaganda or coarse harmful-content labels. We introduce AHA-Memes, which is, to our knowledge, the first large Arabic hateful meme benchmark with fine-grained, multi-label annotations. The dataset includes 5K manually annotated memes using a taxonomy that captures hate types, i.e., attack strategies. We further provide ~66K silver-labeled memes to support future studies. We benchmark text-only, image-only, and late-fusion multimodal models, as well as few-shot in-context learning (ICL) and open- and closed-weight Vision-Language Models (VLMs) under zero-shot and fine-tuning settings. Our results establish strong baselines and highlight key challenges in culturally grounded Arabic hateful meme detection. We release the dataset, annotation guidelines, and evaluation scripts to support future research. (**Resources:** https://github.com/MohamedBayan/AHA-Memes) (**Hugging Face:** https://huggingface.co/datasets/QCRI/AHA-MEMES)

paper.title: Towards Speech ALDi: Predicting the Arabic Level of Dialectness Directly from Speech

author.affiliation: Mohamed bin Zayed University of Artificial Intelligence

paper.abstract: Arabic Dialect Identification (ADI) aims at automatically assigning an utterance—written or spoken—to a single variety, be it Modern Standard Arabic (MSA) or a variety of Dialectal Arabic (DA). To complement ADI, the Arabic Level of Dialectness (ALDi) has been proposed to model the different dialect levels that exist between MSA and Highly Dialectal text. However, current ALDi estimation models operate on text inputs only. This paper presents the first step toward extending ALDi to the speech modality. First, we use the automatically estimated ALDi score of a spoken utterance’s transcript as the silver-standard target score. We then compare the performance of two approaches at automatically predicting these silver-standard ALDi scores from spoken utterances: (1) a cascaded approach where automatic speech recognition is used to generate automatic transcripts that are then fed to a text-based ALDi estimation model, and (2) a direct ALDi estimation from speech. We use SADA—a dataset of 435 hours of manually transcribed Arabic speech—as the fine-tuning source data, and evaluate the two approaches on three datasets that cover different varieties of Arabic. Our results indicate that estimating silver-standard ALDi scores directly from speech is on-par or slightly worse than the cascaded approach for in-domain data. However, the direct approach generalizes better, especially for dialects where the fine-tuned ASR backbone of the cascaded approach has relatively large word-error-rates. This paper paves the way towards predicting ALDi scores directly from speech inputs.

paper.title: Definition-Guided Learning and Root-Stratified Evaluation for Arabic Lexical Semantics

author.affiliation: King Salman International Academy for the Arabic Language
King Salman International Academy for the Arabic Language
King Salman International Academy for the Arabic Language

paper.abstract: We introduce Definition-Guided Learning (DGL), a contrastive training framework that uses dictionary definitions as semantic queries and lemmas as retrieval targets, instantiated here for Arabic reverse dictionary retrieval. We construct a root-stratified Arabic lexical benchmark that limits morphological root overlap between training and test partitions. Zero-shot evaluation suggests a notable gap, with the best pre-trained model achieving only 11.16% Top@1 accuracy on this benchmark. Fine-tuning with DGL yields 41.13% Top@1 and NDCG@10 of 49.32%, an improvement of roughly 3.7 times over the strongest zero-shot baseline we tested. Our results suggest that in-batch negative sampling tends to outperform Triplet Loss in this setting, and that definition length and lexical difficulty appear to trade off in importance across retrieval depth. These findings offer preliminary evidence that lexicographic resources can serve as a useful supervisory signal for Arabic embedding learning, at least within the scope of the benchmark studied here.

paper.title: Real-Time Quranic Recitation Assessment on Mobile Devices Using Streaming Inference and Model Compression
paper.abstract: Automatic Quranic recitation assessment requires accurate detection of phonetic and Tajweed-related pronunciation errors while providing low-latency feedback. However, most speech recognition models are designed for offline processing and are too large for deployment on consumer mobile devices.We present a real-time Quranic recitation assessment system based on a multi-head Wav2Vec2-BERT model trained to jointly predict phonemes and Tajweed Sifat attributes using Connectionist Temporal Classification. To enable streaming inference without retraining, we introduce an Adaptive Eager-Emission framework that combines heuristic output commitment, dynamic context expansion, and overlap recovery, reducing perceived latency while preserving long-range temporal features.For efficient on-device deployment, we propose a structured compression pipeline based on encoder pruning, recovery fine-tuning, and INT8 quantization with ONNX optimization, reducing a 600M-parameter, 2.4 GB model to a 24.5M-parameter, 36 MB model while maintaining recognition performance.The streaming framework consistently outperforms static sliding-window approaches across the accuracy–latency trade-off, achieving responsiveness as low as 1.0 s at roughly 2.1% phoneme error rate (PER), or near-offline performance below 1% PER at 6.0 s average chunk latency, while the production streaming configuration maintains 99.45% average Sifat attribute accuracy. On a mid-range Android CPU, the compressed model runs at a real-time factor of 0.225 with a peak memory of about 600 MB.

paper.title: KASHAF: A Hierarchical Resource and Pipeline for Arabic Interpretable Semantic Textual Similarity

author.affiliation: Al-Imam Mohamed Ibn Saud Islamic University

paper.abstract: We introduce KASHAF, to our knowledge the first interpretable Semantic Textual Similarity (iSTS) resource and end-to-end system for Arabic: a corpus of 7,811 human-annotated sentence pairs (inter-annotator κ=0.83κ= 0.83 κ=0.83 on a doubly-annotated subset) under a three-level hierarchical schema (sentence, phrase, and word), together with a modular pipeline that produces this layered analysis plus a composite similarity score, the KASHAF Hierarchical Similarity Score (KHSS), calibrated to the ordinal SEM scale. On a held-out cross-batch test split (1,002 pairs, disjoint from training and dev), KASHAF reaches macro-F1 =0.659= 0.659 =0.659 (±0.016±0.016 ±0.016, 5 seeds) and Spearman ρ=0.6715ρ= 0.6715 ρ=0.6715; a rule-based antonym/negation polarity gate provides an empirical score-capping rule for high-similarity contradictions, and the MARBERTv2 backbone leads three alternative Arabic encoders. As an off-the-shelf diagnostic rather than a fine-tuned comparison, four contemporary LLMs under matched prompting reach at most macro-F1 0.215 (standard prompting) and 0.336 (chain-of-thought), a 32–44-point gap that reflects systematic over-prediction of SEM-PARA at the expense of the dominant SEM-PARTIAL class. We release the schema, guidelines, code, models, and a reproducibility pipeline; the corpus is available from KSAA on request.

paper.title: Quanta: A Fine-Grained Dataset and Benchmark for Arabic Machine-Translation Error Analysis
paper.abstract: Automatic machine-translation (MT) metrics collapse heterogeneous errors into a single score. For Arabic, no fine-grained resource exists for diagnosing error types and severity. We introduce QUANTA, a 9,032-instance En to Ar MT-error dataset (738 real UNPC + 7,856 synthetic training instances, both structurally validated, plus a held-out 438-instance real Gold test set) annotated with Mizan (ميزان, "scale"), a new 23-class MQM-compatible taxonomy organised in a four-level hierarchy: 23 leaf classes rolling up to 14 subtypes, 5 parent groups, and 4 TQA dimensions. To make the resource usable, we release the Raqeeb (رقيب, "observer") classifier, an AraBERT-v2 model for predicting Mizan 23-class labels (5-fold Gold macro-F1 = 0.614 ± 0.017). Data quality is supported by ETCA (Error Taxonomy Cross-vendor Audit), an LLM-as-judge check in which a different-vendor model audits QUANTA instances for anchor validity and label fidelity, curbing same-family self-preference bias, and by dual-annotator validation (Gwet’s AC1 = 0.97 synthetic; 0.83 real) on core taxonomy criteria. Ablations show that anchor-guided framing is decisive (without it, macro-F1 collapses to 0.114); that 738 structurally validated real samples are ≈12× more sample-efficient than synthetic data; and that, restricted to the classes with real-tier training support, combining both tiers outperforms real (0.656) or synthetic (0.312) alone. Code, data, prompts, and checkpoints are publicly available.

paper.title: Beyond Monolithic Libyan Arabic: A Sub-Regional Speech Corpus and Dialect Identification Benchmark
paper.abstract: Spoken Arabic dialect identification (DID) has advanced quickly, but Libyan Arabic remains under-served and, where it appears, is labeled only at the country level, hiding the variation between the Libyan coast and interior. We present a Libyan Arabic speech corpus annotated at the sub-regional level: Tripolitania (west), Cyrenaica (east), and Fezzan (south). It contains 133.7 hours of single-speaker segments from 645 speakers across 161 channels (YouTube and TikTok sources). An automated pipeline (diarization, speaker embedding, clustering, cross-episode linking) produces silver labels from channel provenance. One annotator then reviewed the resulting speaker clusters and confirmed the provenance region for 95.5% of the kept speakers (a within-annotator figure). We release speaker-disjoint splits. An off-the-shelf Arabic DID model recognizes our verified Libyan speech as Libyan only 74% of the time and cannot resolve the region. On the new three-way task, the encoder matters more than the classifier: a probe over speaker-recognition ECAPA embeddings reaches 0.525 macro-F1, over a language-identification ECAPA reaches 0.660, and fine-tuning that encoder reaches 0.702 (75.5% accuracy), far above the 0.20 floor. A channel-disjoint re-test reaches 0.609, versus 0.702 speaker-disjoint; Fezzan is hardest at 0.313. The task is learnable, but Fezzan performance remains low. We release the corpus, cached embeddings, and code.

paper.title: SALM: Social Arabic Language Model

author.affiliation: George Washington University and Johns Hopkins University

paper.abstract: Arabic NLP faces a fundamental mismatch between training and deployment conditions. While most language models are trained predominantly on Modern Standard Arabic (MSA), real-world communication occurs largely in spoken dialects. To bridge this gap, we leverage social media content from Reddit, Twitter, and YouTube as a scalable proxy for spoken Arabic. We construct a 1.04-billion-token pretraining corpus and train SALM, a compact 336M-parameter decoder-only language model pre-trained via next-token prediction alone, no masked language modelling, no dialect labels, no task-specific signal. Despite an order-of-magnitude smaller training corpus than existing dialectal PLMs and a generative training objective that provides no direct classification signal, SALM matches MARBERT, explicitly pre-trained on one billion dialectal tweets, within 0.7 percentage points on MADAR-26 dialect identification accuracy and outperforms it on macro-F1. Under full fine-tuning, SALM surpasses all baselines, achieving 69.1% accuracy on 26-way city-level dialect classification. Under the same frozen probe on binary Arabic sentiment (AJGT), SALM achieves 92.2% accuracy, topping all Arabic PLMs, encoder and decoder alike. We release the corpus and trained model to facilitate future research on Arabic spoken language modelling.

paper.title: Knowledge Graphs and Distributional Readability of Arabic Documents

author.affiliation: Arab Center for Research and Policy Studies
Arab Center for Research and Policy Studies
Arab Center for Research and Policy Studies
Arab Center for Research and Policy Studies and American University of Beirut

paper.abstract: This paper addresses automatic readability assessment of Arabic documents. It compares classical readability formulae, fine-tuned Arabic encoders, zero-shot large language models and a Co-occurrence Graphs for Arabic Readability (CoGAR). CoGAR, interpretable and LLM-free, represents a document as a co-occurrence network over content lemmas and use topology features such as density, clustering, path length and degree entropy to predict readability. Evaluated on the BAREC corpus over five ordinal levels, the method reaches a quadratic weighted kappa (QWK) of 0.756, on par with a sparse 35B-parameter LLM and well above the surface formulas Flesch and OSMAN.An ablation shows that the signal lies in the graph’s shape rather than size, and that alternative graphs based on relations between named-entity carry almost no readability difficulty signal. We further distill a frontier LLM (Gemini) into a small Arabic encoder (NeoAraBERT) by silver labelling 30k chunks, reaching 0.714 QWK. We show that stacking an LLM with CoGAR improves on the LLM alone, reaching QWK 0.839 with GPT-4.1 and 0.852 with the open-weight Qwen-35B, our best result. The two signals are complementary and the gain does not depend on a proprietary model. Finally, we analyze how eight methods including CoGAR distribute reading levels across seven Arabic text sources ranging from children books to expert research manuscripts showing how the methods align with intuitive difficulty.

paper.title: Why LLM Aggregation Falls Short: Correlated Errors and Selection Gaps in Arabic Punctuation Restoration
paper.abstract: Combining LLMs for Arabic punctuation restoration should help when their errors are complementary, but aggregation failure can reflect either missing coverage, where no predictor proposes the correct label, or failed selection, where the correct label is present but not selected. We investigate this distinction with vote-based, text-blind aggregators that use predictor labels, agreement, position, and neighbouring predictions, but not Arabic words. We evaluate three frontier LLMs and a fine-tuned AraBERT encoder on AraPunc-sub and ABC. The LLMs show strongly correlated errors: when all three are wrong, they choose the same incorrect label in 79.4% of cases on AraPunc-sub and 77.8% on ABC. Yet the four-predictor oracle achieves macro-F_1 scores of 0.857 and 0.778, surpassing the best standalone predictors (0.639 and 0.496). Leave-one-predictor-out analysis shows that AraBERT supplies the largest unique oracle coverage. Standard aggregation recovers only part of this headroom, and no tested aggregator outperforms standalone AraBERT on AraPunc-sub. A selectability probe confirms that some covered disagreements are learnable, but a deployable router offers only modest, corpus-dependent gains. Even a text-aware peer-deliberation step deepens rather than breaks the correlation, as weaker models conform to their peers. Hence, in the tested text-blind regime, the bottleneck is primarily selection rather than coverage, without ruling out text-aware selectors.

paper.title: Child ASR Adaptation with Adult Retention: An Empirical Study
paper.abstract: Automatic Speech Recognition (ASR) systems often underperform for children and non-native speakers, while adapting adult ASR models to child speech can cause adult-speech forgetting. We study child ASR adaptation with adult retention across Arabic and English. We compare full fine-tuning, LoRA, and post-hoc weight-space merging across encoder–decoder, encoder–CTC, and AudioLLM-based ASR systems. Experiments use Arabic native and non-native child speech, English MyST child speech, and adult benchmarks from MGB-2 and LibriSpeech test-clean. We evaluate recognition quality with WER and quantify the adaptation–retention trade-off using Retention Index, Child Adaptation Gain, and Adaptation Recovery. Results show that child adaptation is necessary, especially for non-native Arabic and English child speech, but direct adaptation often reduces adult ASR performance. Bilingual adaptation is more stable than language-specific adaptation. Weight-space merging often improves the trade-off, especially for encoder–CTC, Whisper, and AudioLLM-based ASR, with LERP favoring adult retention and TIES recovering stronger child gains. For the encoder–decoder model, direct bilingual fine-tuning remains strongest in raw WER.

meta.booktitle: Proceedings of The Fourth Arabic Natural Language Processing Conference: Shared Tasks

paper.title: NADI 2026: The Second Multidialectal Arabic Speech Processing Shared Task

author.affiliation: King Abdullah University of Science and Technology
King Fahad University of Petroleum and Minerals

paper.abstract: NADI 2026 is the seventh edition of the Nuanced Arabic Dialect Identification (NADI) shared task series and the second dedicated to multidialectal Arabic speech processing. This edition comprises five tasks and eight subtasks spanning Automatic Speech Recognition (ASR), Spoken Dialect Identification (SDID), Text-to-Speech (TTS), Spoken Language Translation (SLT), and Spoken Language Understanding (SLU). NADI 2026 emphasizes realistic evaluation through low-bandwidth, mixed-dialect, code-switched, out-of-domain, and zero-shot settings, while introducing TTS, SLT, and SLU to the series for the first time. The shared task attracted 21 participating teams from at least 13 countries, with 48 test-phase submissions, and 14 submitted system-description papers. Results show that out-of-domain generalization remain a bottleneck and highlight the effectiveness of recent Arabic-specialized speech models, multimodal dialect identification, and ensemble methods. Overall, NADI 2026 provides a broader and more challenging benchmark for robust Arabic dialect speech processing.

paper.title: Sabaa at NADI 2026 Subtask 1.1: Matching Annotation Conventions for Dialectal Arabic ASR
paper.abstract: This paper describes our submission to NADI 2026 Subtask 1.1, speech recognition for eight Arabic dialects under noisy conditions. Our system adapts whisper-large-v3-turbo with one low-rank adapter per dialect, decodes with tuned beam search, and applies a normalization step that matches the spelling conventions of the reference transcriptions rather than applying generic orthographic rules. We train only on the shared-task data, which places our results well below those of systems built with large external corpora, and we report our numbers with that constraint in mind. Country-average WER falls from 0.804 for the zero-shot backbone to 0.6053 on the test set. We also report three observations that shaped the system: per-dialect adapters outperform a jointly trained adapter on all eight dialects even when the joint model is trained for twice as long; replacing beam search with temperature sampling in order to produce diverse hypotheses for rescoring costs more accuracy than the rescoring recovers; and because the official scorer normalizes hypothesis and reference identically, generic character-level normalization cannot help, whereas learning each dialect’s annotation convention from the training transcriptions does.

paper.title: Aslema at NADI 2026: Data Augmentation for Intent Recognition and Slot Filling

author.affiliation: Hamad Bin Khalifa University and Qatar Computing Research Institute

paper.abstract: We present Aslema, our system for NADI 2026 Shared Task 5, which consists of two subtasks: intent recognition and slot filling. We evaluate four omni LLMs in a zero-shot setting and compare them with fine-tuned models. Our results show that fine-tuning consistently outperforms zero-shot inference. We further explore synthetic data augmentation by using an LLM to generate culturally grounded Tunisian Derja utterances, followed by voice cloning to generate synthetic speech. Incorporating this synthetic data improves performance on both tasks. Our final submitted system, based on Qwen3-Omni-30B and trained with a mixture of original and synthetic data, achieves 86.8% intent accuracy and 34.7 WER on the devtest split. On the official test set it ranks 1st in slot filling (59.5 CoER) and 4th among 5 teams in intent recognition (66.1% accuracy). We release our experimental scripts and the synthetic dataset to support further research.

paper.title: Abjad AI at NADI 2026 shared task: Overcoming Data Scarcity in Arabic Speech Processing through Augmentation
paper.abstract: We describe our submission to three NADI 2026 subtasks: Tunisian Arabic–French–English code-switched ASR (Task 1.3), dialectal Arabic speech translation, and 20-way Arabic dialect identification (ADI). For code-switched ASR, we finetune a 2B-parameter FastConformer encoder-decoder with synthetic Tunisian speech, cross-lingual data, waveform augmentation, and checkpoint averaging, achieving 14.12% WER and ranking first overall. For speech translation, finetuning Whisper Large-v3 yields strong in-domain results but poor generalization (BLEU 5.8 on blind test), illustrating overfitting under limited data. For ADI, a classifier on frozen pretrained ASR representations outperforms full/partial finetuning, reaching 42% accuracy across 20 dialects. We highlight synthetic augmentation, checkpoint averaging, and encoder freezing as effective low-resource strategies.

paper.title: The Nile at NADI 2026 Subtask 1.1: A Two-Phase Acoustic Fine-Tuning Strategy for Robust Dialectal Arabic Speech Recognition
paper.abstract: Two-phase Whisper fine-tuning (broad dialect pre-training + low-LR target annealing) reaches 57.0 WER on NADI 2026 Subtask 1.1, with 8 WER points from the schedule alone.

paper.title: Wifaq at NADI 2026 Shared Task: Data Expansion and System Combination for Robust Arabic ASR
paper.abstract: Wifaq is our entry to NADI 2026 Subtask 1.1, which evaluates country-level Arabic automatic speech recognition across eight dialects under noisy conditions. We fully fine-tune four 600M-parameter W2v-BERT 2.0 CTC models on nested mixtures of task and ex- ternal speech, decode them with a shared 5-gram KenLM, and combine their hypotheses by word voting; each run fits on one 16 GB NVIDIA RTX 4070 Ti SUPER. The submitted four-way ensemble ranked first among nine entries on the blind test with 43.23% WER and 20.0% CER. On a reused 800-utterance local holdout, it lowers WER from 46.12% for the strongest single model to 44.0%

paper.title: NAMAA Community at NADI 2026: Mixed-Dialect and Code-Switched Arabic ASR and Spoken Dialect Identification
paper.abstract: Robust Arabic speech processing must accommodate dialectal variation, multilingual code-switching, and distribution shift. We present NAMAA Community’s systems for three NADI 2026 speech subtasks: Mixed-Dialect Arabic ASR, Code-Switched Arabic ASR, and 20-way Spoken Arabic Dialect Identification. For Mixed-Dialect ASR, an Arabic-specific Conformer–Transformer achieves 0.45 word error rate (WER) on the blind set, outperforming a development-selected normalization and consensus pipeline at 0.49. For Code-Switched ASR, two-stage LoRA adaptation of the Tunisian Whisper-derived FarukSTT checkpoint, with multilingual tokenization and unconstrained decoding, yields 20.38% WER and 8.06% character error rate (CER) on validation and 16.98% blind-test WER. For dialect identification, a four-model ensemble reaches 0.950 development accuracy but 0.31 on the out-of-domain blind set. Label-free class-spread and inter-model agreement diagnostics identify an outlying component; removing it improves blind accuracy to 0.36, and a refined three-model submission reaches 0.38. Across Subtasks 1.2 and 2, development-selected calibration did not reliably transfer to blind data, although the available comparisons do not isolate the causal effect of individual components.

paper.title: CIS-OpenSLU at NADI 2026 Shared Task: ASR-Matched Training and Confidence-Based Rejection for Open-Set Tunisian Arabic Intent Recognition
paper.abstract: Open-set spoken intent recognition for low-resource Arabic varieties must handle both automatic speech recognition (ASR) errors and intents absent from training. We describe CIS-OpenSLU, our NADI 2026 Task 5.1 system, which transcribes Tunisian Arabic speech with Whisper Turbo and classifies the resulting text using word- and character-level TF–IDF features with a LinearSVC. On ASR-transcribed validation audio, training the classifier on Whisper-generated transcripts rather than gold transcripts raises weighted F1 from 49.25% to 69.78%, showing that matching training and inference text distributions is crucial. We rank test utterances by the maximum SVM decision score and reject low-confidence examples as unknown; the final system achieves 71.54% weighted F1 and 72.50% accuracy, ranking second. Auxiliary audio and multi-modal experiments further show that strong unseen-intent detection in leave-one-intent-out simulation does not necessarily transfer to genuinely unseen test intents.

paper.title: CodeZone Research Group at NADI 2026 Shared Task: Cross-Domain Score Calibration for Spoken Arabic Dialect Identification
paper.abstract: We describe the CodeZone Research Group system for NADI 2026 Shared Task 2, spo ken Arabic dialect identification over Modern Standard Arabic and 19 country-level dialects under cross-domain evaluation. Our system ensembles an ECAPA-TDNN language identi fier fine-tuned on the shared task data with a Whisper-large-v3 dialect classifier that we fur ther adapt using waveform- and spectrogram level augmentation, fusing their log-softmax scores. This ensemble reaches 94.35% accu racy on in-domain validation but initially re tained only 25.40% on the official blind test, a collapse that affected every participating team. We show that about a fifth of this gap is a cali bration failure rather than a modelling failure: discarding per-class bias terms fit in domain raised official accuracy from 0.2540 to 0.3918 and lowered the shared task’s average cost from 0.2077 to 0.1515, and a softening temperature reduced cost further to 0.1469; neither change touched either model. Our submission ranked 10th of 16 teams, and we show analytically why uniform additive score shifts cannot affect this metric while temperature scaling can.

paper.title: AI Elites at NADI 2026 Shared Task: Selecting on Out-of-Domain Accuracy for Cross-Domain Spoken Arabic Dialect Identification
paper.abstract: We describe our submission to NADI-2026 Subtask 2, country-level spoken Arabic dialect identification on a blind test set from undisclosed sources. Because the target domain is unknown at development time, we select on out-of-domain accuracy rather than in-domain validation accuracy at every decision point, comparing three backbones under a common pooling-plus-linear head and training the selected Arabic ASR encoder on ADI20-micro mixed with Casablanca. The system reaches 91.54% in-domain, 73.10% on the held-out MADIS-5 corpus (scored five-way), and 52.51% on the blind test set (C_{\mathrm{avg}} 0.11), placing fourth. The criterion helped, choosing an encoder that in-domain accuracy would have rejected by 32 points on a held-out corpus, a gap more than twenty times our measured seed variation, but it was not sufficient: of the 39.03-point in-domain to blind gap, at least 18.44 points are attributable to leaving the training domain. We trace part of the remainder to a corpus that entered the training mixture while still being used for checkpoint selection.

paper.title: Thakaa at NADI 2026 Shared Task: ROVER Ensembling and Multi-Representation Fusion for Robust Arabic ASR and Dialect Identification

author.affiliation: Thakaa, Advanced Company for Information Technology
Thakaa, Advanced Company for Information Technology
Thakaa, Advanced Company for Information Technology

paper.abstract: We describe Thakaa’s systems for NADI 2026 subtasks 1.1 and 1.3 and Task 2, covering noisy country-level Arabic automatic speech recognition (ASR), Tunisian code-switched ASR, and spoken dialect identification. The ASR systems combine heterogeneous connectionist temporal classification (CTC), encoder–decoder, and audio-LLM recognizers through ROVER, with country-aware routing for subtask 1.1 and a frame-rate-corrected CTC anchor for subtask 1.3. The dialect identifier fuses Ara-BEST-RQ acoustic scores with lexical evidence extracted from Cohere and Whisper transcripts by a partially fine-tuned MARBERTv2 model. Our official test scores were 50.41% WER on subtask 1.1, 14.53% WER on subtask 1.3, and 56.15% accuracy on Task 2, ranking third, third, and first, respectively. Across the three systems, the largest gains came from explicit control of alignment, temporal resolution, and evidence diversity rather than from model scale alone.

paper.title: KAND CA at NADI 2026 Shared Task: Multi-Stage Fine-Tuning for Spoken Arabic Dialects
paper.abstract: We describe the KAND CA systems for all five subtasks of the NADI 2026 shared task on multidialectal Arabic speech processing. For the three ASR subtasks, a single family of staged, fully fine-tuned Whisper large-v3 models — broad dialectal adaptation, then only task-matched gold data — is combined with task-specific levers: an mT5 spellingcorrection post-editor trained on the task references (Subtask 1.1, final country-average WER 0.5111), chained continue-fine-tuning through the Subtask 1.1 data before the Mixed- ASR dev split (Subtask 1.2, WER 0.48), and a fresh two-epoch schedule over a 46K-clip external gold Tunisian–French corpus with an accent-only French post-pass (Subtask 1.3, WER 15.21%). For spoken dialect identification (Task 2), where in-domain accuracy anti-predicted blind-test accuracy, our system fuses an architecturally distinct FastConformerencoder classifier, a decorrelated enhancedaudio view, and an ASR-transcript text route, reaching 0.5114 accuracy. For dialectal TTS (Subtask 3) we submitted 4,001 voice-cloned clips across ten dialects (UTMOS 2.72). We also report extensive negative results and release our models, correctors, and code publicly.

paper.title: Lynx at the NADI 2026 Shared Task: Exploring ASR Representations and Transcripts for Dialectal Arabic Speech Understanding
paper.abstract: Speech conveys complementary information through its linguistic content and acoustic characteristics. Speech-related tasks can exploit either source of information or combine them to improve performance. In this paper, we present Lynx_Id and Lynx_In, our systems for the NADI 2026 Spoken Dialect Identification and Intent Recognition tasks, respectively. Both systems build on an automatic speech recognition (ASR) model. Lynx_Id is a late-fusion system for dialect identification. It combines internal representations from the ASR encoder with predictions derived from the ASR transcript. Lynx_In is a two-branch text-based system that uses ASR transcriptions for intent recognition. One branch predicts the intent among the known classes, while the second acts as a gate to detect out-of-scope utterances. Lynx_Id achieved 53.53% accuracy and ranked third in the Spoken Dialect Identification task, while Lynx_In achieved a weighted F1 score of 76.86% and ranked first in the Intent Recognition task.

paper.title: Resonate at NADI 2026 Shared Task: Robust Speech Recognition and Dialect Identification under Acoustic and Domain Shift

author.affiliation: Applied Innovation Center and Nile University
Applied innovation center and Nile University
Applied Innovation Center and Nile University
Applied Innovation Center and Nile University
Faculty of Computers and Artificial Intelligence, Cairo University

paper.abstract: This paper describes the Resonate team’s submission to the NADI 2026 shared task on multidialectal Arabic speech processing. We participated in the robust dialectal Arabic ASR (Subtask 1.1) and spoken Arabic dialect identification (Task 2) subtasks, adding no external labelled speech. Our best single ASR model is a fully fine-tuned Cohere Transcribe Arabic, a 2.07B-parameter Arabic speech model, trained on 239.6K rows derived entirely from the 12.8K official clips through voice conversion, in-corpus noise augmentation and short-clip re-segmentation. Our submitted entry combines nine checkpoints of four sibling runs with a pivot-anchored ROVER vote and a per-dialect orthographic canonicaliser, obtaining 50.29% WER and 24.43% CER on the official test set and ranking second of nine teams. Our dialect identification system is a fine-tuned WavLM Base+ encoder with context-aware multi-head factorized attentive pooling under an angular-margin objective, which obtained 94% accuracy on the validation set and 41% on the out-of-domain test set. The ASR comparisons support augmenting scarce dialectal transcripts with acoustic variation, while ADI highlights the need for evaluation across domains. Code and reproducibility resources for both tasks are available at https://github.com/ResonateResearch/resonate-nadi-2026.

paper.title: Itgan at NADI 2026 shared task: Parameter-Efficient Whisper Adaptation for Robust, Mixed-Dialect and Code-Switched Arabic ASR
paper.abstract: We describe the Itgan systems for the three ASR subtasks of NADI 2026, namely robust country-level ASR (1.1), mixed-dialect ASR (1.2), and Tunisian code-switched ASR (1.3). All three share one recipe, Whisper adapted with LoRA on consumer GPUs, and each was carried by a different addition to it. On 1.1, where the dialect label is given at test time, per-dialect specialists continued from a pooled adapter gave the largest gain, and the submitted system reached 57.1% country-average WER. A post-evaluation linear probe on frozen encoder features routes utterances without the label and recovers 44% of what oracle routing gives. On 1.2 the choice of base model mattered more than adapter capacity, and system combination helped only once we added a decorrelated member, reaching 46.7% WER. On 1.3 our system placed second at 14.49% WER with the lowest CER among the leading submissions, 5.38%. Its last 0.60 WER points came without further training, mostly from an exact weight-space average of independently trained runs, with ROVER voting adding the remainder. Every comparison carries a paired-bootstrap test, and we report eight directions that did not work.

paper.title: BAREC-ST-2026: The Second Shared Task on Arabic Readability Assessment

author.affiliation: Mohamed bin Zayed University of Artificial Intelligence and New York University, Abu Dhabi
Mohamed bin Zayed University of Artificial Intelligence

paper.abstract: We present the results and findings of the BAREC Shared Task 2026, the second shared task on Arabic readability assessment, organized as part of the Fourth Arabic Natural Language Processing Conference (ArabicNLP 2026). The shared task focuses on automatic readability assessment using the BAREC Corpus, addressing fine-grained classification across 19 readability levels. It comprises two subtasks —sentence-level classification and document-level classification— and three tracks: (1) the Strict Track, which permits only the BAREC Corpus; (2) the Constrained Track, which permits the BAREC Corpus, the SAMER Corpus, and the SAMER Lexicon; and (3) the Open Track, which permits the use of any external resources. A total of 14 teams from 12 countries registered for the task, of which 10 submitted system description papers. All participating teams competed only in the sentence-level classification subtask. The top-performing system achieved a quadratic weighted kappa (QWK) of 85.3.

paper.title: HP at BAREC Shared Task 2026: Parameter-Efficient Ordinal Regression and Threshold Optimization for Arabic Readability.
paper.abstract: This paper describes the system submitted by team HP for the BAREC Shared Task 2026 on Arabic readability assessment. Driven by the Quadratic Weighted Kappa (QWK) eval- uation metric, which heavily penalizes dis- tant misclassifications, we reframe the 19- level task as an ordinal regression problem rather than standard multi-class classification. Our approach leverages pre-trained language models (AraBERTv02, ARBERT) optimized via Parameter-Efficient Fine-Tuning (LoRA) and trained with a COnsistent RAnk Log- its (CORAL) loss framework incorporating sample-level class weights. To ensure robust generalization, we consolidate the available datasets and implement a 5-fold stratified cross- validation pipeline. Finally, to optimize the QWK metric on the official blind test, we apply an 18-threshold Nelder-Mead optimizer cali- brated exclusively on blended Out-Of-Fold log- its, yielding a blind test QWK of 0.837. Our solution is released in the Github.

paper.title: thylinao at BAREC Shared Task 2026: Ensembling at the Noise Floor
paper.abstract: Team thylinao entered the Open and Strict tracks of the BAREC 2026 shared task on sentence-level Arabic readability with a deliberately plain system: a fourteen-member equal-weight ensemble of encoder fine-tunes, decoded to the 19-level scale by cutpoints interpolated halfway between validation-tuned thresholds and thresholds that match the blind score distribution to the training label prior. It scored 85.3 QWK on both tracks, first on both. This paper is about how those choices were measured. Three independent estimates place the noise floor of our offline evaluation between 0.09 and 0.44 QWK, as large as the margins that decided the final ranking. In three paired comparisons against the live board, only the smallest of the three offline estimates survived; the other two reversed in sign. We therefore proved that the Open and Strict tracks score identical gold, and made every decision worth a submission from a live board reading. Once the board showed the mean was capped, every candidate we probed came back a tie, bar one that we later withdrew as outside the rules. The full ledger, including four refuted hypotheses, is in the appendix.

paper.title: Northwestern 2 at BAREC Shared Task 2026: CAMeLBERT-Mix for Fine-Grained Arabic Readability Assessment
paper.abstract: This paper presents the Northwestern University in Qatar (NU-Q) submission to Task 1 of the BAREC Shared Task 2026 on fine-grained Arabic readability assessment. The task requires predicting the readability level of Arabic sentences across 19 ordered readability levels. Our system fine-tunes CAMeLBERT-Mix as a 19-class classifier using the official BAREC training data and cross-entropy optimization. We evaluate the proposed system using Quadratic Weighted Kappa (QWK), the official shared-task evaluation metric, together with classification accuracy. Our submitted system achieves a validation QWK of 0.7393 and an accuracy of 45.96%, indicating that pretrained Arabic language models provide a strong baseline for fine-grained Arabic readability assessment.

paper.title: Nile Nexus at BAREC Shared Task 2026: Enhancing Fine-Grained Arabic Readability Assessment through Ordinal-Aware Transformer Ensembling and Decision Calibration

author.affiliation: Chittagong University of Engineering and Technology

paper.abstract: Readability assessment has played a vital role in education, yet most NLP work has focused on English and a few high-resource languages, leaving fine-grained Arabic readability comparatively unexplored. In the BAREC Shared Task 2026, we have addressed sentence-level classification into 19 ordinal readability levels under the Strict Track, fine-tuning four Arabic transformer encoders, MARBERT, CAMeLBERT MSA, AraELECTRA and AraBERTv2, on the official training split under multiple ordinal-aware losses: soft cross-entropy, squared Earth Mover’s Distance, direct ordinal regression and a CORAL-style cumulative-threshold loss. A validation-only greedy ensemble of all resulting models, combined with a learned per-level threshold post-processing step, has raised performance from a best single-model QWK of 0.8341 to a final validation QWK of 0.8507. On the official Blind Test leaderboard, our system has achieved a QWK of 0.848, securing 3rd place in the Strict Track

paper.title: Viper at BAREC Shared Task 2026: Structured Arabic Representations and Robust Multi-Seed Ensembling for Readability Assessment

author.affiliation: University of Information Technology, Vietnam National University

paper.abstract: Fine-grained Arabic readability assessment aims to estimate how difficult an Arabic sentence is for its intended readers by assigning it to one of 19 ordered readability levels. This task is particularly challenging because of Arabic’s morphological complexity and the imbalanced distribution of examples across the levels. To address these challenges, we develop a system for the Sentence-Level Strict Track of the BAREC Shared Task 2026. Using only the official BAREC data, the system combines D3Tok-based morphological information, normalized surface text, and complementary features within a multi-seed ensemble of AraBERTv2-based regression models. Our submission achieved a QWK of 84.1% on the official Blind Test. This result indicates that the proposed combination provides competitive performance for fine-grained Arabic readability assessment.

paper.title: Skywalker at BAREC Shared Task 2026: Multi-Expert PLM Fusion and QWK-Aware Ordinal Decoding

author.affiliation: Mohamed bin Zayed University of Artificial Intelligence

paper.abstract: We present the system of Team Skywalker for the Sentence-level Strict track of the BAREC Shared Task 2026, which requires predicting one of 19 ordered Arabic readability levels for each sentence. Our system integrates complementary public Arabic pretrained language-model (PLM) experts fine-tuned with classification, regression, and ordinal objectives. Their continuous scores, confidence estimates, and rank-based features are combined using cross-fitted LightGBM meta-models. We further incorporate a cumulative ordinal branch that models level-boundary probabilities and a normalized-text branch that improves robustness to Arabic orthographic variation. Finally, a QWK-aware decoder maps the fused continuous score to one of the 19 readability levels using monotonic thresholds selected exclusively on the public validation set. We use only the official training data for supervision and the public validation labels for model selection. In addition to the final fusion system, we report single-PLM baselines and controlled ablations. The final configuration achieves a QWK of 86.30 on the public validation set and 84.20 on the CodaBench blind evaluation, ranking fourth among the submitted systems.

paper.title: NAMAA Community at the BAREC Shared Task 2026: Ordinal-Aware Training for Fine-Grained Arabic Readability Assessment Beyond Architectural Scale
paper.abstract: Fine-grained Arabic readability assessment is challenging due to the language’s rich morphology and the ordered nature of readability labels. We investigate this problem in the sentence-level Strict Track of the BAREC Shared Task 2026, which uses a 19-level readability scale. We evaluate six controlled configurations spanning engineered linguistic and morphological features, TF-IDF/SVD lexical representations, contextual transformer encoders, multi-encoder fusion, output-level ensembling, and ordinal-aware training, followed by a final refinement using a single EmbeddingGemma encoder. Contextual transformer representations provide the largest improvement over classical feature-based baselines, while multi-encoder fusion and voting yield smaller additional gains. In contrast, word-repetition and adjacent-word-swap augmentation degrades performance, indicating that these perturbations do not reliably preserve readability labels. Our strongest configuration combines EmbeddingGemma with Gaussian soft labels, KL-divergence training, expected-value decoding, class weighting, and best-checkpoint selection, achieving 84.0 QWK on the test set and 82.4 QWK on the official blind test set. Overall, the results suggest that explicitly accounting for the ordinal structure of readability labels is a promising alternative to simply increasing architectural or ensemble complexity. We further summarize the resulting design insights into a practical framework for Arabic ordinal readability modeling.

paper.title: ZHR at BAREC Shared Task 2026: Ordinal-Objective Ensembles with Threshold Calibration and Silver-Label Pretraining for Arabic Readability Assessment
paper.abstract: We describe the ZHR systems for the two sentence-level tracks of the BAREC 2026 Shared Task on Arabic readability assessment: Strict, where training is restricted to the BAREC training split, and Open, which allows any public data. Each sentence receives one of 19 ordinal levels, and systems are ranked by quadratic weighted kappa (QWK). Both tracks use one recipe. Arabic encoders are fine-tuned under five ordinal objectives and averaged with weights from greedy selection, and the averaged score is discretized by 18 thresholds fitted to maximize QWK; every fitted quantity uses the development split. The official Strict system, an ensemble of ten train-split models, scores 85.0 QWK on the blind set.
