The official Open system adds pretraining on the silver-labeled BAREC-10M corpus and restricts selection to members whose early stopping never touched the calibration split; it scores 85.2. Both clear the official baseline (82.5) by 2.5 and 2.7 QWK while trailing it in exact accuracy, a trade-off that comes from the metric itself and that we measure directly. Negative results are part of the record: a catalog of 19 changes that did not help, each measured under a held-out protocol.

paper.title: LSI at BAREC Shared Task 2026: A Controlled Study of Training Convergence, Heuristics, and Ensembles for Arabic Sentence-Level Readability
paper.abstract: We present the Linguistic Security Institute (LSI) submission to the BAREC Shared Task 2026 (Task 1): predicting Arabic sentence readability on a 19-level ordinal scale. Our approach uses a logit-level ensemble of three Arabic pre-trained language models, with CAMeLBERT trained using an ordinal Earth Mover’s Distance loss and augmented by six SAMER Lexicon difficulty features. Controlled comparisons show that surface heuristics improve undertrained baselines but degrade converged models, and retrieval-augmented in-context learning yields no gains in this fine-grained setting. Our final ensemble achieves 81.7 QWK, ranking 1st among Constrained-track system submissions and 3rd among Open-track system submissions.

paper.title: Soloeval at BAREC Shared Task 2026: QWK-Aligned Soft-Label Ordinal Classification with Auxiliary Surface Features for Arabic Readability Assessment
paper.abstract: We describe Soloeval’s submission to the Sentence-Level Open Track of the BAREC Shared Task 2026 on fine-grained Arabic readability assessment. Rather than treating the 19-level readability scale as a scalar regression target, we fine-tune pretrained Arabic BERT encoders (MARBERTv2 and CAMeLBERT-Mix) with a soft-label cross-entropy objective whose target distribution is a Gaussian centered on the gold level, chosen to more directly reflect the Quadratic Weighted Kappa (QWK) evaluation metric’s quadratic distance penalty. We combine this with lightweight auxiliary surface features (sentence length, word count, diacritic density) and K-fold cross-validation. Our best single-model configuration, CAMeLBERT-Mix trained with F=3 folds, achieves a QWK of 80.6 on the BAREC 2026 blind test leaderboard for the Open track. We report our full hyperparameter search, discuss the gap between our dev- and test-set results, and outline what we would try next.

paper.title: AraGenre 2026: A Hierarchical Definition-Guided Arabic Genre Classification Shared Task

author.affiliation: King Fahad University of Petroleum and Minerals
University College of Applied Sciences, Islamic University of Gaza and Onaizah Colleges
Hamad Bin Khalifa University and Birzeit University

paper.abstract: AraGenre 2026 is a shared task on hierarchical, definition-guided Arabic genre classification under limited supervision and substantial distribution shift. Systems assign each text a broad label and a specific label using an inventory of six broad branches and 74 defined final genres. The final benchmark contains 27,972 source-derived Arabic segments, spanning Modern Standard Arabic, Classical Arabic, and dialectal material, while the released labelled examples are small and primarily synthetic. Final specific classes are absent from the released labelled data, but their English names and definitions are provided. The task received 46 registrations and 373 submissions, with 17 ranked final entries and 11 system description papers. Thaka achieved the highest official Hierarchical Macro F1 at 73.52, followed by HP at 71.69 and NAMAA-1 at 70.13. Broad classification was consistently stronger than specific classification. The documented systems frequently combine label semantics with multilingual retrieval, LLM judging, pseudo-labelling, reranking, or calibration. We clarify the resource-driven taxonomy and inherited gold labels, distinguish combined distribution shift from isolated unseen-label effects, and provide systematic validation of the final evaluation data.

paper.title: Rabee Al-Qasem at AraGenre 2026: Conformer Based Hierarchical Classifier for Arabic Genres
paper.abstract: This paper presents the first investigation into the performance of the Conformer architecture for hierarchical text classification, specifically applied to predicting two-level Arabic text genres. The proposed system combines multilingual sentence embeddings, target label definition representations, a Conformer projection module, an auxiliary broad-genre classifier, synthetic data augmentation, and seed-based ensembling. Evaluated on the official shared task, the approach achieved a Hierarchical Macro-F1 of 0.4399, demonstrating strong high-level genre classification (Broad Macro-F1 of 0.6288) while highlighting ongoing challenges in distinguishing semantically close specific subcategories (Specific Macro-F1 of 0.2511).

paper.title: HP at AraGenre 2026: LLM-Guided Pseudo-Labeling for Hierarchical Arabic Genre Classification with MARBERT
paper.abstract: This paper presents the system submitted by team HP for the AraGenre 2026 Shared Task on Hierarchical Definition-Guided Arabic Genre Classification. To address the low-resource constraint of the provided dataset (140 labeled training samples), we propose a two-stage pipeline combining LLM-based pseudo-labeling with supervised fine-tuning. In the first stage, we evaluate several models under a 5-fold cross-validation framework, including Gemini 3.5 Flash Lite (0.9413), Qwen2.5 7B (0.7203), LLaMA 3.1 8B (0.6380), and a multilingual NLI model (0.3099). Based on these results, Gemini 3.5 Flash Lite is selected to generate pseudo-labels for the unlabeled test set using a definition-guided few-shot prompt. In the second stage, MARBERTv2 and ARBERTv2 are fine-tuned on approximately 28,000 pseudo-labeled samples. Our experiments show that MARBERTv2 achieves the best standalone score of 0.7169 Hierarchical Macro F1, outperforming both ARBERTv2 (0.7118) and a soft voting ensemble (0.7165), suggesting that Arabic-specialized pretraining of MARBERTv2 is more effective than model ensembling for this task.

paper.title: Northwestern at AraGenre 2026 : Definition-Guided Dense Retrieval Using BGE-M3 for Hierarchical Arabic Genre Classification
paper.abstract: This paper describes the Northwestern University in Qatar submission to the AraGenre 2026 Shared Task on hierarchical Arabic genre classification. We formulate the task as a definition-guided dense retrieval problem by encoding Arabic documents and English genre definitions into a shared semantic space using the multilingual BGE-M3 model. Genre labels are assigned by retrieving the most semantically similar definition without task specific fine tuning. On the development set, the proposed approach achieved a Broad Macro F1 of 0.6125, a Specific Macro F1 of 0.6125, and a Hierarchical Macro F1 of 0.6125. These results show that a lightweight retrieval based framework is an effective approach for hierarchical Arabic genre classification.

paper.title: Phoenix at AraGenre 2026: Transductive Bias Correction and Multi-View Label Representations for Zero-Shot Arabic Genre Classification
paper.abstract: AraGenre 2026 requires hierarchical classification of Arabic texts into evaluation-specific genres unseen during training, using supplied English definitions and taxonomy information. We present a transductive zero-shot system combining multilingual retrieval over multi-view label representations with per-genre z-normalization, calibrated Qwen3-8B candidate reranking, sibling-focused reranking, metric-aware macro-F1 decoding, and margin-gated shortlist widening. On the official 27,972-instance test set, the system achieves 0.5800 Hierarchical Macro F1, comprising 0.749 broad and 0.411 specific macro F1. Per-genre normalization provides the largest build-up improvement (+0.095), while an encoder-only diagnostic attributes +0.082 to LLM reranking. Calibrated log-probability fusion, multi-view labels, and decoding refinements provide further complementary gains.

paper.title: MohannadHendi at AraGenre 2026: Contrastive Cross-Lingual Definition Retrieval for Hierarchical Arabic Genre Classification
paper.abstract: We describe the MohannadHendi submission to the AraGenre 2026 shared task. The system casts hierarchical Arabic genre classification as cross-lingual retrieval between Arabic texts and English genre definitions, allowing it to consider labels unseen during training. We fine-tune multilingual E5-large on 140 texts paired with five deterministic views of their genre definitions. At inference, the nearest normalized definition embedding supplies both the broad and specific labels. The best local configuration achieved 0.9020 specific Macro F1. The submitted system obtained 0.4560 Hierarchical Macro F1 and ranked eighth among 18 final leaderboard entries. Its broad Macro F1 (0.6125) exceeded its specific Macro F1 (0.2995), showing that fine-grained genre discrimination remains the main difficulty.

paper.title: NAMAA Community at AraGenre 2026: From Encoder Baselines to Self-Consistent LLM Ensembling for Hierarchical Arabic Genre Classification
paper.abstract: Hierarchical, definition-guided genre classification places a short Arabic text under a broad genre and, within it, a fine-grained specific genre, using only a natural-language definition of each. We present NAMAA’s submission to AraGenre 2026. Fine-tuned bi-encoder classifiers reached 0.93 hierarchical macro F1 on development via data augmentation and cross-lingual pretraining, but collapsed to as low as 0.22 on the released test set, having specialized to a hand-engineered definition style that missed the test set’s larger, 74-genre taxonomy. We root-caused this gap and switched to zero-shot LLM classification, matching the best fine-tuned ensemble’s test score (0.6899 hierarchical F1) with no training; layering self-consistency sampling and disagreement resolution raised this further to 0.7013, ranking 3rd of 18 teams. Specific Macro F1 (0.5114) lags well behind Broad Macro F1 (0.8913), showing that most remaining errors concentrate in fine-grained genre choices rather than broad-category mistakes. Zero-shot LLM prompting generalizes across this definition and taxonomy shift where fine-tuned, definition-conditioned encoders do not. We release our code and system resources to support reproducibility and further research.[<https://github.com/NAMAA-ORG/Aragenre-Definition-Guided-Genre>].

paper.title: GHADAI at AraGenre 2026: Definition-Guided Classification of Arabic Text Genres via Bi-Encoder Retrieval and Large Language Model Reranking
paper.abstract: We describe the GHADAI approach to the AraGenre 2026 shared task, which requires classifying Arabic text into broad and specific genre categories, including specific genres unseen during training. Our approach is a two-stage pipeline: a fine-tuned multilingual bi-encoder scores all 27,972 test sentences against the 74 candidate definitions, and a large language model reranks the top candidates per sentence using cyclic option rotation to mitigate positional bias. On the hidden test set, the bi-encoder achieves a hierarchical macro-F1 of 0.4213, which increases to 0.5006 with Fanar-9B reranking and to 0.6050 with Qwen-32B reranking over the top 15 candidates using five rotations. The final pipeline ranked fourth on the official leaderboard. These results demonstrate the effectiveness of combining definition-based retrieval with LLM reranking for generalization to unseen Arabic text genres.

paper.title: Nasaq at AraGenre 2026: Definition-Guided Approaches for Hierarchical Arabic Genre Classification

author.affiliation: King Salman International Academy for the Arabic Language
King Salman International Academy for the Arabic Language
King Salman International Academy for the Arabic Language

paper.abstract: We describe SynAnchor, Nasaq’s definition-guided system for AraGenre 2026. The task requires hierarchical Arabic genre classification under disjoint specific-genre inventories across training, development, and test, making generalization to unseen genres a central challenge. SynAnchor addresses this setting by generating Arabic anchor texts from genre definitions using GPT-4o and embedding them with BGE-M3 for similarity-based retrieval. High-confidence cases are classified directly, while ambiguous inputs are selectively adjudicated by GPT-5 among the three highest-ranked candidate genres. On the official test set of 27,972 texts spanning 74 unseen specific genres, SynAnchor achieves a Hierarchical Macro-F1 of 0.6006 on Codabench, compared with 0.2472 for the organizers’ definition-embedding baseline (approximately 2.4). Approximately 25% of test instances are resolved using retrieval alone, without LLM adjudication. The results suggest that combining definition-guided Arabic anchor synthesis with selective LLM reasoning can support hierarchical genre classification under changing label inventories.

paper.title: SAGE at AraGenre 2026: Adapter-Refined Definition Embeddings for Zero-Shot Arabic Genre Classification

author.affiliation: Arab Center for Research and Policy Studies

paper.abstract: We present our system SAGE: \textbf{S}entence \textbf{A}nalysis \textbf{G}enre \textbf{E}valuation for the AraGenre shared task, which assigns Arabic sentences a hierarchical genre label from an English definition alone, with none of the 74 evaluation genres represented in the official training data. Since a definition is not itself an instance of its genre, we fine-tune the encoder generating the embeddings of both the sentences to classify and the candidate genre definitions and train a small adapter that refines those of the definitions. Studying three encoders and four datasets that were generated for training purposes, we find that the adapter’s training data matters more than either encoder choice or adapter hidden layer. Our best system, combining a fine-tuned encoder and an adapter, reached a Hierarchical Macro F1 score of 0.5278, placing seventh.

paper.title: WathiqTeam at AraGenre 2026: Class-Balanced Hybrid Retrieval with Selective LLM Reranking

author.affiliation: Higher Institute for Applied Sciences and Technology

paper.abstract: We present WathiqTeam’s system for the AraGenre 2026 Shared Task on hierarchical Arabic genre classification. The task requires assigning each Arabic text both one of six broad genres and one of 74 fine-grained specific genres organised beneath them. This setting is particularly challenging because many specific genres overlap in topic and vocabulary, while the hierarchy is highly asymmetric: the six broad genres contain substantially different numbers of specific children. We address these challenges with a broad-first retrieval architecture. Multilingual E5 compares Arabic texts with English genre definitions, an Arabic sentence encoder retrieves generated Arabic prototypes, and BM25 preserves exact lexical and structural cues. At the broad level, class-balanced pooling prevents parents with larger prototype pools from receiving more votes. After hard hierarchical gating, Weighted Reciprocal Rank Fusion combines the three independent rankings for the remaining specific labels. Qwen3 reranks only uncertain top-two broad decisions and is constrained by internal ensemble support. The submitted system achieved 0.4559 Hierarchical Macro F1, with 0.6250 Broad Macro F1 and 0.2869 Specific Macro F1. Component-oriented official runs show that class balancing and level-specific fusion produced most of the gain, while selective LLM reranking provided a small final improvement.

paper.title: Thakaa at AraGenre 2026: Definition-Guided LLM Judging with Full-Taxonomy Agreement-Gated Correction for Hierarchical Arabic Genre Classification

author.affiliation: Thakaa, Advanced Company for Information Technology
Thakaa, Advanced Company for Information Technology
Thakaa, Advanced Company for Information Technology

paper.abstract: We report the first-place system in AraGenre 2026 (0.7352 Hierarchical Macro F1, 18 teams). The task assigns each of 27,972 hidden-test Arabic segments one of 6 broad and one of 74 specific genres, given only as English prose definitions, with the specific-label inventory disjoint from training. Our pipeline updates no model parameters but is not free of task-specific effort: the judge prompt carries 74 hand-written cues, and components were selected on the public leaderboard. A family-restricted, definition-guided LLM judge scores candidate genres setwise under a hierarchically constrained decoding scheme, whose five-step pipeline reaches 0.7139. That base led on Specific Macro F1 but trailed on Broad Macro F1, so we add a correction stage: two instruction models re-predict the specific genre, each shown the entire 74-definition taxonomy, and a label is edited only where both agree against the base. That system scores 0.892 Broad Macro F1, alongside fewer topic-trap calls, where the subject a text discusses displaces the genre it instantiates. In a post-evaluation audit of instances that the base labelled as book descriptions, Religious calls fall 394 → 233 → 119 as the prompt adds the type-versus-topic convention and then the full taxonomy. Refinements and an attractor drain reach 0.7352.

paper.title: ArGuard Shared Task: Harmful Content Detection in Arabic Memes and LLM Prompts

author.affiliation: Hamad Bin Khalifa University and University of Massachusetts Boston

paper.abstract: Harmful content appears in diverse forms, ranging from multimodal memes targeting protected groups to textual prompts designed to elicit unsafe responses from large language models. However, existing Arabic resources typically study these settings separately and often rely on coarse-grained labels. We introduce **ArGuard**, a shared task on harmful content detection in Arabic memes and LLM prompts. ArGuard consists of two tracks: Track A focuses on multimodal hate detection in Arabic memes, while Track B addresses harmful prompt detection for Arabic LLM safety evaluation. Overall, 58 teams registered for the shared task, 35 participated in the final evaluation phase, and 27 submitted system-description papers. Participating systems explored a range of approaches, including fine-tuning encoder- and decoder-based models such as AraBERT, Jais, and Qwen3-VL. The best-performing systems achieved macro-F1 scores of 0.823 on Subtask A1, 0.419 on Subtask A2, 0.984 on Subtask B1, and 0.790 on Subtask B2. These results highlight fine-grained meme classification (Subtask A2) as the most challenging setting, partly due to sparse labels and train-test distribution shifts. To facilitate further research on Arabic harmful-content detection, we release the task datasets and associated resources through the shared-task website.

paper.title: dbilianos at ArGuard Shared Tasks: When Does Translation Help in Arabic Harmful Prompt Detection?
paper.abstract: This paper describes the participation of the dbilianos team in the ArGuard 2026 Shared Task on harmful prompt detection for Arabic LLM safety evaluation. We participated in both subtasks: binary safe/unsafe classification (Task B1) and granular harm category classification (Task B2). Our approach systematically tested a central hypothesis: whether translating Arabic prompts into English improves classification performance. We experimented with multiple pipelines, including classical machine learning with TF-IDF features, zero-shot and few-shot prompting with DeepSeek-V4, and hybrid approaches. Our results reveal a divergence across subtasks. For binary classification, DeepSeek zero-shot on English translations achieved 0.89 macro-F1, securing 4th place in this subtask, and confirming that LLM-based prompting is highly effective for coarse-grained safety decisions. For granular classification, however, the best performance came from training a Support Vector Machine directly on original Arabic text using TF-IDF features, which achieved 0.61 macro-F1, placing the team 16th in this subtask. This outperformed our translation-based strategies, suggesting that fine-grained harm categorization is highly sensitive to linguistic and cultural nuance that is lost or distorted during translation. The translation hypothesis was only partially supported locally, and ultimately reversed on the final test set for both subtasks. We discuss implications for cross-lingual safety evaluation and highlight the limitations of translation-based pipelines for tasks requiring subtle intent interpretation.

paper.title: Nile Nexus at ArGuard Shared Tasks: Leakage-Controlled MARBERTv2–SVM Ensemble for Arabic Harmful-Prompt Classification

author.affiliation: Chittagong University of Engineering and Technology

paper.abstract: Arabic harmful-prompt detection has remained challenging due to dialectal variation, implicit expressions and context-dependent intent. In the ArGuard 2026 Shared Task, we have participated in Subtask B1, a binary safe/unsafe classification task scored by macro-F1. We have identified evaluation leakage in an initial pipeline: the development set has been reused for early stopping, threshold tuning and ensemble optimization, which has inflated development scores while masking poor generalization on the blind test set. To correct this, we have introduced a leakage-controlled protocol with separate fitting, checkpoint-selection and tuning splits and have compared a TF-IDF SVM baseline, MARBERTv2 and a stacking ensemble, selecting the best-performing method based on tuning-set results. We have further applied five rounds of error-driven data augmentation to address recurring failure patterns. Our final system has achieved 0.861 accuracy, 0.878 precision, 0.862 recall and 0.860 macro-F1 on the blind test leaderboard, ranking 5th. Manual error analysis has shown that remaining errors have mainly stemmed from false positives on sensitive but non-harmful content, confirming that leakage-controlled evaluation has been necessary for a reliable blind-test estimate.

paper.title: L3IA Morocco at ArGuard 2026: Intent over Words - Uncovering Implicit Harm in Arabic LLM Prompts
paper.abstract: We present the L3IA Morocco team’s system for shared Task B, designed for large language models and focused on detecting harmful prompts in Arabic. In this context, we define two subtasks: B1 and B2, which refer, respectively, to the binary safe/unsafe classification and the classification of harmfulness into 7 categories. Our system combines three fine-tuned Arabic encoders: AraBERTv2, CAMeLBERTmix, and MARBERT, using soft voting that takes into account the predominant classes. It achieves a macro-F1 score of 0.946 for B1 and 0.902 for B2 during the development phase. In contrast, performance drops to 0.639 for B1 and 0.758 for B2 in the blind test. We demonstrate that this generalization divergence is due to a "unsafe” overprediction bias resulting from an unbalanced training corpus (80% unsafe) and not due to alignment of identifiers or dialects. Finally, we observed a negative result: in zeroshot and few-shot, AceGPT-7B, a generative Arabic LLM, performed poorly compared to fine-tuned encoders (0.38-0.42 on Darija).

paper.title: AK_QMUL at ArGuard Shared Tasks: A Single Fine-Tuned JAIS for Arabic Harmful-Prompt Detection
paper.abstract: We present AK_QMUL’s submissions to the ArGuard-2026 shared tasks on Arabic harmful-prompt detection: a binary safe/unsafe task (B1) and a seven-way harm-domain task (B2). Both submissions use one backbone – JAIS-6.7B fine-tuned with 4-bit QLoRA and a linear classification head over its last-token representation. For B1 we train a four-way head that factors the label by dialect register safe, unsafe × MSA, other, we augment the training fold with MSA prompts from AraSafe, and decode with a plain argmax to score safe/unsafe. For B2 we fine-tune the same backbone as a seven-way classifier and average the softmax outputs of five random seeds. Both submissions ranked first on their track, with macro-F1 0.984 on B1 and 0.790 on B2. We report results by dialect and by class: on B1 the model is accurate across all six dialects (93.6–99.8%) and its predicted unsafe rate tracks the true rate closely; on B2 six of the seven classes reach F1 between 0.73 and 0.98, with the residual error concentrated in the Bully class, which overlaps semantically with harassment and harm-to-others.

paper.title: NYUAD at ArGuard Shared Tasks: Multimodal Embedding Models for Detecting Arabic Hateful Memes and Unsafe Prompts
paper.abstract: The rapid growth of social media and generative AI has significantly increased the volume of Arabic textual content, memes, and user prompts shared across online platforms. While these media facilitate communication, creativity, and information exchange, they can also be exploited to disseminate hate speech, harmful content, and unsafe instructions. As a result, there is an increasing need for reliable automated methods to identify hateful Arabic memes and harmful (unsafe) prompts. This paper leverages pre-trained and fine-tuned multilingual embedding models to learn rich semantic representations from textual and visual content. The evaluation is conducted using a dataset of Arabic memes and prompts proposed in the ArabicNLP ArGuard 2026 challenge. The results underscore the capacity of large language model (LLM)-based embedding models to deliver superior performance. Developing robust detection systems is essential for improving content moderation and fostering a more secure and trustworthy online environment for Arabic-speaking users.

paper.title: Lattice AI at ArGuard Shared Tasks: Encoder Ensembles and a Re-Annotated Test Slice in Arabic Harmful-Prompt Detection
paper.abstract: We describe our system for the ArGuard 2026 shared task (Task B), harmful-prompt detection for Arabic, with subtasks B1 (binary safe versus unsafe) and B2 (seven-way harm-domain classification), both scored by macro-F1. Our system pairs a Unicode-normalization front-end with an ensemble of fine-tuned Arabic encoders, treats B2 as topic-domain classification over all prompts, and adds a retrieval-augmented resolver for the confusable interpersonal classes; it reaches development macro-F1 0.907 (B2) and 0.950 (B1), and on the blind test B1 0.9839 (1st, tied) and B2 0.7875 (2nd). Our main contribution explains the large B2 development-to-test gap. One fifth of the B2 test is a "novel" slice: AraSafe prompts re-annotated into the seven ArGuard domains under a fixed cross-taxonomy mapping that the organizers confirmed. Because that mapping does not preserve the training convention and is recorded in no data available during the task, no system can infer it, and the competitive B2 field compresses onto a blind 0.68-0.79 band, far below the ~0.90 reachable in-distribution. On the familiar slice we score macro-F1 0.908, matching development; we argue this is the honest measure of the system.

paper.title: Dynamos at ArGuard Shared Tasks: Multimodal Transformers and Selective Ensembling for Binary and Fine-Grained Arabic Hateful Meme and Harmful Prompt Detection
paper.abstract: For the ArGuard 2026 shared task on harmful content detection in Arabic memes (Task A) and LLM prompts (Task B), we fine-tune Arabic transformer encoders across all four subtasks. Memes additionally use a vision tower (ViT-B/16 for the binary subtask, CLIP ViT-L/14 for the fine-grained one) late-fused with MARBERTv2; ensembling choices and decision thresholds are tuned per subtask throughout. Two methodological choices account for much of our gains: selecting checkpoints by development macro-F1 rather than loss, and aligning the B2 training target with the evaluation distribution. Our largest single effect, however, was diagnostic. The B1 blind test set is approximately class-balanced while its training data is ~80/20, so our dev-tuned threshold collapsed macro-F1 from 0.9557 on dev to 0.6345 on test. We recovered the test class balance algebraically from the aggregate metrics the platform reported to all participants; re-thresholding the same saved probabilities, with no retraining, restored 0.8628. Because this uses only aggregate leaderboard feedback (within the task rules), the B1 figure is not directly comparable to teams that did not use the channel and is not a generalisation estimate. This correction is also not general: on the weaker multi-label classifier (A2), stronger prior matching reduced performance in every setting we tested, so matching the test prior is not necessarily F1-optimal. We additionally report a catalogue of quantified negative results, including external-data augmentation with AraSafe. Final test macro-F1: A1 0.7869, A2 0.3463, B1 0.8628, B2 0.7622.

paper.title: CalibGuard at ArGuard Shared Tasks: Threshold Calibration and Label-Space Constraints for Arabic Multimodal Hate Speech and Harmful Prompt Detection
paper.abstract: This paper describes CalibGuard, our system for the ArGuard 2026 Shared Task on harmful content detection in Arabic memes and large language model prompts. We participate in all four subtasks: binary and fine-grained hateful meme classification (A1, A2) and binary and harm-domain prompt classification (B1, B2). For Task A, we extract frozen embeddings from three vision-text encoder pairs and train a joint two-headed classifier under 5-fold cross-validation with seed averaging. For Task B, we fine-tune AraBERTv02 with class-weighted cross-entropy. CalibGuard obtains 75.53% macro-F1 on subtask A1, 36.53% on A2, 65.38% on B1 and 68.85% on B2, ranking 11th, 3rd, 15th and 13th respectively. We further show that the B1 test split contains 49.3% unsafe prompts against 79.8% in training, and that this distribution shift accounts for a 29-point gap between our development and test scores, concentrated entirely in Modern Standard Arabic. Rethresholding to the test prior recovers 13.7 points without retraining. We additionally report two negative results: constrained decoding marginally reduces A2 performance, and restricting B2 training to unsafe prompts costs 5.7 points.

paper.title: SZED at ArGuard Shared Tasks: Multi-Task Label-Attention and Cross-Modal Fusion for Arabic Hateful Meme Detection
paper.abstract: We present SZED’s submission to ArGuard 2026 Track A: Arabic hateful meme detection. The task has two parts: binary classification (A1) and fine-grained multi-label tagging (A2). For A1, we fuse MARBERTv2 and CLIP ViT-L/14 embeddings, comparing concatenation, self-attention, and ensemble heads. For A2, we use a multi-task label-attention architecture with per-class query vectors and an auxiliary head for cascade calibration. We reach macro-F1 = 0.7597 on A1 and 0.3142 on A2. We report reproducibility across runs, per-class error patterns, and the effect of cascade calibration on the long-tailed A2 labels.

paper.title: LingLab at ArGuard Shared Tasks: A Lightweight Hybrid Classifier for Arabic Harmful Prompt Detection
paper.abstract: The classification of Arabic prompts as Safe or Unsafe is the focus of this submission to ArGuard 2026 Subtask B1. We developed a lightweight hybrid classifier that combines lexical and semantic information. The lexical branch uses normalized word-level and character-level features with a class-balanced LinearSVC classifier. The semantic branch uses frozen multilingual E5 embeddings with a class-balanced logistic regression classifier. We combined the outputs of both branches using late fusion. On the development set, LinearSVC achieved a Macro-F1 score of 0.93, while the frozen E5 branch achieved 0.88. The final hybrid system achieved a Macro-F1 score of 0.93. On the test set, the submitted system achieved 0.78 accuracy, 0.83 precision, 0.70 recall, and 0.72 Macro-F1.

paper.title: Axiom at ArGuard Shared Tasks: Unimodal Text Dominance for Arabic Hate Meme Detection
paper.abstract: Detecting hate speech in social media memes requires disentangling complex cross-modal interactions, a challenge magnified in low-resource and morphologically rich languages like Arabic. We present Team Axiom’s submission to the ArGuard 2026 Shared Task (Task A1) on binary hate meme classification. While conventional multimodal wisdom posits that text and visual features must be jointly fused, empirical evidence across non-English domains reveals that noisy visual backbones and cross-modal space misalignment frequently degrade language signals. We validate this hypothesis by fine-tuning a unimodal MARBERTv2 sequence classifier without external multimodal fusion. Our simple, well-regularized approach achieved a Macro-F1 of 0.770 and an accuracy of 0.818 on the official gold test set, securing 6th place on the global leaderboard and outperforming both the official AraBERTv2 baseline and our own complex multimodal fusion architectures.

paper.title: TextLing at ArGuard Shared Tasks: An Enhanced MARBERT-Based Late-Fusion Model for Multimodal Hateful Meme Detection in Arabic
paper.abstract: The classification task for ArGuard 2026 Track A, Subtask A1, identifies whether an Arabic meme is Hateful or Not Hateful. Our system combines three separately trained models. In the first experiment, we use word-level and character-level features with balanced linear classifiers. In the second experiment, we fine- tune MARBERT for text classification using class-balanced focal loss. In the third experi- ment, we use a frozen SigLIP image encoder with balanced logistic regression. We combine the Class-1 probabilities from the three mod- els using late fusion. On the test set, the fused model achieved a Macro-F1 score of 0.76 and an accuracy of 0.79

paper.title: SATLab at ArGuard Shared Tasks: Character N-Grams for Fine-Grained Categorization of Harmful LLM Prompts in Arabic
paper.abstract: This paper presents SATLab’s participation in the ArGuard 2026 shared sub-task on identifying seven types of harmful LLM prompts in Arabic. The proposed system is language-agnostic and requires no resources other than the training data provided in the shared task. It is based on character n-grams and a logistic regression classifier. Performance on the Test set (Macro-F1 = 0.736) was average, approximately 0.05 lower than that of the top teams (0.790) and approximately 0.05 higher than the baseline (0.687). Notably, this performance was substantially lower than those achieved in cross-validation and on the Development set. Several analyses aimed at understanding these discrepancies are reported. An analysis of the confusion matrix indicates that the “Harm-to-other” category poses the greatest problem, likely because it is partially compatible with all other categories except “Adult-content”.

paper.title: QuadCore at ArGuard Shared Tasks: Ensembling Arabic Encoders with Dialect Conditioning for Harm-Domain Classification

author.affiliation: Chittagong University of Engineering and Technology
Chittagong University of Engineering and Technology
Chittagong University of Engineering and Technology

paper.abstract: We describe the QuadCore submission to Sub task B2 of the ArGuard 2026 shared task, which asks systems to assign an Arabic prompt addressed to a large language model to one of seven harm domains. Our system is a soft-voting ensemble of three Arabic en coders with complementary pre-training cor pora- MARBERTv2, CAMeLBERT-DA and AraBERTv02-Twitter- each fine-tuned under two random seeds, with the annotated dialect prepended to the prompt as a textual condition ing prefix; it uses no external data, no augmen tation and no generative models. It reached 0.7665 macro-F1 on the official test set, rank ing 4th of the 16 teams that submitted to the subtask. Using the gold labels released after the evaluation period, we then show that this sin gle number conflates two regimes: on the first 4,809 test items, whose label prior, dialect mix and lexical profile match the training data, the same predictions reach 0.9044 macro-F1, while on a contiguous final block of 1,170 items they collapse to 0.2073. That block is entirely Mod ern Standard Arabic, contains no adult-content instance, and its nearest-neighbour label agree ment with the training set is 0.1829 against 0.7777 elsewhere- close to the 1/7 chance rate. A substantial portion of our system’s errors on the official test set is therefore attributable to this shift rather than to the difficulty of harm domain classification itself.

paper.title: CompLing at ArGuard Shared Tasks: Dialect-Aware Sparse Fusion for Arabic Prompt Safety Classification
paper.abstract: We present our approach in this submission for ArGuard 2026 Subtask B1, which classifies Arabic prompts directed at large language models as Safe or Unsafe. Our system combines four sparse TF-IDF feature representations with dialect indicators and surface-level features. We trained logistic regression and Naive-Bayes SVM (NBSVM) classifiers and combined their predictions using late fusion. The system achieved a Macro-F1 score of 0.94 and an accuracy of 0.96 on the development set. On the test set, our submission achieved 0.79 accuracy, 0.85 macro precision, 0.71 macro recall, and 0.72 Macro-F1.

paper.title: Bahash-AI at ArGuard Shared Tasks: Multimodal Ensemble Learning for Hateful Meme Detection
paper.abstract: Hateful content in memes is difficult to detect automatically, as harmful intent often emerges from the interaction between image and text rather than either modality alone, a challenge compounded in Arabic by dialectal variation and sarcasm. This paper presents the system submitted by team Bahash-AI to Subtask A1 (binary hateful meme detection) of the ArGuard shared task at ArabicNLP 2026. A late-fusion classifier combining MARBERTv2 and ViT-base is first developed and evaluated as a standalone development-phase system. Building on this, the final submission ensembles a CLIP-based text-image classifier with this same late-fusion classifier, retrained on the combined train, development, and development-test partitions. Class imbalance (approximately 30% Hateful) is addressed via class-weighted losses, oversampling, and threshold selection. The final ensemble achieves a Macro-F1 of 0.7457 and an accuracy of 0.7680 on the blind test set, ranking 12th of 16 teams on the official leaderboard and outperforming the development-phase system by 9 Macro-F1 points. Error analysis using per-class precision and recall shows that the two systems reach a similar Hateful-class F1 gap through opposite error patterns.

paper.title: NLPLab at ArGuard Shared Tasks: Balancing Confidence Scores for Fine-Grained Classification of Unsafe Arabic Prompts Across Harm Domains
paper.abstract: This paper presents the CIC system for ArGuard 2026 Subtask B2, which classifies unsafe Arabic prompts into one of seven harm domains. Our system combines four complementary components: a fine-tuned CAMeLBERT-Mix model, a modified-Huber stochastic gradient descent classifier, a character-level nearest-neighbor model, and a character class-centroid similarity model. On the development set, we achieved a Macro-F1 score of 0.916 and an accuracy of 0.923. On the test set, the proposed model achieved an accuracy of 0.766, a macro precision of 0.760, a macro recall of 0.763, and a Macro-F1 of 0.751. The results show that combining contextual transformer representations, lexical features, and retrieval-based similarity signals can improve fine-grained harmful-prompt classification.

paper.title: iMak AI Lab at ArGuard Shared Tasks: Heterogeneous LoRA Ensembles of Vision-Language Models for Arabic Hateful Meme Detection

author.affiliation: Higher School of Economics and St. Petersburg State University

paper.abstract: We describe our submissions to Task A of the ArGuard 2026 shared task on harmful-content detection in Arabic memes: binary hateful-meme detection (Subtask A1) and fine-grained multilabel categorization (Subtask A2). Our A1 system is a probability-averaging ensemble of 22 fine-tuned models: 18 Qwen3-VL vision-language members (8B and 32B) trained with LoRA and scored via first-token logits, and 4 Arabic text-encoder members (MARBERTv2, AraBERTv02-twitter), combined at a fixed 0.85/0.15 modality mix. The system ranked first on Subtask A1 with 0.8234 macro F1, 2.2 points above our best single member. For A2, six LoRA-tuned VLMs with sigmoid multilabel heads, an A1-consistency mask, and flat 0.5 thresholds scored 0.3900 macro F1. Post-hoc analysis on the released gold labels shows that our single global threshold survived an unannounced 8-point drop in the share of hateful memes in the test set, and that most remaining errors in both subtasks separate benign sarcasm or humor from mockery aimed at a protected target.

paper.title: ANLP-UniSo at ArGuard 2026 Task A: Multimodal AraBERT–ResNet50 with Knowledge Graph Fusion for Arabic Hateful Meme Detection

author.affiliation: Higher Institute of Management, University of Sousse

paper.abstract: Detecting hateful content in Arabic memes is challenging due to dialectal variation, sarcasm, cultural references, and the interplay between visual and textual signals. We participate in ArGuard 2026 Track A (Multimodal Hateful Meme Detection) with a multimodal architecture that fuses AraBERT textual representations, ResNet50 visual features, and a lightweight knowledge-graph (KG) ontology vector derived from domain-specific Arabicbinary keywords. The model jointly optimizes (Hateful / Not Hateful) and multi-label finegrained classification through a gated fusion layer with strong regularization (dropout 0.45, weight decay 0.05, label smoothing 0.1). Gradual unfreezing of AraBERT layers, weighted sampling, and Arabic-specific normalization further improve robustness. On the official development set the system reaches a binary macro-F1 of 0.710; on the blind test set it obtains binary macro-F1 0.717. We analyse the contribution of each modality and discuss remaining challenges of fine-grained multi-label prediction under severe class imbalance.

paper.title: ANLP-UniSo at ArGuard 2026 Task B: Multi-Task MARBERT with Focal Loss and Hierarchical Consistency for Arabic Harmful Prompt Detection

author.affiliation: Higher Institute of Management, University of Sousse

paper.abstract: Detecting harmful prompts directed at large language models is a critical safety challenge, especially in Arabic where dialectal variation, code-switching, and culturally specific expressions of harm complicate classification. The ArGuard 2026 shared task addresses this problem through two subtasks: binary classification of prompts as safe or unsafe (B1) and fine-grained classification of unsafe prompts into seven harm domains (B2). We participate with a multi-task fine-tuning of MARBERT that shares encoder representations across a binary head and a seven-class granular head. Training combines focal loss with class weights and label smoothing, a hierarchical consistency regularizer that discourages contradictory safe/unsafe and granular predictions, a weighted sampler, and light character-level augmentation. On the official development set the system reaches a binary macro-F1 of 0.9618 and a granular macro-F1 of 1.0000; on the blind test set it obtains binary macro-F1 0.688 and granular macro-F1 0.752. We analyse the substantial development–test gap and discuss limitations of the submitted system.

paper.title: RACAI at ArGuard Shared Task: Exploring Self-Taught LLM Reasoners and Fine-Tuned Transformers Classifiers for Arabic Prompt Toxicity Detection

author.affiliation: Research Institute for Artificial Intelligence, Romanian Academy

paper.abstract: This paper presents the systems we developed for ArGuard 2026 Task B, addressing Arabic prompt safety through binary safe/unsafe classification (B1) and fine-grained assignment of unsafe prompts to harm domains (B2). Our central strategy is cross-lingual data augmentation: we machine-translate a large English prompt-safety corpus into Arabic and reuse it across both subtasks. For B1 we fine-tune the Arabic-native ALLaM-7B on self-generated rationales using the granular labels from B2 as signal. We compare against label-only training; our submission ranks 2nd (macro F_1{=}0.924). The experiments show the augmentation drives accuracy and not the self-generated chain-of-thought. For B2 we fine-tune Arabic encoders (full and adapter tuning) with a two-stage "warm’ pipeline that first trains the encoder on the easier binary task, before specialising it to the seven domains; our submission ranks 5th (macro F_1{=}0.762)

paper.title: Ahmed Younis at ArGuard Shared Tasks: Calibration Is Most of What You Tune: Decode-Time Structure and Threshold Transport for Arabic Harmful-Content Detection
paper.abstract: We describe our systems for all four ArGuard 2026 subtasks: binary and fine-grained Arabic hateful-meme detection (A1/A2) and binary and granular harmful-prompt detection (B1/B2). Our systems are deliberately conventional (a LoRA-tuned Qwen3-VL-8B for memes, a nine-encoder ensemble for prompts) because our central finding is that most of the achievable headroom lay not in the model but in decode-time calibration: per-class thresholds refit under structural constraints, rank-based decoding against known or published class priors, and threshold transport under distribution shift. On subtask A2, our submissions rose from 0.248 to 0.419 macro-F1; roughly 0.15 of that gain came from decode-time changes against under 0.03 from model-side interventions, and a fixed-model ablation on the ensemble’s char-ngram member attributes +0.070 to the decode stack alone. On B1, recalibrating a single threshold recovered +0.16 macro-F1 after we detected that the blind test was rebalanced to approximately 49% unsafe against an 80% unsafe training prior. Our final systems ranked 1st on subtask A2 (macro-F1 0.4194; 0.3913 without per-class scoring feedback), 3rd on A1 (0.7889), 3rd on B2 (0.7695), and 7th on B1 (0.7552). We additionally report a benchmark audit conducted during participation: a sequential-id label leak in the Task B development release (macro-F1 1.000 from ids alone), identified before the test release, left unexploited, and absent from the re-indexed test files; latent taxonomy structure that contradicts the task description; and a quantified gap between development and test distributions.

paper.title: NAMAA at ArGuard Shared Tasks: Multimodal Fusion, Vision–Language Model Adaptation, and In-Context Prompting for Arabic Hateful Meme Detection
paper.abstract: Multimodal hate speech detection requires interpreting how an image and its accompanying text jointly construct a target, stance, or derogatory implication. In Arabic memes, this relation is often shaped by locally recognizable public figures, political references, visual analogies, and indirect humor, making either modality insufficient on its own. We tackle this problem in Track A of ArGuard 2026, covering binary hateful meme detection (A1) and fine-grained multi-label classification (A2). Our experiments compare jointly trained dual encoders, parameter-efficient vision–language model (VLM) adaptation, and training-free prompting. We fine-tune Qwen3-VL, Llama 3.2 Vision, and Gemma 4 with QLoRA using task-specific binary and multi-label objectives. We also build CLIP–MARBERTv2 and SigLIP–AraBERT-Twitter cross-attention systems and evaluate frozen VLMs with zero-shot prompting and in-context learning. Qwen3-VL achieves our highest A1 score (0.7610), while SigLIP–AraBERT-Twitter leads A2 (0.3851), where label sparsity and multi-label prediction remain challenging.

paper.title: DetectorAI at ArGuard Shared Tasks: Calibrated Multimodal and Label-Frequency-Aware Systems for Arabic Meme Safety Detection
paper.abstract: We present our systems for ArGuard 2026 Track A, which aims to detect harmful content in Arabic memes. The track includes two tasks: a binary task for identifying hateful memes (A1) and a multi-label task for predicting specific categories (A2). For A1, our approach combines a fine-tuned Qwen3-VL sequence classification model, Arabic text encoders, and a Qwen text LoRA classifier. We then apply top-k calibration and make targeted adjustments based on model disagreements. On the official test set, our system reached a macro-F1 score of 0.7896 and an accuracy of 0.8200. For A2, we found that using thresholds from the development data caused us to overpredict common labels and miss rare ones. Our best A2 submission uses an ensemble of six Arabic text models, with label-frequency-aware top-k calibration and rare-label boosting. This approach achieved a macro-F1 of 0.3601 and a micro-F1 of 0.5150. Overall, we found that careful calibration of a few fine-tuned Arabic and multimodal classifiers contributed more to our results than using larger zero-shot vision-language models.

paper.title: QuadCore at ArGuard Shared Tasks: A Simple Threshold Calibration Approach for Arabic Hateful Meme Detection

author.affiliation: Chittagong University of Engineering and Technology
Chittagong University of Engineering and Technology
Chittagong University of Engineering and Technology

paper.abstract: We describe our system for Subtask A1 (binary hateful meme detection) of the ArGuard 2026 shared task (Alam et al., 2026). Our final system fine-tunes MARBERTv2 with class-weighted loss and macro-F1-based checkpoint selection, then applies a post-hoc decision-threshold calibration to correct for a class-distribution shift we found between the training/development splits (37.8% Hateful) and the held-out test split (29.6% Hateful). This calibration step requires no retraining and adds 3.3 macro-F1 points (0.7286 → 0.7616) on the official test split. On the same test split, this calibrated system also outperforms two alternatives we evaluated there – multi-seed ensembling and naive multimodal late-fusion. They match or exceed backbone-substitution and multi-model-ensemble variants that we were only able to evaluate on local development data. We report our full experimental log, including the negative results, with each result explicitly labeled by evaluation split, and compare our score to the AHA-Memes benchmark, where a much larger vision-language model reaches a similar range. Code and configuration files are released for reproducibility.

paper.title: StanceEval 2026: The Second Stance Detection Shared Task

author.affiliation: King Fahad University of Petroleum and Minerals and University of Tabuk
King Fahad University of Petroleum and Minerals
King Fahad University of Petroleum and Minerals
King Fahad University of Petroleum and Minerals
King Fahad University of Petroleum and Minerals
SDAIA-KFUPM Joint Research Center for Artificial Intelligence

paper.abstract: StanceEval 2026 is the second edition of the StanceEval shared task series on stance detection in Arabic social media text. Stance detection aims to identify a writer’s stance toward a given topic. Given a tweet and a target, participating systems must determine whether the writer’s stance is Favor, Against, or None. This edition focuses on cross-target generalization across two distinct evaluation tracks: Track 1 evaluates thematically related cross-target transfer (testing on Women Driving, related to Women Empowerment in the training data), while Track 2 evaluates cross-domain transfer to completely unseen targets (E-Cars and Trimester System). The shared task attracted 80 registered teams from 12 countries. During the evaluation phase, 30 unique teams submitted entries, with 21 teams officially ranked in Track 1 and 13 in Track 2 following validation filtering, and 20 teams submitting system-description papers. Participating teams employed diverse methodologies, including fine-tuned pretrained language models, prompt-based and retrieval-augmented large language models (LLMs), fine-tuned LLMs, and hybrid cascades. Top systems achieved impressive F_{avg2} scores of 0.8994 on Track1 and 0.9400 on Track2, substantially outperforming the strongest baselines (0.7366 and 0.7475, respectively), where F_{avg2} denotes the macro-averaged F1 score over the Favor and Against classes. Counterintuitively, performance on the unseen targets was higher than on the related target, a disparity could be driven by extreme target polarization, class imbalance, and dialectal or sarcastic nuance across topics.

paper.title: TTLab at StanceEval-2026: A Cloze-Style Prompting Approach for Arabic-Language Stance Detection (CLASP-Ar)

author.affiliation: Johann Wolfgang Goethe Universität Frankfurt am Main
Johann Wolfgang Goethe Universität Frankfurt am Main and Johann Wolfgang Goethe Universität Frankfurt am Main
Johann Wolfgang Goethe Universität Frankfurt am Main

paper.abstract: Arabic-language stance detection remains challenging, and previous shared-task systems have largely relied on multitask learning and ensembles. While these systems achieve state-of-the-art performance, their applicability and transferability are limited by the additional complexity introduced by multitask learning. To reduce this complexity, we introduce \texttt{CLASP-Ar}, which reformulates the task as cloze-style masked language modeling. In this approach, the target, predicted sentiment, and text are combined into a single prompt whose \texttt{[MASK]} prediction is restricted to a verbalizer-constrained label vocabulary. When evaluated on the StanceEval-2026: Arabic Stance Detection Shared Task, our proposed approach achieves an F_{\text{avg2}} score of 71.36% on Track 1 and 74.14% on Track 2 test sets.

paper.title: Razan Alsulieman at StanceEval-2026: Validation Under Target Shift for Arabic Stance Detection
paper.abstract: We describe our systems for both StanceEval- 2026 Arabic stance-detection tracks. Our MARBERT-centered pipeline optimized the primary macro-F1 over AGAINST and FAVOR directly, combining target-aware fine-tuning, probability ensembles, and guarded transfer experiments. We report one official test sub- mission per track. The Track 1 target-routed MARBERT system scored 0.8925 on devel- opment and 0.6743 on the official test set. The Track 2 MARBERT/Fanar/Qwen3 system scored 0.8360 on development and 0.8100 on the official test set. The released Track 1 evaluation input contained only Women Driv- ing, absent from its labeled train and develop- ment targets, making the nominal seen-target track an effective target-transfer test for our system. These results show that validation pro- tocols must reflect the intended target-transfer setting; otherwise, same-target development scores can substantially overstate transfer per- formance.

paper.title: Axiom at StanceEval-2026: A Two-Stage Hybrid Cascade for Arabic Stance Detection
paper.abstract: Cross-target Arabic stance detection presents a unique challenge due to the rich morphological complexity, regional dialects, and heavy reliance on sarcasm within social media discourse. In this paper, we describe the system submitted by Team Axiom for Track 1 (Seen Targets) of the StanceEval-2026 shared task. Our primary contribution is a resource-efficient, Two-Stage Hybrid Cascade architecture. This system utilizes a fine-tuned MARBERTv2 encoder as a high-confidence gatekeeper, dynamically routing uncertain and complex tweets to a locally hosted, 4-bit quantized Large Language Model (Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct). To prevent label bias and ground the LLM’s reasoning, the fallback stage incorporates a dynamically balanced, class-specific TF-IDF sub-word retriever. Our official submission achieved an F_{avg2} score of 0.6910 (Rank 18), demonstrating a measurable improvement over our standalone encoder baseline (0.6722).

paper.title: Tarjih at StanceEval-2026: Argument-Guided Arabic Stance Detection
paper.abstract: We present Tarjih, our proposed system for the Stance Detection in Arabic Language shared task (StanceEval-2026). Rather than predicting stance directly, Tarjih formulates the task as verification among competing arguments. An instruction-tuned LLM generates one steelman argument for each stance label, and a second blind pass evaluates each argument against the tweet without access to the gold label. Each argument–tweet is then jointly encoded with AraBERT to model their compatibility. From this pipeline, we derive three systems: a gated classifier, a pair scorer, and a ranking read-out. The pair scorer achieves the best seen-target test Favg2 of 0.73, while the gated classifier performs best on the unseen-target track with 0.77. Overall, the lower test performance and ranking among the submitted systems indicate limited generalization across targets.

paper.title: rabia_naz at StanceEval-2026: An Ensemble of Fine-Tuned Open LLMs for Arabic Stance Detection on Seen Targets
paper.abstract: This paper presents a system for StanceEval-2026 Track 1, Arabic stance detection on seen targets. Systems in this track are trained on the provided targets and evaluated on a related target within the same thematic domain. Open large language models are fine-tuned with QLoRA on the original Mawqif training data and adapted to the test target through transductive self-training, in which unlabeled test tweets are added to training only when independent models agree on their label. The final prediction is a majority vote over three fine-tuned models, Qwen2.5-7B, the Arabic-native ALLaM-7B, and a sarcasm-aware variant that predicts the official sarcasm label before the stance label. The system scored 0.7564 Favg2 and placed 12th of 21 teams on the official leaderboard. Across seventeen scored variants, task fine-tuning outperformed zero-shot prompting at every model scale, heterogeneous fine-tuned models converged on 98% of test predictions, and further gains required decorrelated ensemble members. The sarcasm annotation supplied this decorrelation and improved the vote, while the sentiment annotation degraded it.

paper.title: JLShen at StanceEval-2026: Cross-Lab LLM Ensembles and a Break-Even Rule for the Excluded Class
paper.abstract: Our two systems for StanceEval-2026, Arabic stance detection on Mawqif-XT, placed 1st of 31 on Track 1 (Favg2 = 0.8994) and 2nd of 22 on Track 2 (0.9357). Track 1 averages six zero shot readings of each tweet by frontier models from two providers, and calls a fine-tuned Arabic pipeline only to break exact ties. Track 2 is one reader, given a short generated description of the target so it can score stance expressed through a related topic. The leaderboard publishes three aggregate scores over the same predictions, and reading them shows that about 60% of our errors on both tracks are tweets annotated NONE that we placed in a stance class. Because the score ignores that class, the gain from moving such a row is fixed before the row is read. We derive the precision a repair must reach, and nine rankings plus an oracle from the corpus’s own annotation columns all fall short of it.

paper.title: SRK AI Lab at StanceEval-2026: Multi-LLM Few-Shot Prompting with Evidence-Guided Auditing for Arabic Stance Detection

author.affiliation: Indian Institute of Information Technology Kottayam, Indian Institute of Information Technology Kottayam

paper.abstract: This paper presents the SRK AI Lab system for Arabic stance detection in the StanceEval 2026 shared task using the Mawqif-XT benchmark. We employ a few-shot multi-LLM framework with GPT-5.5 Instant, Gemini 3.6 Flash with Extended Thinking, and Qwen 3.7 Plus to classify target–post pairs as Favor, Against, or None. The models independently predict stance, followed by GPT-5.5 Instant auditing based on target–post relation, linguistic context, and stance evidence. The audit results are combined with cross-model comparison to select the final label. Our system achieves an official Favg2 of 0.8420 in Track 1 and 0.9192 in Track 2, ranking 8th and 3rd, respectively. These results demonstrate the performance of multi-LLM few-shot prompting with GPT-5.5 auditing for Arabic stance detection.

paper.title: phonghoang at StanceEval-2026: A Two-Stage Framework for Arabic Stance Detection via Multi-Task Regularization and LLM-Guided Data Augmentation
paper.abstract: This paper describes the system submitted by the phonghoang team for Track 1 (Seen Tar- gets) of the StanceEval-2026 shared task on Arabic stance detection, where models are trained on provided targets and evaluated on a related target within the same thematic do- main. We propose a two-stage framework to address this within-domain target shift. In the first stage, we fine-tune a Multi-Task MAR- BERT model that jointly learns stance, senti- ment, and sarcasm, further regularized with R- Drop and Stochastic Weight Averaging (SWA), achieving Favg2 of 0.8561 on the development set. In the second stage, we adapt to the test target (“Women Driving”) by combining con- trastive few-shot pseudo-labeling via a Large Language Model, fusion with an external Ara- bic stance dataset, and high-confidence samples filtered from a thematically related training tar- get. The resulting augmented training set is used to adapt our optimal Stage 1 architecture, achieving an official Favg2 of 0.8431 on the test set.

paper.title: NAMAA at StanceEval-2026: From Encoder and Decoder Model Fine-Tuning to Data-Centric Retrieval-Augmented In-Context Learning for Arabic Stance Detection

author.affiliation: King Salman International Academy for the Arabic Language

paper.abstract: Stance detection identifies an author’s position toward a specified target, yet Arabic social-media text remains challenging because stance is often implicit and shaped by dialect, sarcasm, informal expression, and culturally specific references. StanceEval-2026 evaluates this problem in two transfer settings: a related target within a seen thematic domain (Track 1) and entirely unseen topics (Track 2). We compare four modeling strategies: single-task Arabic encoder fine-tuning, multi-task learning with sentiment and sarcasm supervision, 4-bit QLoRA adaptation of the ALLaM-7B model, and Retrieval-Augmented In-Context Learning (RAG-ICL) with frozen large language models (LLMs). Our strongest single-backend configuration is a data-centric RAG-ICL pipeline combining label-balanced retrieval, hashtag and negation adaptation, text cleaning, similarity filtering, and target descriptions. A majority-vote ensemble of this configuration across three LLM backends obtains official F_{avg2} scores of 0.8719 on Track 1 and 0.9016 on Track 2, ranking 3rd and 7th, respectively. Under the shared-task test conditions, the retrieval-based systems substantially outperform the supervised systems evaluated here, particularly on Track 2.

paper.title: Saigum at StanceEval-2026: Evaluating LLM-ensemble models and Retrieval Augmented Classification for Arabic Stance Detection
paper.abstract: Arabic stance depends on quotation, sarcasm, negation, hashtags, and target scope, which surface polarity may miss. For StanceEval-2026, we study Codex and Gemini prompting through two submission systems: a replicated contextual Codex predictor and a gated judge that retrieves labeled examples using seven AI-generated discourse cues. On 619 Dev examples, cue retrieval changes Favg2 from 0.8580 to 0.8613 for GPT-5.6-luna, 0.8767 to 0.8844 for Gemini 3.5 Flash, and 0.8646 to 0.8554 for Flash-Lite. Random and semantic controls show no consistent retrieval advantage. On the 352-row hidden set, the best retained Codex member scores 0.8685 Favg2 and currently ranks fourth, while gated retrieval scores 0.8604. Codex and OPUS-MT translation pipelines score 0.7848 and 0.7304, and a synthetic-data classifier scores 0.7334. These results support replication and retrieval as auditable system components, not as general performance gains.

paper.title: HardStance at StanceEval-2026: Error-Driven Prompt Calibration for Arabic Stance Detection
paper.abstract: We present our system for StanceEval-2026 Track 1, which focuses on Arabic stance detection toward Women Driving using the Mawqif-v2 dataset with three labels: Favor, Against, and None. We compare fine-tuned AraBERT models with zero-shot Gemma-4-31B. We refine the Gemma prompt using recurring development-set errors, focusing on dialect and indirect meaning, target identification, sentiment versus stance, hashtags, sarcasm, and the distinction between reporting and endorsement. We also compare the calibrated system with several alternative inference strategies, including self-consistency, model debate, and dialect-interpreter pipelines. The final Gemma-4-31B system achieves 86.61% Favg2, 67.46% Favg3, and 82.67% accuracy on the official blind test, ranking 5th. Our results show that target-specific context and clear decision rules can be more effective than adding additional inference stages or model interactions. The main remaining challenge is distinguishing Against from None, particularly when stance is indirect, ambiguous, or expressed through humor.

paper.title: Nabra at StanceEval-2026: Exploring Fine-Tuning Strategies for Arabic Stance Detection
paper.abstract: We present Nabra, a system submitted to StanceEval-2026 Track 1 for Arabic stance detection. Our approach fine-tunes MARBERTv2 on the Mawqif-v2 dataset, exploring seven configurations including class weighting, regularization, data augmentation via back-translation, resampling strategies, and zero-shot inference with Qwen2.5-7B. Our best model by the primary metric Favg2 is M1 (Baseline), achieving 0.837 on the development set and 0.6704 on the official blind test set. Error analysis reveals that Favor→Against misclassification accounts for 84.6% of errors, driven by negative sentiment words co-occurring with supportive stances. We find that metric choice (Favg2 vs. Favg3) significantly impacts model selection decisions.

paper.title: Meta_Labs at StanceEval-2026: Calibrated Routing and Pseudo-Label Self-Training for Cross-Target Arabic Stance Detection
paper.abstract: We present CaRPS, our system for Track 1 of StanceEval-2026. CaRPS combines a target-conditioned encoder with an LLM-based labeling and verification process to handle targets that are not seen during encoder fine-tuning. The encoder takes both the target and the tweet as input, while the LLM is used to generate labels and verify difficult predictions. These LLM-generated labels can then be used as pseudo-labeled data to further fine-tune the encoder, with the goal of gradually reducing the need for LLM calls. On the development leaderboard, our target-conditioned encoder alone achieves 87.19% Favg2, 76.56% Favg3, and 85.30% accuracy. For the official evaluation, we used adversarial LLM prompting for the target not seen during encoder fine-tuning, achieving 82.89% Favg2, 62.67% Favg3, and 78.98% accuracy. Additional experiments show that adversarial verification improves stance and sarcasm classification over one-shot prompting, while pseudo-label self-training helps adapt the encoder to a held-out target. Overall, CaRPS explores a practical combination of efficient encoder-based prediction and LLM-based labeling and verification for Arabic stance detection.

paper.title: U4RASD at StanceEval 2026: Fine-Tuning, Prompting, and Ensembling for Unseen-Target Arabic Stance Detection

author.affiliation: Arab Center for Research and Policy Studies
Arab Center for Research and Policy Studies
Arab Center for Research and Policy Studies
Arab Center for Research and Policy Studies and American University of Beirut

paper.abstract: This paper describes our system for StanceEval 2026 Track 2, which requires predicting stance toward targets not seen during training. We explored fine-tuning different Arabic BERT encoder models, using class weighting techniques, incorporating auxiliary sentiment and sarcasm tasks in sequential and parallel multi-task setups, and focal and margin-based contrastive losses. We also tried zero-shot and few-shot prompting, self-consistency with escalation, LoRA fine-tuning, and an ensemble approach. Our best-performing submission on the official blind test set was a training-free few-shot prompting approach using Gemini 2.5 Flash with an extended prompt, achieving an F_{avg2} of 87.41 and an F_{avg3} of 76.94, and ranking 8th out of 13 teams. This result shows that a simpler, training-free prompting approach can generalize to unseen targets more effectively than fine-tuned and ensemble systems.

paper.title: saliyah at StanceEval-2026: Few-Shot Arabic LLMs and Complementary-Model Fusion for Stance Detection across Seen and Unseen Targets
paper.abstract: We describe our entry to both tracks of StanceEval-2026, an Arabic stance-detection task built on the Mawqif-XT corpus. Track 1 (Seen Targets) is evaluated on Women Driving, while Track 2 (Unseen Targets) is evaluated on Electric Cars and the Trimester school calendar system. Rather than committing to a single approach, we compare two paradigms: fine-tuned Arabic encoders trained with multi-task learning using Mawqif-XT’s sentiment, sarcasm, and rationale annotations, and native Arabic LLMs used in a few-shot setting without any fine-tuning. For each track, we build the final system around the stronger approach. Across more than forty experimental configurations, few-shot LLMs consistently outperform fine-tuned encoders on both tracks. Our final systems achieve an Favg2 of 0.834 on Track 2 (ranked 9th) and 0.747 on Track 1 (ranked 13th), the latter through a complementary fusion of ALLaM-7B and Fanar-9B. We further observe that model performance may be related to how well pretraining coverage aligns with a target’s cultural and linguistic domain, that fusing two comparably strong models can outperform either model individually, and, perhaps most importantly, that more elaborate methods never surpass a strong LLM with a simple prompt. We release our code and prompts to support reproducibility.

paper.title: Orni at StanceEval-2026: Arabic Stance Detection with Reasoning-Augmented LLM Prompting and Encoder Ensembles

author.affiliation: Chittagong University of Engineering and Technology, Chittagong University of Engineering and Technology and Chittagong University of Engineering and Technology

paper.abstract: Arabic stance detection is a task that identifies whether an Arabic text expresses Favor, Against, or None toward a given target. It is important for understanding public opinion and social media discourse, particularly in Arabic where dialectal variation, sarcasm, and informal expressions make stance interpretation difficult. To address this, we took part in StanceEval-2026 Track 1, where models are trained on provided targets and evaluated on a related target from the same thematic domain. We investigate two complementary approaches: fine-tuning-based systems using Arabic encoders and parameter-efficient LLM adaptation, and prompted GPT-4o without fine-tuning. Our experiments include encoder ensembles, multi-task and contrastive learning, attention aggregation, augmentation, calibration, QLoRA, and prompted LLMs with few-shot demonstrations, target-specific context, structured reasoning, and self-consistency voting. The best fine-tuning-based system achieves 0.701 Favg2, while GPT-4o v4 reaches 0.827 Favg2, 0.630 Favg3, and 0.784 accuracy, ranking 11th on the official leaderboard. The results show that prompted GPT-4o transfers more effectively to the related-target setting, while additional prompt complexity does not always lead to further improvement.

paper.title: Thakaa at StanceEval-2026: Inference-Time Target Grounding for Arabic Stance Detection

author.affiliation: Thakaa, Advanced Company for Information Technology
Thakaa, Advanced Company for Information Technology
Thakaa, Advanced Company for Information Technology

paper.abstract: StanceEval-2026 tests Arabic stance classification under target shift, with evaluation targets absent from the labelled task data. We test two ways to supply target information at inference time. For Track 1, we retrieve eight labelled Women Driving demonstrations from the external ArabicStanceX corpus and score the three label tokens with Gemma-4-31B-IT. For the unseen-target track, we prepend cached target context prompted to be factual and non-evaluative, then fuse label predictions and label-token scores from multiple LLMs, with final assignments constrained by published class totals. The systems obtain 85.22 and 91.78 F_{\mathrm{avg2}} on Tracks 1 and 2, ranking sixth and fourth in the final standings. On held-out ArabicStanceX tweets, direct prompting scores 79.45 F_{\mathrm{avg2}}; eight random Women Driving demonstrations raise it to 84.78, and similarity retrieval reaches 89.04. Across three target-held-out Mawqif evaluations, a fixed target card raises Gemma-4-31B-IT from 86.54 to 86.93, whereas QLoRA lowers Gemma-4-12B-IT from 84.43 to 83.77. In these separate public evaluations, same-target demonstrations and retrieval improve performance, factual target context provides small, target-dependent gains, and the tested source-only adapter does not improve.

paper.title: ZHR at StanceEval-2026: Surface-Matched Synthetic Demonstrations and Metric-Aware Decoding for Arabic Cross-Target Stance Detection
paper.abstract: We describe the ZHR system for both tracks of StanceEval-2026, Arabic stance detection on Mawqif-XT, where Track 1 evaluates on seen targets and Track 2 on unseen ones. The system combines fine-tuned Arabic encoders, a few-shot classifier that retrieves labelled examples for a served instruction model, and generative models adapted with LoRA, and turns their blended probabilities into labels with a threshold rule that abstains to None unless one stance class is probable enough, with thresholds fixed on the development split. We report the whole sequence of experiments, including eight that lowered F_{\mathrm{avg}2} and were not adopted. The main finding is that transfer to a new target is carried by the demonstrations, the labelled examples retrieved into the prompt, rather than by the model itself. Generated on-target tweets in the example pool gave the largest gain on both tracks, matching the surface form of the test tweets helped where the target has a distinctive style, and doubling the examples hurt. Our official results are F_{\mathrm{avg}2} 0.896 with accuracy 0.855 on Track 1, and F_{\mathrm{avg}2} 0.940 with accuracy 0.922 on Track 2. The strongest official baselines reach 0.8425 on the Track 1 development set and 0.7475 on the Track 2 test set.

paper.title: ImageEval 2026: Culturally Grounded Arabic Multimodal Evaluation

author.affiliation: Hamad Bin Khalifa University and Qatar Computing Research Institute
Department of Computer Science, University of Toronto
Hamad Bin Khalifa University and Birzeit University

paper.abstract: We present an overview of the **ImageEval 2026** shared task on culturally grounded Arabic multimodal evaluation. It includes two tasks: (i) **AynVQA**, covering spoken visual question answering and image-grounded hallucination detection in English and Modern Standard Arabic (MSA), and (ii) **CRAI-Bench**, evaluating the cultural accuracy of text-to-image generation. A total of 14 teams participated in the test phase, with 12 teams submitting system description papers. Participating systems used a range of approaches, including zero-shot prompting, fine-tuning of vision-language models, speech-recognition pipelines, ensembling, and score calibration. We describe the task setup, datasets, evaluation procedure, and participating systems, and summarize the main results across the different tracks. All datasets and evaluation scripts from the shared task are released to the research community. The shared task highlights challenges in culturally grounded multimodal evaluation, particularly for Arabic speech and image-text reasoning.

paper.title: Dynamos at ImageEval 2026 Shared Tasks: Metric-Aligned Selection and Cross-Family Ensembling for Vision-Language Hallucination Detection in English and Arabic
paper.abstract: We describe the Dynamos submission to ImageEval 2026 Task 1b, image-grounded hallucination detection: given an image and three statements, exactly one of which is grounded, a system must label each true or false. The official ranking metric, Contrastive Instability (CI, lower is better), reduces exactly to one minus the accuracy of picking the grounded statement once a system always outputs a single true label, which removes an entire failure mode (marking zero or several statements true) at no cost. Building on this reduction, we score each statement with an open vision-language model and always output the highest-scoring one as true. Starting from zero-shot Qwen2.5-VL, we low-rank fine-tune the model with a selection objective, train multiple random-seed adapters, and average their scores. Our main finding is that the strongest single model is not the strongest ensemble member: a 32B adapter trained on more data performs substantially better on the labelled devtest split but generalises worse than smaller 7B adapters to the blind test set, yet combining the two model families improves over either pure-family ensemble on both languages, despite the 32B family generalising worse on its own. Our final submitted systems reach CI 0.033 in English (2nd of 8 teams on the official leaderboard) and 0.056 in Modern Standard Arabic (3rd of 6 teams), both well below our zero-shot baselines of 0.058 (English) and 0.110 (MSA).

paper.title: NYUAD at ImageEval Shared Tasks: A Multimodal LLM for Audio-Visual Question Answering and Hallucination Detection in English and Modern Standard Arabic
paper.abstract: The increasing adoption of multimodal large language models (MLLMs) has enabled more natural interaction with visual and spoken information, creating new opportunities for intelligent audio-visual question answering (AVQA) and hallucination detection systems. AVQA extends traditional visual question answering by requiring models to jointly understand an input image and a spoken question to generate accurate, context-aware responses. Despite recent advances, AVQA and hallucination detection tasks remain challenging for modern standard Arabic (MSA) due to the limited availability of multimodal datasets and the need to reason across Arabic speech and text modalities alongside visual inputs. In this paper, we present an MLLM-based framework for AVQA that takes an image and a spoken question as input and generates answers. In addition, we utilized this framework to detect hallucination in text-image pairs. The proposed approach is evaluated on the ImageEval 2026 Task (Ayn-VQA) benchmark, which focuses on culturally grounded Arabic AVQA. Experimental results demonstrate that the proposed framework effectively understands spoken queries, grounds their responses in the visual content, and produces accurate answers. The results underscore the capacity and limitations of different LLM architectures for both English and MSA and under various conditions.

paper.title: Nile Nexus at ImageEval 2026 Shared Tasks: Single-Choice Reformulation and Confidence-Calibrated Refinement for Culturally Grounded Hallucination Detection

author.affiliation: Chittagong University of Engineering and Technology

paper.abstract: Visual hallucination detection in culturally grounded images has remained challenging due to fine-grained visual distinctions and knowledge-dependent statements. In the ImageEval2026 / ArabicNLP26 AynVQA Shared Task, we have participated in Task 1b by developing a system based on Qwen2.5-VL-7B Instruct with 4-bit quantization. We have reformulated hallucination detection as a single choice selection problem to enforce the exactly one-correct-statement constraint and have introduced confidence-based selective refinement using paraphrase ensemble voting.
