Our final system has achieved 0.942 accuracy, 0.058 CI, 0.000 CFHR,0.942 Q+accuracy and 0.971 Q−accuracy, ranking 6th in the English track. Error analysis has revealed that the remaining failures have mostly stemmed from fine-grained cultural and visual grounding challenges rather than prediction inconsistency.

paper.title: Team Falcons at ImageEval 2026 Shared Tasks:Structure-Constrained QLoRA Fine-Tuning and Dual-Model Consensus Verification
paper.abstract: We present the Team Falcons system for the ImageEval 2026 Task 1b English track. The task provides culturally grounded images from the OASIS/EverydayMMQA resource family and three English statements per image, exactly one of which is visually supported(CITATION). Rather than treating the statements as independent binary decisions, we exploit this structural constraint and formulate each item as image-conditioned three-way classification. In Stage 1, we fine-tune Qwen3-VL-8B(CITATION) with 4-bit QLoRA(CITATION) and estimate uncertainty from the first-token probabilities assigned to A, B, and C. Stage 2 we send only examples whose top-two probability margin is below 0.90 to Gemini 3.6 Flash and GPT-5.4-mini. Their answer replaces the Stage 1 prediction only when both verifiers return the same valid option. On the official test set, Stage 1 obtains a Contrastive Instability (CI) of 0.0360 and Combined Accuracy of 0.9640. Consensus verification improves these scores to 0.0290 and 0.9710, respectively, placing our submission first on the Task 1b English leaderboard. After test labels were released, we found that the verifiers agreed on 91 of 138 routed items and changed 17 predictions: 12 corrections and 5 harmful revisions. These results show that structure-aware fine-tuning and conservative uncertainty routing can effectively combine a local open-weight VLM with proprietary multimodal verifiers.

paper.title: Ahmed Ayman at ImageEval 2026 Shared Tasks: Measurement-First Systems for Spoken VQA and Cultural Accuracy Evaluation
paper.abstract: We describe our systems for both ImageEval 2026 shared tasks. On Subtask 1a (spoken visual QA) we reach 0.962 on English and 0.834 on Modern Standard Arabic against baselines of 0.664 and 0.398, ranking first on the English track and second on MSA, while on Task 2 (CRAI-Bench) our judge ensemble reaches a test Spearman of 0.673 against 0.533 for our reproduction of the organizer baseline. Three effects account for most of these margins: answer-token bias (digit labels suppress the answer 0, and ordinal words are worth 0.35 accuracy), Arabic speech recognition (isolated from visual reasoning by the parallel track design), and tie-breaking (calibration collapses ranks and a second judge separates them, while error correlation of 0.89 rules out cancellation). A post-submission study on degraded audio finds four transcript-level interventions null and measures a 9% answer-flip rate between identical runs at temperature 0, a noise floor for single-run ablations.

paper.title: VisionEval at ImageEval 2026 Shared Tasks: Forced-Choice Reformulation for Hallucination Detection and a Version-Prior Baseline for Cultural Relevance
paper.abstract: We describe the VisionEval submissions to ImageEval 2026, covering Task 1b in the English and MSA tracks and Task 2 (CRAI-Bench). For Task 1b the three statements of an item share a stem and exactly one is grounded, so we replace the three independent True/False calls of the released baseline with a single three-way forced choice, read from the logits of the candidate digit tokens. The output then satisfies the one-true constraint by construction, and contrastive instability falls from the baseline 0.2674 to 0.0670 in English and from 0.4277 to 0.1010 in MSA. The organisers’ baseline is Qwen2.5-VL-3B prompted one statement at a time, and it identifies the grounded statement about as often as our 7B system does in English (0.9310 against 0.9330), so most of that gap is the output format rather than perception or scale. Task 2 is handled by a six-parameter model over the caption version, which placed first of five teams at Spearman 0.8258; an analysis of what that model reads shows the version field is recoverable from the released instance identifiers, so the result characterises the benchmark more than the system. We also show that the five reported Task 1b columns collapse to one degree of freedom for any system marking one statement true per item, an identity satisfied exactly by all fourteen rows of the final standings.

paper.title: HALDETECT at ImageEval 2026 Shared Tasks: Answer-First Contrastive Grounding with QLoRA

author.affiliation: Center for Computation and Data Sciences,IUB

paper.abstract: Large multimodal models tend to hallucinate visual detail fluently, which limits their deployment for fine-grained interpretation. We present HALDETECT, our system for the English hallucination-detection track (Task 1b) of ImageEval 2026, in which a system must identify, from an image and three culturally plausible statements, the single visually grounded one. We frame the item as one contrastive decision, emit the answer before its explanation, and structure reasoning around colour/texture, shape/form, and context. Our best submitted adapter fine-tunes Qwen2.5-VL-7B-Instruct with 4-bit QLoRA while freezing the vision encoder and reaches Contrastive Instability (CI) 0.035 on the 1,000-item test set; we placed third of eight teams. Development experiments show that answer order can matter more than model scale and that adaptation beats prompting alone. Retrospective paired analysis of the released gold labels confirms the QLoRA gain over the best prompt but not the small gap between the devtest-selected and best-test adapters, and reseeding all four training sizes shows that the apparent data-scaling curve does not survive a seed change. The 35 residual errors are culturally plausible function, material, and recognition distinctions; naive adapter voting does not help.

paper.title: alkhder at ImageEval 2026 Shared Tasks: Constrained Selection and Rotation-Averaged Logit Scoring for Multimodal Hallucination Detection

author.affiliation: Imperial College London and University of Sheffield

paper.abstract: We describe our submission to Subtask 1b of ImageEval 2026. The task consists of selecting the single visually valid statement from three candidates paired with an image, and is in both English and Modern Standard Arabic (MSA). Our system uses a pre-trained 7B vision–language model in a zero-shot setting, without task-specific training or fine-tuning. We formulate the task as a constrained selection problem and choose the answer using next-token log-probabilities. To reduce answer-position bias, we apply a Latin-square rotation to the candidate statements. Our system achieves CI scores of 0.0510 on the English test set and 0.0960 on the MSA test set, reducing CI relative to the official 3B baselines reported on devtest by 83.7% and 80.4%, respectively.

paper.title: CUET_InferX at ImageEval 2026 Shared Tasks: Audio-Visual LoRA Adaptation of Qwen2.5-Omni for Culturally-Grounded Spoken VQA
paper.abstract: We present CUET_InferX, our submission to Subtask 1a (Spoken VQA, English-audio) of the ImageEval 2026 shared task on the AynVQA dataset. The task requires predicting the correct answer option solely from an image and a raw audio clip containing both a spoken question and three candidate options. We fine-tune Qwen2.5-Omni-3B with LoRA applied exclusively to the language reasoning backbone, keeping both audio and vision encoders frozen, under a single 16 GB Kaggle T4 GPU. Training uses a time-budgeted, class-stratified subsample of 2,055 examples. Our system achieves 91.20% test accuracy (Balanced Accuracy 87.72%, Macro-F1 80.50%), placing 3rd position, with gains of +7.20 accuracy and +15.95 Macro-F1 over the zero-shot base. We compare against a cascaded ASR\toVLM alternative and zero-shot 3B/7B baselines, and explain with devtest evidence why we submitted the end-to-end fine-tuned model despite lower raw test accuracy than the cascade.

paper.title: Ahmed Younis at ImageEval 2026 Shared Tasks: The Judge Needs a Prior and the Task Needs a Constraint
paper.abstract: Across two ImageEval 2026 tracks, our best results came from analyzing the evaluation machinery rather than from a stronger model, yielding 1st place on hallucination detection (Task 1b, Modern Standard Arabic) and 4th on CRAI-Bench (Task 2). On CRAI-Bench, which asks systems to predict human cultural-accuracy scores for AI-generated images of Qatari scenes, a blind frequency prior that never looks at an image reaches dev Spearman 0.6878, above the organizers’ GPT-4-as-judge baseline of 0.625; adding two vision judges, with blend weights tuned against the global ranking metric rather than by scene-level cross-validation, reaches 0.7806 on the blind test. The weighting correction alone is worth +0.0296 test Spearman, because scene-level cross-validation is structurally blind to the within-cell ranking that judges contribute. On Task 1b, reframing "label three statements true/false" as "select the one grounded statement" makes invalid labelings structurally impossible and reaches 0.964 combined accuracy on the blind test, against an official baseline of 0.508. A matched-model ablation shows most of that headline gap is the underlying judge, but the constraint still adds +0.026 combined accuracy and eliminates the 4.0% of items that otherwise receive structurally invalid labelings; meanwhile upgrading to a stronger judge is worth nothing measurable and a three-model vote scored lower.

paper.title: DATALabKU at ImageEval 2026 Shared Tasks: Metric-Aware Cultural Evaluation for CRAI-Bench
paper.abstract: We present a reference-based evaluation framework for CRAI-Bench, Task 2 of ImageEval 2026. The method uses GPT-5.4 to extract cultural evidence from the reference image, caption, and generated image. This evidence is converted into metric-specific numerical features and mapped to CRAI scores using a small regressor trained on the released data. On the development set, the proposed approach improves composite Spearman correlation over direct GPT-5.4 scoring, with strong gains on certain metrics. We also analyze performance across caption versions and show that evaluation becomes less reliable for some dimensions as captions become more generic.

paper.title: Digilians at ImageEval 2026 Shared Tasks: Modular Speech Parsing and Joint Multimodal Reasoning for Arabic Spoken VQA
paper.abstract: We describe the Digilians submission to Task 1a (Spoken Visual Question Answering, MSA track) of the ImageEval 2026 shared task (Abdaljalil et al., 2026). Our system splits the problem into independently cacheable stages: speech recognition, schema-constrained transcript parsing that recovers a question and three candidate answers from continuous Arabic speech, a conditional repair mechanism that escalates to a larger ASR model only for semantically degenerate parses, and a joint multiplechoice visual reasoning stage that evaluates all three candidates against the image simultaneously rather than scoring them independently. On the labeled development split (500 records, synthetic voice-cloned audio), our production configuration reaches 79.0% accuracy against a 39.8% official baseline, with nearly the entire gain over an earlier configuration coming from a single change to the answer-selection model. On the blind final test split (1,000 records, human-recorded audio), the same frozen configuration scores 65.6% accuracy / 57.4% balanced accuracy / 50.4% macro F1, a substantial drop we attribute to the dev-to-test recordingcondition shift and report as our most important finding. We also surface a caching-related reproducibility issue uncovered during development and discuss what both findings imply for pipelines built the same way.

paper.title: AlexandriaX 2026: The First Shared Task on Dialectal Arabic Machine Translation

author.affiliation: King Fahad University of Petroleum and Minerals
Hamad Bin Khalifa University and Birzeit University
King Abdullah University of Science and Technology
King Abdullah University of Science and Technology

paper.abstract: Dialectal Arabic machine translation (MT) remains challenging despite recent progress in Arabic language technologies, particularly because effective translation requires modeling not only semantic content but also dialectal variation, conversational context, speaker and addressee characteristics, and sociolinguistic appropriateness. Moreover, conventional MT metrics provide limited insight into the linguistic errors produced by dialectal systems. We present the AlexandriaX 2026 Shared Task on Dialectal Arabic MT, which addresses these challenges through three complementary subtasks: (1) context-aware English-to-Dialectal Arabic dialogue translation across 13 Arabic varieties, (2) cross-dialect Arabic translation in the financial domain covering six Arabic dialects, and (3) span-level MT error detection and classification using linguistically motivated error categories across five Arabic varieties. The shared task attracted 38 registrations for Subtask 1, 33 for Subtask 2, and 35 for Subtask 3. Twelve unique teams submitted their system description papers, all of which we accepted for publication. The best system on Subtask 1 achieved 30.42 spBLEU in the constrained track and 33.49 spBLEU in the unconstrained track. On Subtask 2, the top system obtained 28.40 spBLEU. On Subtask 3, the best system achieved an overall score of 49.82, outperforming the 24.29 baseline. Taken together, the results of the leading systems across the three subtasks highlight the benefits of explicit dialect modeling, context-aware generation, retrieval and reranking, and specialized approaches to interpretable MT error analysis. All the resources of AlexandriaX 2026 shared task are publicly available, including data, baselines, and evaluation code on our project page: https://alexandriax.dlnlp.ai.

paper.title: TTLab at AlexandriaX-2026: A Fine-Tuned Surface Tagger for Arabic Machine-Translation Error-Span Detection and Classification

author.affiliation: Johann Wolfgang Goethe Universität Frankfurt am Main and Johann Wolfgang Goethe Universität Frankfurt am Main
Johann Wolfgang Goethe Universität Frankfurt am Main
Johann Wolfgang Goethe Universität Frankfurt am Main

paper.abstract: We present TTLab’s submission to the AlexandriaX-2026 Subtask 3 on Arabic MT error span detection and classification. Our system frames the task as token-level classification over surface forms, preserving character offsets to ensure exact alignment with the evaluation metric. To handle severe label imbalance, we employ a focal loss with class weighting and dialect-specific decoding thresholds. Among six Arabic pre-trained encoders, MARBERTv2 achieves the best overall performance of 40.8 and 40.91 on the development and test set, respectively, ranking 3rd out of all participating teams. While our system localizes error spans effectively, classification of rare error types remains challenging, highlighting the need for data augmentation for tail categories.

paper.title: Rosetta at AlexandriaX-2026: LoRA-Adapted NileChat for Context-Aware Dialectal Arabic Dialogue Translation
paper.abstract: This paper describes the Rosetta system for Subtask 1 (Context-Aware English-to-Dialectal Arabic Dialogue Translation) of the AlexandriaX shared task, participating in both constrained and unconstrained tracks. The approach fine-tunes a LoRA adapter on NileChat-3B using structured system/user prompts that condition generation on dialect and dialogue context. For the unconstrained track, the adapter is additionally pretrained on MADAR and PADIC. Rosetta ranked 4th in the constrained track (spBLEU 26.10) and 5th in the unconstrained track (spBLEU 25.09). The experimental results demonstrate that external pretraining helps only two of thirteen dialects while slightly hurting overall performance, suggesting negative transfer.

paper.title: Axiom at AlexandriaX-2026: Confidence-Thresholded Dialectal Encoder Fine-Tuning for MT Error Span Detection and Classification
paper.abstract: This paper describes the "Axiom" team’s submission to the AlexandriaX-2026 Shared Task, focusing on Subtask 3: MT Error Detection and Classification. We frame the task of predicting fine-grained error spans and their corresponding LQM categories as a joint token classification problem using a BIO tagging scheme. Evaluating multiple Arabic encoders, we find that dialect-specific pretraining significantly outperforms generative extraction baselines. To address severe label imbalance across error categories, we apply a square-root scaled inverse-frequency class-weighted loss. Furthermore, we introduce a confidence-thresholded decoding strategy at inference to reduce false-positive span over-prediction. Our final system achieved highly competitive performance, ranking 5th on the official leaderboard. We highlight that while overlap-based detection is robust, exact span matching remains a persistent challenge due to the non-standardized nature of dialectal Arabic orthography.

paper.title: CUNI at AlexandriaX-2026: Finetuning LLMs for dialectal Arabic Translation
paper.abstract: We describe the Charles University (CUNI) submission to the AlexandriaX-2026 Subtask 1, a shared task on English-to-Arabic dialectal conversation translation covering 13 Arabic varieties. Our approach fine-tunes Gemma-4-31B-it with QLoRA on the Alexandria training data at the conversation level, using rich contextual prompts that include domain metadata, participant names and speaker labels. We explore multiple training data mixes and hyperparameters, yielding a pool of candidate translations for the test set. These are reranked with a genetic-algorithm-enhanced minimum Bayes risk (GA-MBR) decoding using sentence-level spBLEU as the fitness function. Fine-tuning improves over the unmodified base model by approximately 5.2 ChrF points on the development set (from 45.2 to 50.4 ChrF for the best single checkpoint, or 25.1 to 32.6 spBLEU); GA-MBR reranking over a 40-candidate development pool yields 51.3 ChrF / 34.0 spBLEU, a further improvement of 0.9 ChrF points over the best pool member. Our submission ranked second in the unconstrained track.

paper.title: NAMAA Community at AlexandriaX-2026: Prompting, Fine-Tuning and Agreement Voting for Dialectal Arabic Translation and Evaluation
paper.abstract: Arabic encompasses diverse spoken varieties with limited parallel data, making both translation and automatic evaluation difficult beyond Modern Standard Arabic. We present the NAMAA Community submissions to all three AlexandriaX-2026 subtasks: English-to-dialect dialogue translation, cross-dialect translation, and dialectal MT error detection. Our systems combine few-shot prompting, fine-tuned encoder-decoder and decoder-only models, and encoder- and LLM-based span detection. Held-out ablations show that minimum-Bayes-risk consensus can suffer from model-family imbalance; we therefore use per-dialect routing for translation and 2-of-3 character-level agreement for error-span detection. Our systems rank fourth and fifth of six in the unconstrained and constrained Subtask 1 tracks, third of four on Subtask 2, and second of six on Subtask 3. The Subtask 3 system achieves 0.5448 overlap-F1, exceeding the overall winner on span localization, with category assignment remaining the main weakness. Code and resources are publicly available.[<https://huggingface.co/collections/NAMAA-Space/namaa-at-alexandriax-2026>]

paper.title: ArabicMTDiagnostics at AlexandriaX-2026: Detecting and Classifying Errors in Dialectal Arabic Machine Translation Outputs
paper.abstract: Dialectal Arabic MT error detection asks a sys tem to locate error spans in a machine trans lation and label each with a linguistic error category. It is hard because the dialects lack a standardised orthography and the error cate gories are severely imbalanced. In Subtask 3 of the AlexandriaX 2026 shared task, the in put is an English sentence and its machine translation into one of five Arabic dialects, and the output is character-level error spans with their LQM categories. The central difficulty is collapse onto the majority sociolinguistics class, 58% of training spans, leaving rare cat egories undetected. To address this, we fine tune NileChat-3B-Base with QLoRA on a sin gle 8 GB consumer GPU, casting the task as schema-prompted JSON generation and com bining character-position annotations that let the model copy offsets rather than count them, a category guide with one worked example per error type, and self-consistency decoding merging five samples by character-level union voting. Our system scores 0.3484 Overall on the official test set. We report two negative results: early stopping on validation loss de grades performance, since rare categories are acquired only in later epochs, and fine-tuning on the skewed distribution lowers macro-F1 be low the un-fine-tuned baseline until the cate gory guide is added

paper.title: ALEXIS at AlexandriaX-2026 Subtask 2: Capacity Discovery and Calibrated Preference Optimization for Cross-Dialect Arabic MT
paper.abstract: Cross-dialect Arabic machine translation asks for translation between Modern Standard Arabic and regional dialects with almost no parallel text. We present a system for Subtask 2 of AlexandriaX-2026, built on two findings about where the gains come from. First, data was not the binding constraint: once our mined-and-synthetic recipe had decelerated to +1.8\% relative spBLEU per round, a single increase in LoRA capacity beat three further data-tuning rounds combined (+8.9\%). Second, planned epoch budgets were consistently too short, and training past them was the largest single lever at every stage. We fine-tune NLLB-200-distilled-600M on a three-tier corpus of real, mined and synthetic pairs, then refine it with Direct Preference Optimization. Ablating three reward designs isolates a third finding: rewarding agreement with self-distilled references regresses real quality despite healthy training dynamics. Restricting the reward to references we trust, with a reference-free substitute for the two zero-resource dialects, yields a real gain that a further iteration gives back. Every configuration was scored on the official leaderboard. Our submission reached spBLEU 25.84 and chrF++ 39.02, ranking 2nd of 4 teams; post-evaluation experimentation reached 28.04.

paper.title: REGLAT at AlexandriaX-2026: A Two-Stage Multi-Encoder Framework for Character-Level Error Detection and LQM Classification in Dialectal Arabic Machine Translation

author.affiliation: ElSewedy University of Technology -POLYTECHNIC OF EGYPT and Faculty of Computer and Artificial Intelligence
Prince Sattam bin Abdulaziz University and Benha University

paper.abstract: We describe REGLAT’s submission to AlexandriaX-2026 Subtask 3, which requires character-offset error spans in dialectal Arabic machine translations and a Linguistically Motivated Multidimensional Quality Metrics (LQM) category for each span. The system separates localization from classification. Four CAMeLBERT-DA and MARBERTv2 BIO taggers project token probabilities to a shared character grid; whitespace-segment probabilities are then thresholded, bridged, and optionally dilated. A second four-member ensemble classifies detected spans using the marked hypothesis, English source, and translation direction, with class weighting and fitted logit biases. REGLAT ranked fourth out of six teams with an official Overall Score of 0.4021 (Overlap F1 0.4272; Error-Class score 0.3770). Its Exact Match F1 of 0.0041 exposes severe boundary imprecision. We document a scorer mismatch in development-time selection and therefore treat earlier development values as proxy-metric results, not official-metric estimates.

paper.title: FCDS at AlexandriaX-2026: Improving Context Aware Dialogue English To Dialectal Arabic Machine Translation Via Context Strategies And Quality Aware Decoding
paper.abstract: Translating English dialogue into dialectal Arabic depends on the target dialect, conversational context and speaker attributes, and these challenges are compounded by the scarcity of dialectal parallel data. We present our system for the AlexandriaX-2026 Context-Aware English-to-Dialectal Arabic Dialogue Translation constrained track, which restricts participants to the provided Alexandria dataset and models of \leq5B parameters. We fine-tune open LLMs, exploring different context composition strategies for training and inference, and find that mismatched strategies can outperform matched ones depending on the model. We further apply quality-aware decoding (QAD) via Minimum Bayes Risk, tuning the utility function and candidate pool size for consistent gains over greedy decoding. Our final system, a fine-tuned Gemma-3-4B-it with spBLEU-based QAD and a pool size of 50 samples, achieves 26.48 spBLEU and 42.3 chrF++, ranking third on the constrained-track leaderboard.

paper.title: LahjaMT at AlexandriaX-2026: A Context-Aware English-to-Dialectal Arabic Machine Translation System with Lightweight Routing of LoRA Experts
paper.abstract: Dialectal Arabic dialogue translation requires modeling both regional variation and conversational context under uneven supervision. We introduce LahjaMT, a compact system for translating English dialogue into thirteen country-level Arabic varieties. LahjaMT adapts the 3.12B-parameter NileChat-3B-Base model with LoRA, conditions translation on dialogue history and metadata, and routes each dialect to a checkpoint–prompt expert selected on the held-out selection set. The constrained system shares one backbone across all varieties; the unconstrained system changes only the Libyan and Sudanese routes, replacing them with specialists trained on auxiliary data. LahjaMT ranked second in the constrained track with 28.30 spBLEU and third in the unconstrained track with 28.54 spBLEU.

paper.title: alkhder at AlexandriaX-2026: Context-Aware English-to-Dialectal Arabic Dialogue Translation with QLoRA-Fine-Tuned NileChat-3B

author.affiliation: Imperial College London and University of Sheffield

paper.abstract: This paper describes team Alkhder’s submission to Subtask 1 of the AlexandriaX-2026 shared task, which asks systems to translate English dialogue turns into thirteen Arabic dialects. We fine-tune NileChat-3B-Base with QLoRA on the Alexandria parallel dialogue corpus, training one set of adapter weights for all dialects. Each turn is translated conditioned on the target country and dialect, the domain, the participant roles, the speaker–addressee gender direction, and the preceding dialogue context. At inference, conversations are translated autoregressively and the model is fed its own previous outputs back as context without using any gold target-side test information. Under the constrained-track, using only Alexandria data, it trains in about one hour and translates the private test set in under two hours. The system reaches a country-macro-averaged spBLEU of 20.36 and chrF++ of 36.64, on both tracks.

paper.title: Thakaa at AlexandriaX-2026: Who Gets the Final Say? Assigning Output Authority in Dialectal Arabic Machine Translation and Error Detection

author.affiliation: Thakaa, Advanced Company for Information Technology
Thakaa, Advanced Company for Information Technology
Thakaa, Advanced Company for Information Technology
Thakaa, Advanced Company for Information Technology

paper.abstract: We report first-place systems for all four evaluated AlexandriaX-2026 settings: both English-to-dialect translation tracks, cross-dialect translation, and translation-error detection. In unconstrained translation, our minimum Bayes risk (MBR) selection restricts output authority: four local systems can supply the translation, while seven additional systems contribute only reference evidence. Candidate-constrained MBR beats the strongest complete candidate in all 13 dialects and gains 1.2554 macro spBLEU overall, reaching 33.4891. It also surpasses a retrospective oracle selecting the best whole candidate system per dialect. In the constrained track, country-routed LoRA adapters over a shared NileChat-3B-Base backbone incorporate the released Libyan and Sudanese supervision absent from the training and development splits, raising macro spBLEU from 29.5969 to 30.4233. Post-evaluation, a single adapter trained on all released Alexandria data reaches 30.4733 macro spBLEU; averaging model weights across three training seeds raises this to 30.9726 while retaining one model for inference. For cross-dialect translation, nonparallel target-dialect retrieval guides deliberation, raising Gemma-4-31B-IT without fine-tuning from 24.6898 to 28.4011 spBLEU. For translation-error detection, GPT-5.5 proposes semantic error regions, while MARBERTv2 controls their character boundaries and corroborates additional spans, raising Overall from 0.4691 to 0.4982.

paper.title: Arabic Sentence Segmentation Shared Task 2026

author.affiliation: Mohamed bin Zayed University of Artificial Intelligence and New York University, Abu Dhabi
Mohamed bin Zayed University of Artificial Intelligence

paper.abstract: We present the findings of the Arabic Sentence Segmentation (AraSEG) Shared Task, organized at the Fourth Arabic Natural Language Processing Conference (ArabicNLP 2026). Given an Arabic document, the task requires systems to identify sentence boundaries and segment the text into coherent sentences. Systems are evaluated on the genre-diverse AraSEG corpus under four input settings that vary in punctuation availability and paragraph structure, each with a Closed Track restricted to the provided training data and an Open Track permitting publicly available external resources. 22 teams from 13 countries registered, 16 submitted systems, and 14 submitted system-description papers. Across the eight subtask-track combinations, the best systems achieve F1 scores ranging from 89.1 to 95.3. Performance declines as segmentation cues are removed, with the largest drop occurring when both punctuation and paragraph structure are unavailable. Pretrained-encoder ensembles and careful prediction calibration emerge as the most effective approaches, while gains from LLMs, external data, and complex architectures vary across systems and settings.

paper.title: MostafaElAraby at Arabic Segmentationtitle Shared Task 2026: Combining Lexical and Punctuation Evidence across Aligned Text View
paper.abstract: Arabic sentence segmentation without punctuation or paragraph breaks requires predicting boundaries from context. The AraSeg Open Track supplies a parallel punctuated view, but its marks do not consistently indicate sentence endings. We train two CAMeLBERT-MSA ensembles, one for the target No-Punctuation No-Paragraph view and one for the auxiliary No-Paragraph view. A discrete rule combines their boundary decisions with punctuation classes projected onto the target words. Model fitting and selection use only the 174-document official training split: five-fold cross-validation selects the training duration, and out-of-fold predictions calibrate the decoders and fusion rule. Development is reserved for evaluation, and the public test is unused. The system achieves 84.61 document-macro F1 on development and 84.88 on the official blind test, with blind precision of 81.87 and recall of 89.50. It predicts too many boundaries in 80.6% of development documents, although some of its lowest scores result from missed boundaries.

paper.title: NAMAA Community at AraSeg Shared Task 2026: Model Diversity, Conditional Decoding, and Missing Punctuation in Arabic Sentence Segmentation
paper.abstract: We present NAMAA Community’s systems for the four closed-track Arabic sentence-segmentation subtasks of AraSeg 2026. Heterogeneous ensembles combining LoRA-adapted bidirectional language models, XLM-R variants, a character-level SaT model, and punctuation-aware models outperform their development-selected single-model baselines. Large weights assigned to weaker but architecturally distinct members are consistent with complementary errors, although they do not establish causality. A training-only logistic MEMM improves F1 by +0.9 and +0.6 points on the punctuation-free subtasks but degrades both punctuated ones; the same directional pattern appears on the blind split. Aligning punctuated and punctuation-free inputs reveals F1 points of oracle headroom against the contemporaneous NoPnx locks, while only 52.5% of removed tokens are covered by the restoration label inventory. Genre-proxy analysis localizes the largest degradation to scriptural text. On the blind split, in the closed track, our systems achieved F1 scores of 94.4/91.3/89.9/87.0 on PA, NP, NoPnx-PA, and NoPnx-NP, respectively, ranking 6th/3rd/4th/3rd. The same systems, entered unchanged in the open track, rank 4th/2nd/3rd/3rd. Implementation and experimental resources are publicly available.[<https://github.com/NAMAA-ORG/NAMAA-Community-AraSeg-2026>]

paper.title: Axiom at AraSeg Shared Task 2026: A Regularized Dual-Model Ensemble with Domain-Adaptive Pretraining for Arabic Sentence Segmentation
paper.abstract: Identifying sentence boundaries in Arabic text is a challenging token classification task due to extreme dialectal variations, the absence of rigid punctuation rules, and document lengths that frequently exceed the capacity of standard transformer models. In this paper, we describe Team Axiom’s submission to the Paragraph-Aware Open track of the AraSeg Shared Task 2026. We propose a highly regularized, dual-model ensemble combining MARBERTv2 and CAMeLBERT-MSA. To address the challenge of excessively long documents, we employ a sliding-window tokenization strategy. Furthermore, we adapt our base models to the task corpus using Domain-Adaptive Pretraining (DAPT). Our final system achieved a Macro-F1 score of 90.2% (Precision: 91.9%, Recall: 89.5%), securing 7th place in the shared task.

paper.title: iMak AI Lab at AraSeg Shared Task 2026: Greedy-Selected Arabic Encoder Ensembles with Structural Constraints for Sentence Segmentation

author.affiliation: Higher School of Economics and St. Petersburg State University

paper.abstract: We describe the iMak AI Lab submissions to the closed track of the AraSeg Shared Task 2026 on Arabic sentence segmentation, covering all four subtasks: Paragraph-Aware (PA), No-Paragraph (NP), No-Punctuation Paragraph-Aware (NOPNX-PA), and NoPunctuation No-Paragraph (NOPNX-NP). Our system treats segmentation as binary token classification with pretrained Arabic encoders finetuned only on the 128K-token AraSeg training split. The single-model recipe encodes documents in overlapping 512-token windows and trains for three times more epochs than the standard schedule, which is the largest source of improvement in our pipeline. Per-subtask ensembles are then built by greedy forward selection over a pool of seven encoder families, several seeds, and multi-variant joint-training variants. Decoding applies deterministic structural constraints and a decision threshold tuned on the development set; no open-test labels or leaderboard feedback enter any modeling decision. The systems reach blind-test F1 scores of 94.1 (PA), 91.0 (NP), 89.5 (NOPNX-PA), and 85.8 (NOPNX-NP), above the official baseline on all four subtasks. We report ablations for each design decision, including several that did not help.

paper.title: NLPBeasts at AraSeg Shared Task 2026: A Character-Word BiLSTM-CRF for Paragraph-Aware Arabic Sentence Segmentation
paper.abstract: We describe NLPBeasts’ submission to the Paragraph-Aware (PA) Closed track of the AraSeg 2026 shared task, which frames Arabic sentence segmentation as per-token binary boundary classification. We compare two closed-track-compliant systems trained with out any pretrained embeddings or language models: (1) a feature-based CRF using handcrafted punctuation, brackets, and paragraphs distance features, and (2) a character- and word-level BiLSTM with a linear-chain CRF decoder, both trained entirely from scratch on the shared task’s training and development splits. The feature-based CRF plateaus at a hard recall ceiling (≈82–83%) regardless of regularization strength, while the BiLSTM-CRF captures substantially more boundary cases through learned context. Our BiLSTM-CRF system, using only permitted training data with the development split reserved strictly for model selection, achieves P=86.37, R=90.51, and F1=87.60 on the blind test set. We additionally report ablations on chunk length and training hardware (CPU vs. GPU), neither of which meaningfully changes development F1, suggesting our system’s performance ceiling on this closed-track data size is data-limited rather than compute- or context-length-limited.

paper.title: knights-ST at AraSeg Shared Task 2026: Cross-Family Ensembling with Task-Adaptive Pretraining for Arabic Sentence Segmentation
paper.abstract: We describe our submission to the AraSeg 2026 shared task on Arabic sentence segmentation (Paragraph-Aware, Closed track). We cast segmentation as binary token-boundary classification and build a system around three ideas: (i) task-adaptive pretraining (TAPT) of encoders on the task’s own training text, (ii) regularized fine-tuning with R-Drop and boundary smoothing, and (iii) a hand-designed cross-family ensemble of architecturally diverse Arabic encoders. Our final system reaches a boundary F1 of 94.8 on the blind test set (ranking 3rd of 12 teams, 0.5 points from the top-ranked team). Beyond the score, we report a practical finding backed by a series of blind submissions: on a small development set, a compact diversity-first ensemble generalizes better to unseen data than ensembles selected by exhaustively maximizing development F1, and TAPT helps only under-adapted backbones while hurting a heavily-pretrained one. We also report five techniques that did not help, to save future practitioners the effort. Our code is publicly available at https://github.com/Body123/araseg-2026-knights-st.

paper.title: ENSAR at AraSeg Shared Task 2026: An Ensemble of Encoders With Agentic Error Refinement
paper.abstract: We describe ENSAR, our submission to the AraSeg 2026 shared task on Arabic sentence segmentation, where a system must decide, for every word in a document, whether a sentence ends there. The four tracks strip punctuation, paragraph breaks, both, or neither. We start from an ensemble of five fine-tuned encoders decoded with a length-aware semi-Markov program. It is strong, but most of its mistakes are places where all five models are wrong and all five assign high confidence, so averaging them or moving a threshold changes nothing. ENSAR adds a reasoning stage on top. Two LLM juries, each holding a written policy learned from its own graded errors on the training split, debate every document and apply only the edits both endorse. Our system ranked first on three of the four tracks in both the closed and open settings.

paper.title: DxMultiHead at AraSeg Shared Task 2026: Alignment-Safe Sequence Labeling and Weighted Ensembling for Arabic Sentence Segmentation

author.affiliation: Digital Egypt for investment co. and Independent

paper.abstract: Sentence boundary detection in Arabic is inherently challenging due to ambiguous orthographic punctuation conventions, prolific coordinating conjunction clitics, and extensive stylistic variability across literary, religious, news, and web domains. In this paper, we present our system submission to the Closed Track of the AraSeg 2026 Shared Task. We formulate sentence boundary detection as a token-level sequence classification problem utilizing an ensemble of fine-tuned Arabic Transformer encoders: AraBERTv02, CAMeLBERT-MSA, and ARBERTv2. Our pipeline integrates an alignment-safe normalization strategy that strictly preserves gold token spans, overlapping sliding-window logit margin aggregation to counteract chunk-boundary degradation, stochastic punctuation masking during training, and calibrated positive-class loss weighting. In the official blind evaluation across eight diverse genres, our framework demonstrated strong boundary recovery across all four task tracks, securing 2nd place in both the Paragraph-Aware setting (F_1 = 95.0\%) and the No-Paragraph setting (F_1 = 91.3\%).

paper.title: AUC DL Lab at AraSeg Shared Task 2026: Syntax-Aware Graphs, Bidirectionalized Decoders, and Encoders for Arabic Sentence Segmentation
paper.abstract: The AUC DL Lab system addresses the AraSeg 2026 shared task on Arabic sentence segmentation across four conditions: paragraph-aware (PA), no-paragraph (NP), no-punctuation paragraph-aware (NOPNX-PA), and no-punctuation no-paragraph (NOPNXNP), in both the closed and open tracks. We cast segmentation as imbalanced word-level boundary classification and pair fine-tuned Arabic encoders with two complementary architectures: HDP-GRAPH, which models syntactic structure via dependency-graph message passing, and a quantized decoder-only LLM using Just Pass Twice (JPT) with QLoRA for contextual boundary classification. Predictions are calibrated and combined through differential-evolution ensemble weighting. On the blind test set, our closed track systems reach 94.5, 90.8, 89.2, and 86.0 F1 (ranking 5th, 6th, 6th, 7th), and our open-track systems reach 94.6, 90.9, 89.7, and 86.0 F1 (ranking 3rd, 4th, 4th, 5th) on PA, NP, NOPNX-PA, and NOPNX-NP, respectively. Architectural diversity grows more valuable as punctuation and paragraph cues are removed, while external data yields only marginal gains once in-domain coverage is adequate.

paper.title: Wathiq-SPU at AraSeg Shared Task 2026: Calibrated Transformer Ensembles for Arabic Sentence Segmentation across Punctuation and Paragraph Conditions

author.affiliation: Higher Institute for Applied Sciences and Technology

paper.abstract: Arabic sentence segmentation becomes substantially more difficult when punctuation and paragraph boundaries are unavailable. The AraSeg Shared Task 2026 provides a controlled benchmark for studying this problem under four conditions that progressively remove structural information. We present the Wathiq-SPU submission to all four closed-track conditions: Paragraph-Aware (PA), No-Punctuation Paragraph-Aware (NoPnx-PA), No-Paragraph (NP), and No-Punctuation No-Paragraph (NoPnx-NP). We formulate sentence segmentation as token-level binary boundary classification using pretrained Arabic Transformer encoders and combine calibrated predictions with track-specific ensemble strategies that adapt to the amount of available structural information. CAMeLBERT-MSA serves as our primary encoder, while the most challenging NoPnx-NP condition additionally benefits from AraELECTRA-based backbone diversity. Our experiments reveal that the most effective source of model diversity depends on task difficulty: diversity among independently trained models provides robust gains when some structural information is available, whereas backbone diversity becomes increasingly important when both punctuation and paragraph cues are removed. The selected systems achieve F1 scores of 93.4, 87.9, 90.0, and 84.8 on the PA, NoPnx-PA, NP, and NoPnx-NP tracks, respectively

paper.title: FAAMG at AraSeg Shared Task 2026: Cross-Architecture Ensembling for Punctuation-Free Arabic Segmentation
paper.abstract: Arabic sentence segmentation without punctuation or paragraph boundaries requires models to infer boundaries only from lexical, syntactic, and discourse context. We describe FAAMG’s submission in the closed track of AraSeg 2026 Subtask 4 (NoPnx-NP), restricted to only 174 training documents for fine-tuning. Our system is a weighted ensemble of eight models based on AraBERT, SaT, and CAMeLBERT BiLSTM-CRF. The ensemble covers a variety of regularization, encoder capacity, and sequence modeling. The resulting system achieves 86.7 document-macro F1 on the Blind Test set ranking fourth on the leaderboard. Through leave-one-out ablations we show that the ensemble contributes complementary information over the individual models.

paper.title: Itgan at AraSeg Shared Task 2026: Diversify, Don’t Curate – Learned Ensemble Combination for Arabic Sentence Segmentation
paper.abstract: We describe our submissions to the four subtasks of the AraSeg 2026 shared task in both tracks. Our components are conventional word-level boundary taggers, and our contribution is a measurement of what combining them is worth. Averaging 21 members gains +0.89 F1 over the best single model, and replacing the uniform probability average with a learned logistic combiner adds a further +0.23 (+1.12 in total), reaching significance only on the two subtasks that lack punctuation. Both are smaller than the encoder swap (+1.82). What the combiner buys is freedom from curation. Added to the base encoder, each of six different pretrained encoders helps under the combiner (+0.12 to +0.72, mean +0.34), whereas under averaging three of the six are harmful, by as much as 0.62. Another seed of an existing encoder is worth nothing under either rule; members should therefore be diversified rather than curated, provided the weights are learned. We also report three null results for inference-time structure, including a semi-Markov CRF whose failure we trace to a length prior that is uninformative at corpus level. Our closed-track systems placed fifth and seventh where ranked. In the open track, pretraining on 3.2M tokens of silver boundaries from Arabic Wikipedia before fine-tuning on the gold training split is worth +0.58 F1, and two of the closed-track findings reproduce on that external data.

paper.title: Abjad AI at AraSeg Shared Task 2026: Auxiliary Loss for Arabic Sentence Segmentation
paper.abstract: This paper describes the Abjad AI team’s sub- mission to the AraSeg 2026 Shared Task on Arabic sentence segmentation, covering the two punctuated tracks: Paragraph-Aware (PA) and No-Paragraph (NP). Rather than substituting a larger encoder, we retain the CAMeLBERT- MSA reference system and ask how much head- room remains in the task’s formulation. Our system combines four components: boundary labels aligned to each word’s final sub-token, an auxiliary classification head on the penul- timate encoder layer trained jointly with the final-layer head, class-weighted cross-entropy for boundary sparsity, and overlap-averaged decoding that scores documents of arbitrary length without truncation. We ablate each com- ponent in isolation, including the two that the reference system already uses. Our solution achieves F1 scores of 91.7 and 89.7 in the blind tests of the PA and NP sub-tasks, respectively.

paper.title: Al-Qahera at Arabic Segmentation Shared Task 2026: Genre-Conditioned LLM Prompting versus Supervised Multi-Backbone Ensembling
paper.abstract: We submit systems to both the closed and open divisions of all four tracks of the AraSeg 2026 shared task (PA, NP, NoPnx-PA, NoPnx-NP): a supervised 3-backbone ensemble (CAMeLBERT-MSA, AraBERTv02, and AraELECTRA, each with a gated-residual head, R-Drop regularization, and stochastic weight averaging), and a zero-shot LLM system prompted with explicit, track-specific segmentation rules instead of labeled examples. The ensemble uses no external resources, so it is entered in both divisions everywhere; for NoPnx-NP specifically, where every structural cue is stripped away, we additionally blend its predictions with the LLM system’s, in a real-data-only variant (closed-eligible) and a wiki-augmented variant trained with added pseudo-labeled Wikipedia data (open-only). On the officially-scored blind test, our best submission per track reaches 94.70 F_1 (PA), 91.00 (NP), 91.20 (NoPnx-PA), and 87.40 (NoPnx-NP). The supervised ensemble is the stronger, more consistent choice overall; the one exception is NoPnx-PA, where our LLM system’s unmodified seed prompt outperforms it and combining the two systems does not help—the only track where that happens. We report in full the structural annotation ambiguities we uncovered while building the LLM system.

paper.title: IslamicEval 2026: The Second Shared Task of Capturing LLMs Hallucination in Islamic Content
paper.abstract: We describe the main findings of the second IslamicEval shared task on hallucination detection in LLM-generated Islam related text (IslamicEval 2026). While the first occurrence of the task in 2025 separately evaluated hallucination detection/correction in quoted Quranic verses and Hadiths alongside a distinct QA retrieval subtask, this year integrates these objectives into four fine-grained subtasks with a much larger provided training set. Given an Islamic question and an LLM response, systems must: 1) detect all cited Quran and Hadith references (including verse numbers and narrators); 2) identify hallucinated citations; 3) correct the hallucinated content; and 4) assess the relevance of every citation to the prompt. Sixteen teams participated in the final phase across the four subtasks, utilizing diverse pipelines that highlight both the challenge of the task and the necessity of mitigation strategies in Islamic AI applications.

paper.title: Northwestern 9 at IslamicEval 2026: Fine-Grained Span Detection in Arabic Islamic Content Using CAMeLBERT-Mix
paper.abstract: This paper describes our submission to the IslamicEval 2026 Task 1 (Span Detection) shared task, which aims to identify and classify evidence spans in AI-generated Arabic Islamic answers. We formulate the task as token-level sequence labeling and fine-tune CAMeLBERT-Mix using BIO tagging, overlapping-window inference, and prediction reconciliation to detect four evidence categories: Ayah, matn, isnad, and claimed_source. On the official development set, our approach achieves a Precision of 95.55%, Recall of 97.06%, F1-score of 96.30%, and Token Accuracy of 98.66%. Multi-seed and qualitative analyses demonstrate the robustness of the proposed framework for Arabic evidence span detection.

paper.title: HIAST at IslamicEval 2026: Context-Aware Hallucination Detection and Evidence-Guided Verification for Arabic Islamic Question Answering

author.affiliation: Higher Institute for Applied Sciences and Technology

paper.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) have significantly improved general-purpose question answering but remain prone to hallucinations in fact-sensitive domains such as religion. IslamicEval 2026 addresses these challenges by providing a fine-grained benchmark for evaluating hallucination and relevance in Arabic Islamic citations. This paper presents our approaches to three tasks: Citation Span Detection (Subtask 1), Hallucination Identification (Subtask 2), and Answer Relevance (Subtask 4). For Citation Span Detection, we formulate the problem as BIO-based token classification and fine-tune AraBERT using overlapping sliding-window encoding to process long responses effectively. For Hallucination Identification, we introduce a segment-level verification framework that augments each citation with adaptively extracted contextual evidence and citation-type information. For Answer Relevance, we combine hybrid lexical-semantic retrieval over authenticated Qur’anic and Hadith corpora with Transformer-based classification, enriching retrieved evidence with citation-specific context such as neighboring Ayat and explicit Surah–verse references. On the official test set, the proposed solutions achieved an F1 of 0.9725, an accuracy of 86.62%, and a macro-F1 of 0.7721 for Subtasks 1, 2, and 4, respectively, demonstrating the effectiveness of the proposed approaches.

paper.title: AhmedNLP at IslamicEval 2026: Learning Answer Relevance from Within-Response Citation Preferences
paper.abstract: IslamicEval 2026 Subtask 4 asks whether a Qur’anic or Hadith citation is useful for answering an Arabic question, rather than merely related to its topic. We treat this decision as ranking under shared response context. An Arabic instruction prompt is scored by the first answer-token logit difference between na’am ("yes") and la ("no"). We adapt ALLaM 7B with LoRA and a response-balanced RankNet loss over 1,063 positive-negative pairs drawn from 348 mixed-label responses. At inference, the model uses deterministic logits and one calibrated threshold; it does not generate or sample an answer. On Development, the frozen checkpoint obtained 0.867761 Question Macro-F1 under question-grouped out-of-fold threshold calibration, compared with 0.777935 for zero-shot ALLaM. Our primary submission, AhmedNLP_AllamR, scored 0.767880 on the official test and was the best of our three submitted runs. The largest Development-to-test drop occurred on all-negative questions. This result suggests retaining pairwise supervision while adding direct supervision for homogeneous negative groups.

paper.title: Yaqeen at IslamicEval 2026: From Contextual Detection to Retrieval-Based Verification and Canonical Correction of LLM-Generated Arabic Islamic Citations
paper.abstract: Large language models are increasingly used to answer questions about religious texts, yet their fluent responses may contain misquoted, misattributed, or fabricated citations. Detecting such hallucinations requires identifying citation components, verifying their correctness, and recovering the canonical text when a quotation is incorrect. We present Yaqeen’s submission to the IslamicEval 2026 shared task, which evaluates these capabilities through three subtasks: detection of Qur’anic verses, Hadith text, chains of narration, and claimed sources; identification of incorrect citation fragments; and correction of erroneous Qur’anic and Hadith quotations. We develop task-specific systems combining AraBERT-based character-level sequence labeling with retrieval-based matching, classification, and reranking. Our systems achieve 96.78% character-level Macro-F1 on Task 1, 91.07% accuracy on Task 2, and 78.02% accuracy on Task 3. The results show that combining contextual Arabic representations with retrieval-based evidence is effective for fine-grained hallucination detection and correction in Arabic Islamic content.

paper.title: HaDe at IslamicEval 2026: Evaluating Prompted Judgment and Fine-Tuned Encoders for Islamic Citation Relevance
paper.abstract: This paper presents our participation in IslamicEval 2026 Subtask 4, citation relevance classification for Qur’an and Hadith spans. We propose two independent systems for this task. The first is a generative large language model prompted to produce a structured, step by step relevance judgment. The second is a domain pretrained sentence encoder fine tuned with triplet loss on citation relevance data. Our evaluation compares two generative backends and three encoders pretrained on different Arabic varieties, using macro averaged F1 as the metric. Results show on development set that chain of thought judgment with ALLaM-7B consistently outperforms our embedding similarity ensemble, reaching 0.774 macro F1 against 0.357 for the ensemble, and outperforms an equivalent Fanar-S-1-7B system on seven of eight prompting strategies. Additionally, AraBERT-v02, pretrained on Modern Standard Arabic, is the consistently strongest encoder, outperforming Classical Arabic pretrained encoders in this citation relevance task. Our best submitted system, ALLaM with few shot prompting without chain of thought, scores 0.748 macro F1 on the blind test set, narrowly ahead of the same backend with chain of thought added, at 0.744.

paper.title: SanadAI at IslamicEval 2026: Detecting Hallucinations in Arabic Islamic Citations through Span Detection and Hybrid Verification
paper.abstract: We present SanadAI, a modular system for the IslamicEval 2026 shared task on fine-grained hallucination detection and correction in Arabic Islamic content. We participate in Subtasks 1 and 2, which address citation span detection and hallucination detection, respectively. For Subtask 1, we fine-tune AraModernBERT as a BIO sequence tagger to identify Quranic verses ayah, Hadith text matn, transmission chains isnad, and claimed sources. Controlled Quranic and Hadith augmentation, together with Shamela-based hard-negative selection, substantially improves citation span detection over training on competition data alone. For Subtask 2, we use source-specific verification pipelines: Quranic evidence is verified through Arabic normalization and approximate matching, while Hadith evidence is verified using BGE-M3 dense retrieval, FAISS candidate search, lexical reranking, and semantic and entity-level evidence. SanadAI achieves 97.35% Macro-F1 on Subtask 1 and 86.66% official macro-accuracy on Subtask 2 on the hidden test set. Quranic verification is strongest at 96.89%, whereas isnad verification remains the most challenging at 77.42%, reflecting the difficulty of verifying transmission chains when the system relies on narrator compatibility with a retrieved Hadith rather than explicitly modeling narrator order and chain continuity.

paper.title: Tathabbut at at IslamicEval 2026: Canonical-Provenance Evidence Fusion for Fine-Grained Citation Hallucination Verification
paper.abstract: Islamic question-answering systems can produce fluent Arabic while altering Qur’anic wording, Hadith text, narrator chains, or source attribution. We present Tathabbut for two IslamicEval 2026 settings: fine-grained verification and canonical correction. For verification, Canonical-Provenance Evidence Fusion (CPEF) classifies Ayah, matn, isnad, and claimed-source segments by combining canonical retrieval with collection, narrator, response-level, contradiction, and exact-matn provenance evidence. CPEF achieves 0.9452 macro accuracy on the official Test set. For correction, Type-Aware Selective Canonical Retrieval (TASCR) reranks authoritative Qur’anic and Hadith candidates using lexical, memory-based, contextual, and source evidence, and abstains when confidence is insufficient. TASCR achieves 86.29% Test accuracy. A post-hoc Development diagnostic finds the gold correction for 319/327 (97.55%) recoverable cases in an expanded candidate pool, indicating that candidate discrimination and abstention are larger bottlenecks than retrieval recall. Neither submitted component invokes a generative LLM at inference time.

paper.title: Bayan_CU at IslamicEval 2026: Fine-Grained Hallucination Span Detection in Arabic Quranic and Hadith Texts

author.affiliation: Faculty of Computers and Artificial Intelligence, Cairo University

paper.abstract: Mitigating factual hallucinations in Large Language Model (LLM) responses is critical, especially when handling sacred Islamic text. This paper presents our system for the IslamicEval 2026 Shared Task-Subtask 1 (Span Detection), which requires extracting exact character-level spans and fragment labeling of religious citations in Arabic LLM-generated responses. We frame this as a supervised token-classification task, fine-tuning a monolingual bidirectional encoder (AraBERTv2). To process long sequences, we implement a sliding window chunking mechanism with an overlapping stride. We reconstruct final character boundaries using a post-processing heuristic that resolves overlapping token predictions. Furthermore, we apply a cascading false-positive filter using cross-type conflict resolution and category-specific minimum length thresholds. Our pipeline yields highly competitive results, achieving a Macro-F1 score of 0.9652 on the development set and a peak evaluation score of 0.9736 on the official-task test set.

paper.title: Qahera at IslamicEval 2026: Corpus-Grounded Retrieval and Iterative Harness Search with a 4B-Parameter LLM for Islamic Citation Verification
paper.abstract: We describe the Qahera system for the four IslamicEval 2026 subtasks: (1) detecting Qur’an/Hadith citation spans in LLM-generated Islamic answers, (2) judging citation authenticity, (3) correcting inauthentic citations against reference corpora, and (4) judging whether an authentic citation answers the question asked. Under a 13B-parameter open-model constraint, running entirely on free Kaggle GPUs, we combine a lightweight token-classification model with character-level auxiliary features (Sub-task 1), corpus-grounded fuzzy retrieval (Sub-tasks 2–3), and a 4B-parameter instruction-tuned LLM (Gemma-3-4B) used only where retrieval alone cannot discriminate (Subtasks 3–4). Rather than hand-designing LLM prompts once, we develop them through an iterative propose-evaluate-diagnose search loop that reads full prediction traces after every candidate and hunts for systematic biases before each change. This surfaces small-model failure modes – a near-universal “reject” bias in isolated yes/no verification, and an “always name something” bias in numbered-list prompts – that would otherwise silently cap performance, and shows that validating candidates on small subsets can be actively misleading. Our final system reaches 0.9716 F1 (Subtask 1), 0.906 accuracy (Subtask 2), 0.773 accuracy (Subtask 3), and 0.673 macro-F1 (Subtask 4) on the official test sets.

paper.title: Taqwatech at IslamicEval 2026: Contextual Span Detection and Corpus-Grounded Verification of Islamic Citations
paper.abstract: Reliable use of large language models in religious settings requires more than fluent text, since a generated answer may misquote Qur’anic verses or Hadiths, assign them to the wrong source, or provide an inaccurate narrator chain. This paper presents the Taqwatech systems for Subtasks 1 and 2 of IslamicEval 2026. For Subtask 1, we fine-tune CAMeLBERT-Mix as a BIO sequence-labeling model to detect Ayah, Hadith matn, isnad, and claimed-source spans. The predicted token labels are then converted into the character offsets required by the task. For Subtask 2, we develop a corpus-grounded verification system that combines Arabic normalization, lexical retrieval, character-level TF–IDF, Qur’anic verse matching, source validation, and narrator matching. On the official test set, our systems achieved a character-level macro-F1 score of 0.9683 for Subtask 1 and a macro accuracy of 0.9050 for Subtask 2. The results show strong performance in span detection and Qur’anic citation verification, while isnad verification remains the main area for improvement.

paper.title: Namaa Community at IslamicEval 2026: Retrieval-Grounded Verification of Qur’anic and Hadith Citations for Hallucination Identification
paper.abstract: Large language models may generate inaccurate Islamic citations when answering religious questions. We present the Namaa Community system for Subtask 2 of IslamicEval 2026, which identifies hallucinations in Qur’anic verses (Ayah), hadith texts (matn), chains of narration (isnad), and claimed sources. We formulate the task as retrieval-grounded verification: citation spans are normalized and matched against the Qur’an and the six major hadith collections using character n-gram retrieval and edit-distance re-ranking. Type-specific verifiers assess Ayah and matn similarity, while claimed sources and isnads are checked against their parent citations. The deterministic pipeline requires no language model or GPU, and every decision is traceable to a canonical record. It achieves a macro accuracy of 0.\devMacro on the development set, 17.9 percentage points above a per-type majority-class baseline, and 0.\testMacro on the official blind test; we trace most of that shortfall to a submission-time configuration error and decompose the remainder by segment type. Our code and submissions are publicly available.[]

paper.title: Halluscoring 2026: The First Shared Task on LLM Hallucination Detection Answer Verification

author.affiliation: King Fahad University of Petroleum and Minerals
King Fahad University of Petroleum and Minerals

paper.abstract: We present HalluScoring 2026, a shared task for evaluating hallucination detection and factual verification in Arabic question answering under challenging generalization settings. The shared task is organized into two main tasks, each comprising two subtasks, for a total of four subtasks. Task 1 evaluates binary hallucination detection, considering generalization to unseen questions (Subtask 1.1) and responses generated by unseen LLMs (Subtask 1.2). Task 2 extends the evaluation beyond detection by requiring the systems to additionally identify the correct factual answer from six related candidates, covering Islamic knowledge (Subtask 2.1) and general knowledge (Subtask 2.2). The shared task is based on two Arabic datasets: HalluScore and HalluTruthQA. A total of 13 teams participated in the shared task, 10 of which submitted system description papers. The results of Task 1 demonstrate that hallucination detection remains challenging under distribution shift, with the winning team achieving AUC-ROC test scores of 0.772 and 0.767 for Subtasks 1.1 and 1.2, respectively. For Task 2, the winning team achieved scores of 0.882 and 0.857 in the Islamic and general-knowledge subtasks, respectively, under assisted evaluation.

paper.title: Hashtag AI at HalluScoring-2026: Distilling Knowledge-Graph Retrieval into Gemma 4 for Arabic Hallucination Detection
paper.abstract: We describe our submission to HalluScoring 2026 for Arabic hallucination detection in general-culture and Islamic-knowledge question answering. Our system adapts the instruction-tuned 12B-parameter Gemma 4 model with QLoRA. Its central idea is to use the Hashtag AI knowledge-graph retrieval system only during offline data construction: we query facts related to development-set failures, create contrastive training examples, and distill them into the model parameters. The submitted model is closed-book and uses no retrieval, search, or external knowledge at evaluation time. On organizer-provided test annotations, it obtains 73.59 macro-F1 on the 400-example Islamic set and 77.56 on the 1,600-example mixed-domain set; answer-option accuracies are 75.25% and 81.13%. Analysis shows strong science performance but lower recall for subtle hallucinations in history, geography, and Islamic knowledge.

paper.title: Vescera at HalluScoring 2026: Privileged-Information Distillation with Contrastive Representation Alignment for Arabic Hallucination Detection

author.affiliation: Consiglio Nazionale delle Ricerche and Université de Biskra

paper.abstract: HalluScoring 2026 Subtask 2.2 (Hallucination Detection & Find the Truth) requires systems to judge whether an Arabic generated answer is hallucinated and to select the correct one among six candidates, without access to the reference answer that would make both judgments trivial. We treat that withheld reference as privileged information: a teacher is fine-tuned with it in the prompt, then never deployed, and its advantage is transferred to a blind student through two channels knowledge distillation over the teacher’s output distribution, and a contrastive privileged-information (CPI) term that aligns the student’s hidden representation with the teacher’s gold-conditioned one. Our fine-tuned ALLaM-7B attains 84.62 combined score (Comb) on the official test set and 83.47 on the dev set.

paper.title: AyahVerse at HalluScoring-2026: Category-Aware Arabic Hallucination Detection with Multi-Layer Representations
paper.abstract: We present our submission to HalluScoring 2026, an ArabicNLP shared task on hallucination detection and answer recovery in Arabic LLM outputs. For Track 1, our submitted baseline fine-tunes CAMeLBERT for binary hallucination detection, achieving 0.921 and 0.763 AUC-ROC on the development and test sets of Task 1.1, and 0.749 and 0.729 on Task 1.2, respectively. We further conduct post-submission ablations with intermediate-layer supervision and category embeddings to study their effect on generalization. The combined model achieves 0.929 AUC-ROC on Task 1.1 and 0.777 on Task 1.2 development sets. For Track 2, we separate hallucination detection from answer selection, using CAMeLBERT for detection and a decoder-based, QLoRA-tuned AceGPT-v2-8B-Chat for option selection. The system achieves combined scores of 0.784 on Task 2.1 and 0.829 on Task 2.2 on the validation sets, improving substantially over the corresponding zero-shot baselines.

paper.title: NAMAA Community at HalluScoring 2026: Beyond Predictive Performance: Reliability and Generalization in Arabic Hallucination Detection
paper.abstract: Reliable Arabic hallucination detection requires not only strong ranking performance but also robustness to distribution shift, calibrated probabilities, and useful uncertainty for selective prediction. We present the NAMAA Community’s submission to HalluScoring 2026 Task ~1.1 and a set of post-submission diagnostic experiments. The scored, template-compliant system is a CAMeLBERT cross-encoder over the question and generated answer; it achieves 0.7596 ROC-AUC on the hidden test set, ranking third among seven teams. We compare this template-defined input path with reference-aware answer-pair models that use the gold answer. A CAMeLBERT input-framing ablation raises the unseen-question ROC-AUC from 0.8713 to 0.9272, while similar gains appear across ARBERT and MARBERTv2. Reference-free distillation recovers only a small portion of this advantage, whereas LoRA-InfoNCE substantially improves direct cosine discrimination. On a separately trained CAMeLBERT reliability replicate, temperature scaling reduces expected calibration error from 0.0993 to 0.0562, and MC-Dropout variance reduces retained-set error from 14.08% to 8.35% when the 30% most uncertain cases are deferred. These results motivate reporting distributional generalization, calibration, and selective risk alongside ROC-AUC. Code and checkpoints for the scored submission are publicly available. [<https://github.com/NAMAA-ORG/HalluScoring-Arabic-Hallucination-Detection>]

paper.title: REGLAT at HalluScoring-2026: A Multistage Approach for Arabic Hallucination Detection

author.affiliation: ElSewedy University of Technology -POLYTECHNIC OF EGYPT and Faculty of Computer and Artificial Intelligence
Prince Sattam bin Abdulaziz University and Benha University

paper.abstract: This paper presents a multistage ensemble-based approach developed for the HalluScoring-2026 shared task on Arabic hallucination detection. The proposed system combines three Arabic pretrained language encoders: MARBERTv2, CAMeLBERT, and ARBERT. The diverse linguistic representations captured by these models enable the ensemble to improve the robustness and discriminative capability of hallucination detection compared to the individual encoders. On the development set, the ensemble achieved an AUC-ROC of 0.9413, Macro-F1 of 0.8704, and an AUC-PR of 0.9610, outperforming the individual models. On the official test set, the system achieved an AUC-ROC of 0.7717, Macro-F1 of 0.6576, and an AUC-PR of 0.9181. These results secured the highest overall ranking among all submitted systems, placing our system first in the HalluScoring-2026 shared task. Further analysis reveals substantial variation in detection performance across generator models and linguistic phenomena, with subtle factual deviations, dialectal and culturally specific expressions, and unusually long responses posing particular challenges. Overall, the findings demonstrate the effectiveness of combining distinct Arabic-specific pretrained encoders for robust Arabic hallucination detection.

paper.title: Anhnamxtanh at HalluScoring-2026: Counterfactual Cross-Checking for Hallucination Detection and Answer Verification in Islamic Knowledge

author.affiliation: University of Electro-Communications, Tokyo Institute of Technology

paper.abstract: Hallucination detection in Arabic Islamic question answering is challenging because fluent answers may misstate a verse, narration, ruling, attribution, or historical fact. The task jointly requires detecting hallucination and recovering the factually correct option. We introduce C3R, a Counterfactual Cross-Check Recognition framework that models this relation with two role-conditioned predictions from one Arabic language model: a truth role selects the factual option, while a match role selects the candidate that best represents the generated response. Training uses targeted counterfactual responses, hard distractors, option-order permutations, and completion-likelihood supervision without a cross-view consistency loss. At inference, C3R scores valid structured completions, maps predictions from permuted presentations back to semantic option identities, and derives the hallucination label from argmax agreement between the two roles. The cross-check is applied only at inference. With a QLoRA-adapted ALLaM backbone, C3R ranks first on the official test leaderboard with a final score of 0.8824, comprising 0.8673 macro-F1 and 0.8975 option accuracy. These results demonstrate the effectiveness of structured cross-role agreement for knowledge-sensitive hallucination detection and answer verification.

paper.title: SCaLAR@NITK at HalluScoring-2026: A Reference-Free Generative Approach to Hallucination Detection via Teacher-Student Distillation
paper.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) produce fluent but factually incorrect outputs which become significant when such models are applied to local languages, such as Arabic, because of the language’s complex morphology, dialectal richness, and the insufficient material available for training and evaluation. The competition HalluScoring-2026 Track 1 aims to address these problems and consists of two tasks that demand hallucination detection in Arabic question-answering settings. To solve this issue, we transfer the knowledge of a powerful reference-based teacher that is a stacked ensemble of five fine-tuned encoder classifiers with dynamic lexical, embedding, and entailment characteristics onto a simpler reference-based student model.

paper.title: HelsinkiTeam at HalluScoring-2026: Domain-Adaptive Arabic Hallucination Detection and Answer Selection with ALLaM

author.affiliation: Qutwo and Ecole Nationale Supérieure de l'Electronique et de ses Applications

paper.abstract: The rapid advancement of large language models (LLMs) has enabled powerful AI applications, yet hallucinations remain a major challenge to their reliability. As part of Track 2 of the HalluScoring 2026 shared task at ArabicNLP 2026, we present a system for detecting hallucinated answers and selecting the correct answer from six closely related candidates. We adapt the Arabic–English ALLaM-7B-Instruct model using Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) with domain-specific supervision from Qur’anic text, Hadith, Islamic law and inheritance, Islamic history, and general knowledge. The system jointly performs hallucination detection and answer selection, achieving 88.9% accuracy and 88.6% macro-F1 for hallucination detection, and 91.1% answer selection accuracy on the 800-instance development set. Error analysis identifies geography and structured-output parsing as the main remaining weaknesses.

paper.title: DzairVerse at HalluScoring-2026: Leak-Free QLoRA Fine-Tuning for Arabic Hallucination Detection and Truth Selection
paper.abstract: Large language models answer fluently but not always truthfully, and catching a wrong answer is hardest in knowledge-sensitive domains such as Islamic question answering, where a confi dent but fabricated citation of Qur’an, Hadith, or jurisprudence is easy to produce and costly to miss. We study this through our participation in the HalluScoring 2026 shared task, Task 2 (Islamic Knowledge) (Alansari et al., 2026): given a question, a baseline-generated answer, and six candidate options, a system must de cide whether the answer is hallucinated and then select the correct option. Our system is a single QLoRA adapter fine-tuned on Fanar-1 9B to reproduce the organizers’ two-step infer ence, under a strictly leak-free setup, where no answer information beyond the question and generated answer enters the detection prompt, following our hypothesis that answer exposure inflates detection scores through leakage rather than judgment. On the official leaderboard our submission placed second of five teams, scor ing 0.7582 on the blind track we targeted and 0.7881 on the assisted track. Controlled follow up experiments support it: showing the options during detection is worth +0.047 Macro-F1 on both splits, and detection ability comes entirely from supervision, the frozen generator accept ing its own output on all 400 test items. A 1,200-item probe, however, corrects our own initial diagnosis. The model is not blind to clean falsehoods, catching 80.5% of them; it is biased toward rejection, wrongly flagging 32.5% of verified-correct answers, and that sin gle bias is the central limitation of the approach.

paper.title: ShadowDZ at HalluScoring-2026: A Fine-Tuned Fanar Approach for Islamic Knowledge Hallucination Detection
paper.abstract: Large language models used for question answering can produce fluent but factually incorrect answers, a problem that is acute in knowledge-sensitive domains such as Islamic religious knowledge. We describe our system for the HalluScoring 2026 shared task (Islamic Knowledge track), which requires jointly detecting hallucinated answers and selecting the correct option among six candidates. We fine-tune Fanar-1-9B-Instruct with LoRA and decompose inference into two independently-prompted steps, judging hallucination before revealing the candidate options, to prevent a textual-similarity shortcut where one option is a near-verbatim restatement of the generated answer. Our system scores 0.7149 (Assisted) and 0.6222 (Blind) on the official hidden test set, ranking 5th of 5 reported teams; a controlled comparison shows this shortcut-resistant design costs roughly 10 points against a single-pass variant on a held-out development subsample (0.7625 vs. 0.8639 Combined Score). We release our code and model to support further work on this trade-off.

paper.title: KnowledgeGraphEval 2026: The First Shared Task on Arabic Knowledge Graphs

author.affiliation: Birzeit University and Palestine Technical University - Kadoorie
Hamad Bin Khalifa University and Birzeit University

paper.abstract: We present KnowledgeGraphEval 2026, the first Arabic shared task dedicated to knowledge graph (KG) construction from text. The task focuses on extracting named entities and semantic relations from Arabic text to build structured, machine-readable knowledge representations. It includes two subtasks: (i) AdaptNER, which evaluates cross-domain named entity recognition (NER), and (ii) Relation Extraction (RE), which predicts semantic relations between predefined entity pairs. For AdaptNER, we release Konooz MSA, an Arabic NER benchmark annotated with 21 entity types across 10 domains. For RE, we release WojoodRelations, an Arabic RE dataset annotated with 40 relation types. At test time, 14 teams participated, of which 13 submitted system description papers; and one RE paper was subsequently rejected. The best systems achieve F1 scores of 76% and 96% on AdaptNER and RE, respectively. Results show that cross-domain NER remains challenging, while RE systems continue to face difficulties with rare and semantically confusable relations. We release the datasets, baselines, and evaluation tools for reproducible research in Arabic information extraction and KG construction.

paper.title: AdaptLinker at KnowledgeGraphEval 2026: Cross-Domain Arabic Named Entity Recognition with Adversarial and Self-Training

author.affiliation: University of Information Technology, Vietnam National University
