paper.abstract: This paper presents the submission of team AdaptLinker to the AdaptNER shared task (Subtask 1: Cross-Domain Named Entity Recognition) at KnowledgeGraphEval 2026. To address nested entities and domain shift across 10 unseen target domains, we propose a multi-head token classification framework built on the AraBERT backbone. Our approach inte- grates: (1) 21 parallel linear classifiers to pre- dict overlapping named entities; (2) a Domain Adversarial Neural Network (DANN) using a Gradient Reversal Layer (GRL) to align feature spaces; (3) confidence-gated pseudo-labeling on unlabeled target text; and (4) Stochastic Weight Averaging (SWA). Our final system achieved a Precision of 75.48%, Recall of 71.21%, a Micro F1 of 73.29%, and a Macro F1 of 63.37% on the official blinded test set, outperforming the shared-task baseline (0.7329 vs. 0.622 Micro F1) and ranking 6th out of all participating teams

paper.title: NAMAA Community at KnowledgeGraphEval 2026: Entity-Span Voting and Constrained LLM Ensembles for Arabic Knowledge Graph Construction
paper.abstract: Arabic knowledge graph construction is a challenging problem due to the linguistic complexity of Arabic and the need for robust generalization across domains. This paper presents our systems for the KnowledgeGraphEval 2026 shared task on Arabic knowledge graph construction and domain adaptation, covering two subtasks: AdaptNER for cross-domain named entity recognition and relation extraction (RE). For AdaptNER, we employ an entity-span ensemble combining two BIO sequence taggers with constrained conditional random field (CRF) decoding and a GlobalPointer span classifier. Our system achieved a micro-F1 score of 76.00%, ranking first in the official evaluation. For relation extraction, we use a majority-vote ensemble of three LoRA-fine-tuned causal language models. This approach achieved a micro-F1 score of 93.48%, ranking fifth. These results demonstrate the effectiveness of model ensembling and complementary prediction strategies for Arabic named-entity recognition and relation extraction.

paper.title: PTUK-NLP at KnowledgeGraphEval 2026: Cross-Domain Nested Arabic NER with ArBERT and Targeted Data Augmentation
paper.abstract: This paper presents the PTUK-NLP submission to KnowledgeGraphEval 2026 Subtask 1 (AdaptNER), evaluating cross-domain and cross-dialect nested Arabic Named Entity Recognition (NER). Models trained on Wojood are evaluated in a zero-shot setting on Konooz, spanning ten unseen domains and sixteen Arabic dialects. Our system fine-tunes ArBERT with targeted augmentation for rare entity types and lightweight inference-time post-processing, using Konooz strictly for evaluation and never for training or adaptation. The submitted system achieves 91.07% micro-F1 and 83.11% macro-F1 on Wojood, and 71.84% precision, 66.59% recall, 69.11% micro-F1, and 60.70% macro-F1 on the official Konooz blind test, ranking fourth on the final leaderboard and achieving a micro-F1 score 6.11 points above the organizers’ baseline. A post-submission ensemble of ArBERT and AraBERTv2 does not improve over the best single model. Overall, targeted data-centric modifications provide useful gains for rare entity types, while a standard MSA-pretrained encoder remains competitive under substantial domain and dialect shift.

paper.title: ISNAD at KnowledgeGraphEval 2026: Arabic Relation Extraction via Entity-Aware AraBERT and Imbalance-Aware Resampling
paper.abstract: Relation extraction (RE) is a fundamental component of knowledge graph construction, question answering, and text summarization. Although recent RE models achieve strong overall performance through the fine-tuning of pretrained language models, their aggregate performance can obscure substantial disparities across relation types, particularly under long-tailed distributions. This issue remains largely unexplored for Arabic RE. In this work, we investigate the effectiveness of class-balancing strategies for long-tail relation extraction in Arabic by fine-tuning AraBERT with entity markers on Wojood^{Relations}. Our system, submitted to the KnowledgeGraphEval 2026 shared task, achieves a Micro-F1 score of 92.73 on the official test set. Further analysis shows that errors are disproportionately concentrated among low-frequency and semantically overlapping relation types, indicating that imbalance-handling strategies developed primarily for English benchmarks do not fully address the challenges posed by the long-tailed relation distribution in Arabic.

paper.title: Wasl at KnowledgeGraphEval 2026: Multi-Head Nested BIO Tagging and Constraint-Aware Relation Classification for Arabic Knowledge Graph Construction

author.affiliation: Maryam Abacha American University of Nigeria

paper.abstract: We describe Team Wasl’s systems for the KnowledgeGraphEval 2026 shared task at ArabicNLP 2026, which decomposes Arabic knowledge-graph construction into two evaluated stages: nested NER under domain shift and relation extraction between given mentions. For Subtask 1 (AdaptNER), we train a multi-head BIO tagger (one three-way O/B/I head per entity type over a shared pretrained Arabic encoder) on Wojood and combine three random seeds by span-level majority vote. For Subtask 2, forced-choice classification over the 40 WojoodRelations relation types, we fine-tune a typed-marker classifier with type-constraint decoding, ensembling five grouped folds by logit averaging. Our submissions scored 0.7483 micro-F1 on AdaptNER’s blind Konooz slice (ten unseen domains), 4th of the eight officially ranked teams and 11.8 points above the official baseline, and 0.9571 micro-F1 on relation extraction with the no-relation class masked at decoding, 2nd at the results release; re-scored by the organizers over all 41 classes, the same ensemble reaches 0.9328, 4th in the organizers’ final ranking. We analyze where the 18.6-point domain-shift tax on NER falls: chiefly on recall. We further show that type-constraint decoding and ensembling are partially redundant (+0.9 points on a single RE model, +0.1 on the ensemble) and that the surviving errors share an argument-type signature that no type constraint can separate.

paper.title: McMasterNLP at KnowledgeGraphEval-2026: Heterogeneous Expert Systems for Arabic Knowledge Graph Construction
paper.abstract: Automated knowledge graph (KG) construction involves two core components: nested named entity recognition (NER) and relation extraction (RE). In this work, we address cross-domain nested NER alongside RE. We integrate domain adaptation methods within a mixture-of-experts ensemble system for nested NER from Arabic text, evaluated in a cross-domain setting. The system combines multiple Arabic pretrained encoders for token- and span-level classification with domain data augmentation, and integrates their predictions using a vote-based ensemble routing with a complementary XLM-R expert. For RE, we employ an adversarially trained relation classifier backed by auxiliary entity types, NLI reranking, and structural schema rules, treating no_relation as a standard relation label. We additionally study a positive-relation setting that excludes no_relation from both training and inference. Our NER system reaches 0.7438 micro F1 on the hidden test set. For RE, the positive-relation setting achieves 0.9608 micro F1, while the no_relation-aware system achieves 0.9295.

paper.title: YafaRE at KnowledgeGraphEval 2026: A Relation Extraction ArBERTv2-based Approach for Arabic Knowledge Graph Construction
paper.abstract: Relation extraction (RE) identifies semantic relations between entities, converting unstructured text into structured facts for downstream applications such as knowledge graph construction. Arabic RE remains challenging due to rich morphology, complex syntax, dialectal variation, and the scarcity of high-quality annotated resources. We present Yafa’s Team submission (ranked 7th) to Subtask 2 of the KnowledgeGraphEval 2026 Shared Task, which frames Arabic RE as multiclass classification over 40 relation types from the dataset. We propose an ArBERTv2-based entity-marker classifier that fuses global sentence context ([CLS]) with entity-specific representations (h_e1, h_e2) into a joint representation for relation prediction. Building on this baseline, we exploit a transductive self-training step that pseudo-labels the released test inputs at a softmax confidence threshold of 0.95 and retrains on them, raising Micro-F1 from 70.20% to 91.92%. We further conduct a systematic analysis of cross-backbone ensembling with MARBERTv2 and AraBERTv2, finding that ensembling does not outperform the single transductive model. Our results highlight transductive self-training as a simple yet effective strategy for improving Arabic RE robustness.

paper.title: YafaNER at KnowledgeGraphEval 2026: AraBERTv2-based Approach to Cross-Domain Adaptation for Arabic NER
paper.abstract: Cross-domain Arabic Named Entity Recognition (NER) remains challenging because models trained on one domain can lose performance when applied to unseen domains with different vocabulary, writing styles, and entity distributions. This paper addresses this challenge, and presents Yafa’s Team submission (ranked 7^{th}) to Subtask 1 of the KnowledgeGraphEval 2026 Shared Task. Our system leverages an AraBERTv2-based model for nested Arabic NER to approach it. The proposed approach combines task-adaptive (TAPT) pretraining on unlabeled Konooz data, R-Drop fine-tuning on Wojood, strong data augmentation, teacher-student knowledge distillation, span-level confidence and entropy filtering, and an entity-specific confidence-aware weighted-logit ensemble. Three teacher models generate soft labels for Konooz, and three distilled student models are combined in the final ensemble to produce the final predictions. Wojood contains approximately 448K tokens and 72K entity mentions across 21 entity types, while Konooz contains data from 10 domains for cross-domain evaluation. The final system achieves a Micro F1 of 71.33% on the official Konooz test set, improving over the non-adapted AraBERTv02 baseline of 61.00% by 10.33 points. The results show that combining domain adaptation, filtered knowledge transfer, and entity-specific ensembling can improve cross-domain Arabic NER performance.

paper.title: ANLP_UniSo at KnowledgeGraphEval 2026: Domain-Adaptive Nested Named Entity Recognition for Arabic via GlobalPointer Ensembling

author.affiliation: Higher Institute of Management, University of Sousse

paper.abstract: The ANLP_UniSo team submitted a system to Subtask 1 (Named Entity Recognition) of KnowledgeGraphEval 2026, which focuses on nested NER in Arabic and evaluates crossdomain and cross-dialect generalization from the Wojood corpus to the multi-domain Konooz benchmark. The system is a combination of an Efficient GlobalPointer decoder with rotary position embeddings and a MARBERT backbone. To reduce the domain gap, first domainadaptive pretraining (DAPT) is performed on unlabeled Konooz text, and then a pseudolabeling self-training stage is applied. A second model based on AraBERT is trained and combined to the other model using a stacking ensemble to improve prediction diversity. As for the Wojood test set, the best ensemble achieves a micro F1 of 0.9288, increasing to 0.9292 when entity-type-specific decision thresholds are used, compared with 0.9211 for the single MARBERT model. On the official blind Konooz test set, however, the submitted system obtains a micro F1 of 0.7106 (macro F1 = 0.6101, weighted F1 = 0.7013, P = 0.8143, R = 0.6304, accuracy = 0.9948). The lower recall suggests that the decoding threshold chosen based on the Wojood validation data was too strict for the domain-shifted Konooz data. the system study the difference and propose a threshold-recalibration strategy to improve the performance under the target-domain distribution.

paper.title: ArmyForRE at KnowledgeGraphEval 2026: Typed Entity Markers and Imbalance-Aware Training for Arabic Relation Extraction
paper.abstract: In this paper, we present a relation extraction system developed for Subtask 2 of KnowledgeGraphEval 2026. The system fine-tunes a single ARBERTv2 encoder on inputs with typed entity markers that expose entity boundaries and types, also classifies each entity pair from the encoder’s classification token ([CLS]) state concatenated with the states at the subject and object start markers. It is trained over the full 41-label space, including no-relation, with focal loss, class-balanced sampling, label smoothing, and no-relation down-weighting to counter severe class imbalance. Our submission ranked third of seven teams with a micro-F1 of 0.9332, 0.23 points above the official baseline, which fine-tunes the same encoder. We also report an analysis of seed-dependent behaviour on fine-grained geopolitical relations from our earlier development experiments and discuss the limitations of our evaluation.

paper.title: U4RASD at KnowledgeGraphEval-2026: Ontology-Constrained Encoder and LLM Systems for Arabic Relation Extraction

author.affiliation: Arab Center for Research and Policy Studies
Arab Center for Research and Policy Studies
Arab Center for Research and Policy Studies
Arab Center for Research and Policy Studies
Arab Center for Research and Policy Studies and American University of Beirut

paper.abstract: This paper details our submission to KnowledgeGraphEval 2026 Subtask 2 on directed Arabic relation extraction. We explored encoder-based and large language model approaches for predicting one of 40 relations or no_relation from an Arabic sentence and a subject–object pair. Our encoder systems use typed entity markers and separate relation-existence and relation-classification heads, while our LLM systems fine-tune Yehia and Qwen3.5 with QLoRA and ontology-constrained prediction. Our best system, an ensemble of Yehia-RE, Qwen-RE, and TypedPair, achieved a micro-F1 score of 94.06 and ranked 1st in Subtask 2. Yehia-RE (full-vocabulary) achieved 92.98, while the best encoder and Qwen-RE achieved 92.69 and 91.94 respectively. Our results highlight the importance of constrained prediction and complementary modeling approaches for Arabic relation extraction.

paper.title: ArmyForNER at KnowledgeGraphEval 2026: Multi-Stage Domain Adaptation and Self-Training Ensemble for Arabic Nested Named Entity Recognition
paper.abstract: This paper presents the ArmyForNER system for Subtask 1 of the KnowledgeGraphEval 2026 shared task on Arabic named entity recognition (NER). We address nested, cross-domain Arabic NER with a multi-stage pipeline built on ARBERTv2: (1) domain-adaptive pre-training (DAPT) via masked language modelling on unlabelled Konooz text, (2) fine-tuning with a multi-head BIO tagging architecture on the Wojood nested NER corpus, and (3) self-training on pseudo-labels produced by an intermediate DAPT ensemble over the Konooz domains. Soft-voting three self-trained checkpoints obtains 74.85 micro-F1 and 65.20 macro-F1 on the official test set, against a 63.00 / 44.00 base- line. Because both adaptation stages consume the blind Konooz test sentences, our system is listed among those that used Konooz during training, and its score is not comparable to systems that used Konooz for evaluation only. We state this setting explicitly and find that self-training gives consistent gains across seeds, whereas the benefit of DAPT is configuration- and seed-dependent.

paper.title: Daleel 2026 Shared Task on Arabic Argumentative Discourse Mining
paper.abstract: This paper presents Daleel 2026, the first shared task on argument mining in Arabic news editorials and competitive debates. Daleel includes two tasks: Task 1 identifies which of six argumentative discourse unit (ADU) categories are present in a paragraph, while Task 2 locates the units with their labels and exact text spans. The tasks are performed using a new corpus of 30 documents, 1,042 paragraphs, and about 76k words. Twenty-nine teams registered, 12 participated, and 10 submitted system papers. Both tasks have Closed and Open tracks. The best results for the Closed track were 0.7117 macro-F1 in Task 1 and 0.7547 modified overlap F1 in Task 2. The results show different insights: the best Closed-track score of each team was higher on debates than on editorials. A broad range of approaches was used in Task 1 submissions, including Arabic encoders, large language models, rules, and ensembles. Task 2 systems, in particular the top-ranked ones, were more similar and mainly used CRF or Viterbi decoding with combinations of models or training runs. The rare ADU categories remained difficult in both tasks, and identifying exact span boundaries was an additional challenge in Task 2.

paper.title: BME-Daleel at Daleel 2026: Joint Modeling, Structured Decoding, and Domain-Routed Ensembles for Arabic Argument Units

author.affiliation: Budapest University of Technology and Economics

paper.abstract: We present BME-Daleel, our system for both Daleel 2026 Arabic argumentative discourse mining tasks. A joint Transformer predicts paragraph-level label presence and token-level BIO states; constrained decoding and domain-routed ensembles map spans to original character coordinates. Repeated out-of-fold comparisons gate domain specialists, while routing selected decoded outputs preserves other-genre rows exactly. Using organizer annotations and public pretrained models, our Closed-track system scores 0.7117 macro-F1 for paragraph classification and 0.7547 modified F1 for span detection.

paper.title: TTLab at Daleel 2026: STAR-Ar, Sequence Tagging for Argument Recognition in Arabic

author.affiliation: Johann Wolfgang Goethe Universität Frankfurt am Main
Johann Wolfgang Goethe Universität Frankfurt am Main and Johann Wolfgang Goethe Universität Frankfurt am Main
Johann Wolfgang Goethe Universität Frankfurt am Main

paper.abstract: Argument Mining (AM) is a critical NLP task that remains significantly under-resourced in Arabic. This paper presents STAR-Ar, a BERT-BiLSTM-CRF architecture for argument discourse detection and classification, as our system for Daleel 2026, the inaugural Arabic argument mining shared task. The task requires the identification and classification of argumentative discourse units (ADUs) in debate and editorial texts. We jointly model these two objectives as a token-level sequence labeling task using a BERT-BiLSTM-CRF architecture that combines contextual transformer embeddings with structural transition constraints to support accurate span detection. STAR-Ar achieves an F1-score of 72.69 on validation and 73.7 on test data. Our domain-specific analysis shows that models trained exclusively on editorials underperform those trained on debates, a disparity we primarily attribute to the smaller size of the editorial dataset.

paper.title: SalahAbdo at Daleel 2026: Routing Each Label to LLM Votes, a Fine-Tuned Encoder, or Sequence Structure
paper.abstract: We describe the SalahAbdo closed-track systems for both Daleel 2026 subtasks: deciding which argumentative-unit types appear in an Arabic paragraph (Task 1) and locating their exact spans (Task 2), in editorials and debates. No single method was best for all six argumentative-unit types, so our Task 1 system routes each type to the method that measured best for it: assumption (AS), testimony (TE), and statistics (ST) are detected by sampling a gemma-4-31b classifier five times and firing when enough samples agree; anecdote (AN) and other (OT) by a fine-tuned CAMeLBERT classifier; and the lowest-agreement type, common ground (CO), by ranking paragraphs and firing a fixed count. A final verifier shows the LLM examples of true and false ST paragraphs and removes likely false positives. Task 2 first extracts spans as verbatim LLM quotes, then re-labels them by blending encoder probabilities with label-sequence statistics under Viterbi decoding, with zero additional LLM calls. Every design change had to clear an adoption bar set before its result was read: 29 recorded decisions produced six adoptions, and composition arithmetic over already-scored legs predicted two development scores digit-for-digit. Development scores are 0.7089 macro-F1 (Task 1) and 0.7247 span F1 (Task 2); the pinned recipes scored 0.6499 and 0.7055 on test, and our final official submissions scored 0.712 and 0.7316: first of ten and fifth of eight closed-track teams (Section 6 discloses the evaluation-phase protocol). Residual errors track the scheme’s measured human agreement (kappa as low as 0.114): types whose definitions a model can check against the text improved under LLM verification, while types defined by annotation convention resisted every prompting attack and were learned only from supervision and sequence structure.

paper.title: RabeeQasem - ImpactAi at Daleel 2026: Conformer-Based Arabic Argumentative Discourse Mining
paper.abstract: We present our system for Daleel 2026 Task 2 on Arabic Argumentative Discourse Unit (ADU) detection. Our main contribution is a Conformer-based tagging architecture that combines a pretrained AraBERT encoder with a Conformer head to capture both global discourse context and local span-boundary cues. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first application of a Conformer-based architecture to Arabic ADU detection. The system also uses overlapping token windows, class-weighted training, character-level span reconstruction, and lightweight post-processing. On the official hidden test set, our system achieved an overall F1 score of 0.732, substantially outperforming the official baseline of 0.285 and ranking fourth in the closed track.

paper.title: Durham-Jazan at Daleel 2026: Domain-Routed Ensembles, LLM Augmentation, and the Limits of Decision-Rule Tuning for Arabic Argument Mining

author.affiliation: University of Waikato and University of Alberta

paper.abstract: We describe the Durham-Jazan submissions to the Daleel 2026 shared task on Arabic argumentative discourse mining, which comprises multi-label paragraph classification (Task 1) and argumentative span detection (Task 2), each with a Closed and an Open track. Our Task 2 Closed system routes the Modern Standard Arabic editorials to CAMeLBERT and the noisier debate transcripts to MARBERTv2. The Open system blends the two families at character level and adds synthetic training data from a large language model for rare-class generalisation, generated by a segment-concatenation recipe that makes span offsets exact by construction. The Task 1 systems add back-translation, targeted augmentation of the rare classes, and a QLoRA-tuned Qwen3-32B for the editorials. Everything else trains on one 16 GB consumer GPU. Our official test scores are 0.729 and 0.736 overlap-F1 on Task 2 and 0.657 and 0.669 macro-F1 on Task 1 (Closed and Open). We placed first of two on Task 1 Open, first of one on Task 2 Open, fifth of ten on Task 1 Closed, and sixth of eight on Task 2 Closed. Our central finding concerns our own systems on this data. Recalibrating per-class thresholds on validation outputs overfits them. Under a controlled protocol the held-out effect is negative at every tuning-set size we tested, while the apparent in-sample gain shrinks as the tuning set grows. An audit of eighteen interventions from our campaign is consistent with this, though observational. A size-matched study links the editorial deficit that every team showed to the genre composition of the training data. We release our code and synthetic data.

paper.title: Northwestern 12 at Daleel 2026: CAMeLBERT-Mix for Multi-Label Arabic Argumentative Discourse Unit Classification
paper.abstract: This paper presents our submission to Task 1 (Argumentative Discourse Unit Classification, Closed Track) of the Daleel 2026 Shared Task. The task addresses Arabic multi-label argumentative discourse unit classification at the paragraph level. Our system fine-tunes CAMeLBERT-Mix using a class-weighted Binary Cross-Entropy loss, paragraph-type-aware input representation, head-tail tokenization for long paragraphs, and label-specific threshold optimization. On the official development set, the proposed system achieves a Macro F1-score of 0.6121, a Micro F1-score of 0.7509, and a Samples F1-score of 0.6387. These results suggest that a carefully optimized CAMeLBERT-Mix framework provides a competitive and reproducible approach for Arabic argumentative discourse unit classification under the Closed Track setting.

paper.title: AIDAL-ARG at Daleel 2026: Hybrid and Multitask Approaches for Arabic Argument Mining
paper.abstract: This paper presents our systems for the Daleel 2026 Shared Task. We explore multitask learning, domain-specific ensembles, and a two-stage BIO segmentation and classification pipeline with LLM-based disambiguation, alongside classical machine-learning, Transformer, and LLM baselines. Results show that supervised Transformers outperform standalone LLM prompting, while LLMs are more effective for selectively resolving ambiguous predictions. The multitask model generalizes best on Task 1, achieving 0.599 F1, while the ensemble multitask model reaches 0.683 F1 on Task 2. Our results show the potential of LLM integration within Transformer-based systems for Arabic argumentative discourse mining.

paper.title: NU_Analytics at Daleel 2026: Independent Label Scoring and Structured Span Prediction for Arabic Argumentative Discourse Mining
paper.abstract: We present our closed-track systems for both subtasks of Daleel 2026, which targets Arabic argumentative discourse unit (ADU) mining over editorials and competitive debates. Task 1 is an imbalanced multi label paragraph classification problem, and Task 2 requires character-level detection and classification of ADU spans. For Task 1 we investigate two parameter-efficient decoder-LLM formulations: joint label generation with Qwen3.5-9B and independent label scoring with ALLaM-7B. The latter decomposes each paragraph into six explicit Yes/No decisions, giving every label direct supervision and a separate decision score; it achieves 0.6714 Macro-F1 on the evaluation phase and ranked 4th, while ablations show that additional class-balanced weighting degrades performance. For Task 2 we combine task-adaptive pretraining, Beginning-Inside-Outside Conditional Random Field (BIO-CRF) sequence labeling, boundary-jitter augmentation, character-space ensembling, and span post-processing over AraBERT-large, achieving an official F1 of 0.7523 (0.7931 on debates, 0.6417 on editorials) and ranking second. Across both tasks, our results support explicit label-wise supervision and span-level ensemble decisions as effective ways to handle label imbalance and boundary noise without aggressive reweighting, while short spans, rare classes, and genre variation remain challenging.

paper.title: BURHAN at Daleel Shared Task Subtask-1: A Multi-Label Transformer Pipeline for Arabic Argumentative Discourse Unit Classification

author.affiliation: University College of Applied Sciences, Islamic University of Gaza and Onaizah Colleges

paper.abstract: This paper presents our system for Task 1 of the Daleel 2026 shared task, which assigns multiple discourse-function labels to Arabic paragraphs from editorials and debate transcripts. We fine-tune a monolingual Arabic encoder (MARBERTv2) with a label-weighted focal loss, multilabel-stratified k-fold crossvalidation, out-of-fold per-label threshold calibration, k-fold ensembling, and a genreconditioning prefix, in a two-stage protocol that first trains on the training split alone and then retrains on training+development. Internal cross-validation macro-F1 rises from 0.667 to 0.680 across the two stages. On the official test set, the system attains micro-F1 = 0.766 and macroF1 = 0.560, with markedly stronger micro-F1 on debate paragraphs (0.825) than editorials (0.633), and a smaller but consistent macro-F1 gap (0.554 vs. 0.456). Assumption is classified most reliably (F1 = 0.88–0.94) and Common Ground least reliably (F1 ≤ 0.12), mirroring the low inter-annotator agreement reported for the same category in the source English scheme. We find a ∼0.12 gap between internal cross-validation and official test macro-F1, concentrated in low-support, genre-sensitive categories. Our code is publicly available at https://github.com/EidAhmed1/daleel2026_task1_project.

paper.title: Solodiscourse at Daleel 2026: Lexically-Augmented Focal-Loss Ensembling for Arabic Argumentative Discourse Unit Classification
paper.abstract: We describe our submission to Task 1 (Argumentative Discourse Unit Classification) of the Daleel 2026 shared task on Arabic argument mining, in the closed track. Given a paragraph from an Arabic editorial or debate transcript, the task is to predict the multi-label set of argumentative functions it contains, drawn from six classes: common ground, assumption, testimony, statistics, anecdote, and other. Our system fine-tunes a pretrained Arabic encoder, comparing AraBERT, MARBERT, and CAMeLBERT-mix, augmented with a small side-channel of hand-crafted lexical features motivated directly by the task’s class definitions (e.g., reporting verbs for testimony, digit/percentage patterns for statistics), trained with a class-balanced focal loss and combined into a 5-fold cross-validation ensemble; CAMeLBERT-mix was selected as the final encoder for all submitted configurations. In the dev phase, our Both-domain configuration achieved an overall macro-F1 of 0.5600 (editorial 0.4350, debate 0.4900). On the official test-phase Codabench leaderboard, our Both-domain configuration achieved an overall macro-F1 of 0.5265 (editorial 0.3838, debate 0.4943), ranking 10th; our Editorial-only configuration reached an overall macro-F1 of 0.4544 (editorial 0.3249, debate 0.4509). We report two findings grounded in these results: overall (pooled) macro-F1 consistently exceeds the macro-F1 computed on either genre subset alone, and our editorial-only model unexpectedly scores higher macro-F1 on the out-of-domain debate subset than on its own in-domain editorial subset. We discuss both as likely artifacts of per-class support sparsity at the smaller genre-subset scale rather than genuine cross-domain superiority, though we did not conduct a formal ablation study or systematic error analysis to confirm this, which we flag as the primary limitation of this report. Our code is available at https://github.com/turab-usmani/daleel-task1-closedtrack.

paper.title: DialectSentEval 2026: Arabic Dialect Sentiment Analysis and Swapping Shared Task

author.affiliation: King Fahad University of Petroleum and Minerals
University College of Applied Sciences, Islamic University of Gaza and Onaizah Colleges
King Fahad University of Petroleum and Minerals
King Fahad University of Petroleum and Minerals

paper.abstract: Sentiment analysis is a fundamental problem in Natural Language Processing (NLP). Standard sentiment classification for the Arabic language remains challenging due to the high volume of dialectal Arabic. To advance research in this area, this paper proposes the Shared Task on Sentiment Analysis and Swapping in Arabic Dialects (DialectSentEval), hosted with the Arabic Natural Language Processing Conference (ArabicNLP 2026). This shared task consists of two subtasks: Subtask 1 focuses on multi-class and multi-dialect sentiment analysis, requiring models to identify sentiment polarity across various Arabic dialects. Subtask 2 introduces a generative task for Arabic sentiment swap, challenging models to invert sentiment polarity while preserving core semantics. In this overview paper, we present the motivation, dataset creation, and summarize the main findings from participating models.

paper.title: Sabaa at DialectSentEval Shared Task Subtask-2: Classifier-Guided Candidate Reranking for Arabic Dialectal Sentiment Swap
paper.abstract: Sentiment swap asks a system to rewrite a sentence so that its polarity is inverted while everything else stays the same, two halves of an instruction that pull against each other. This paper describes how the Sabaa system navigates that trade-off for Arabic dialects in Subtask 2 of DialectSentEval 2026. Rather than asking one model for a single correct rewrite, we ask two fine-tuned Arabic sequence-to-sequence models to each propose several, then choose among the pooled proposals with a scoring function built from the signals the task grades us on. The system scores 49.07 BLEU, 69.33 chrF, and 0.7447 sentiment accuracy on the official test set. That last figure is the most informative result here: the system places 90.37% of its outputs at the polarity it was aiming for, and the shortfall traces to inferring each sentence’s original polarity, which the test data withholds. Measured against gold labels on development, that inference is correct only 74.07% of the time, and sixteen points of sentiment accuracy separate our submission from a perfect estimator.

paper.title: AKARROUCH at DialectSentEval 2026: A Generate-and-Rerank Approach for Arabic Dialect Sentiment Swapping
paper.abstract: We describe the AKARROUCH submission to DialectSentEval 2026 Subtask 2, which requires reversing the sentiment of an Arabic dialect sentence while preserving its content. We fine-tune AraT5v2 for direction-controlled generation and use it to produce multiple candidates. We then rerank these candidates using CAMeLBERT target-sentiment probabilities and source-to-candidate chrF. The system ranked second in the official evaluation, achieving 78.51% sentiment accuracy, 49.82 BLEU, and 70.12 chrF.

paper.title: NileNLP at DialectSentEval 2026: SWAPPER Sentiment SWAPping with Parameter-Effcient adapteRs for Arabic Dialects
paper.abstract: We describe our participation in Subtask 2 of the DialectSentEval 2026 Shared Task, whose goal is to rewrite an Arabic dialectal sentence so its sentiment polarity is reversed while its meaning, entities, and dialect are preserved. Our system, SWAPPER (Sentiment-SWAPping with Parameter-Efficient adapteRs), is an ensemble of LoRA-adapted mBART-50 checkpoints in which the adapters are extended beyond attention into the feed-forward sub-layers, where the actual lexical rewriting is learned. Three design choices carried most of the weight: (i) a minimal Arabic instruction prefix that reserves encoder capacity for content; (ii) feed-forward LoRA; (iii) forcing the decoder’s beginning-of-sequence token to ar_AR so mBART-50 does not drift into other scripts. On the official blind test SWAPPER reaches Sentiment-Style Accuracy 0.6732, BLEU 41.38, and chrF 65.84. As a secondary contribution, we introduce the J-Gap (\Delta J = J_{tgt} - J_{src}), a Jaccard-based copy-collapse diagnostic that cleanly separates genuine sentiment swappers from models that merely copy their input, and explains why superficially strong backbones such as AraT5v2 fail the task despite high surface metrics.

paper.title: LahjaSensei at DialectSentEval 2026: Few-Shot Prompting and Model Merging for Sentiment Swap
paper.abstract: Arabic dialect sentiment swapping requires systems to reverse the affective orientation of an utterance while preserving its core meaning, dialectal form, and fluency. This task is particularly challenging because sentiment may be conveyed through dialect-specific vocabulary, negation patterns, and spelling variation. We present LahjaSensei, our system for Subtask 2 of the DialectSentEval shared task. We investigate two complementary approaches: prompt-based generation with GPT-5.6 and parameter-efficient fine-tuning of Qwen2.5-7B. We evaluate GPT-5.6 under zero-shot, retrieved few-shot, stronger Arabic instructions, and direction-aware configurations. The direction-aware GPT-5.6 pipeline explicitly predicts source polarity before retrieving direction-matched demonstrations and generating the rewrite. For Qwen2.5-7B, we compare pooled QLoRA with linear and TIES merges of direction-specific adapters. Direction-aware GPT-5.6 prompting achieves the highest test sentiment accuracy and remains stable across development and test. Pooled QLoRA produces the highest development BLEU and chrF, while linear merging obtains the highest test BLEU and chrF but lower sentiment accuracy. These findings highlight the central trade-off between sentiment control and preservation of semantic content and demonstrate the value of explicit direction modeling for Arabic dialect sentiment swapping.

paper.title: Northwestern at DialectSentEval 2026: A Comparative Study of MARBERTv2 and AraBERT for Arabic Dialect Sentiment Analysis
paper.abstract: This paper describes our submission to Subtask 1 of DialectSentEval 2026, which focuses on three class sentiment classification for Arabic dialectal text. The task aims to classify sentences written in five Arabic dialects into positive, negative, or neutral sentiment categories. We investigate the effectiveness of transformer-based Arabic language models through a series of controlled experiments. Specifically, we compare MARBERTv2 and AraBERT while maintaining identical pre processing, training, and evaluation settings to ensure a fair comparison. In addition, we examine whether explicitly providing dialect information as part of the input improves classification performance.Experimental results on an internal validation split show that MARBERTv2 consistently outperforms AraBERT on this task. Furthermore, removing the explicit dialect tag from the input slightly improves performance, suggesting that MARBERTv2 can effectively capture dialect-specific linguistic patterns directly from the sentence. Our best configuration, which uses MARBERTv2 with sentence-only input, achieves a Macro F1-score of 0.9394 and an accuracy of 94.24%. These findings demonstrate the effectiveness of dialect-aware pre-trained language models for Arabic sentiment analysis and establish a strong baseline for the official shared task evaluation.

paper.title: Gradient Descenders at DialectSentEval 2026: A Comparative Study of Pretrained Arabic Transformers for Multi-Dialect Sentiment Analysis

author.affiliation: University of Information Technology, Vietnam National University

paper.abstract: This paper presents the Gradient Descenders system for DialectSentEval Subtask 1 on multi-dialect Arabic sentiment analysis. Because general-purpose models often miss dialectal nuances, we compare three pretrained encoders with distinct linguistic orientations: MARBERTv2, DarijaBERT, and AraBERT. We formulate the task as three-class classification, employing a parameter-efficient head-only adaptation strategy that freezes encoder parameters. Our results show MARBERTv2 outperforms the others, achieving a Macro F1 of 80.11% and Accuracy of 81.90%, securing fifth place overall. These findings emphasize that backbone selection is critical; specifically, broad dialect-oriented pretraining yields the most transferable representations for multi-dialect generalization.

paper.title: Axiom at DialectSentEval 2026: Dialect-Aware Ensembling of MARBERTv2 and AraBERTv2 for Arabic Sentiment Analysis
paper.abstract: Sentiment analysis of regional Arabic dialects presents a formidable challenge due to severe orthographic variation, morphological complexity, and a scarcity of annotated resources. To tackle these linguistic hurdles within Subtask-1 of the DialectSentEval 2026 Shared Task, team Axiom proposes a heavily regularized, dialect-aware ensemble framework combining two domain-complementary language models: MARBERTv2 and AraBERTv2. Our pipeline incorporates preprocessed dialect tags appended directly to input sequences, Stochastic Weight Averaging (SWA) for flat-minima convergence, and simple probability averaging across model outputs. Empirical results on the hidden test set demonstrate the robustness of this approach, with our system securing 2nd place overall and achieving an official Macro F1-Score of 0.8211.

paper.title: PTUK-NLP at the DialectSentEval 2026 Shared Task: MARBERT-Based Sentiment Classification, Missing-Dialect Effects, and Error Analysis
paper.abstract: We present our system for Subtask 1 (three-class sentiment classification) of the DialectSentEval 2026 shared task, which evaluates five Arabic dialects using the Multi-Dialect-Sent (MDS-3) hotel-review corpus. Our approach fine-tunes MARBERT with a stratified train/validation split and class-weighted cross-entropy loss. On the official test set, our system achieves an F1 score of 0.8175 and an accuracy of 0.8419, ranking 3rd on the official leaderboard. We identify a substantial dialect mismatch in the dataset: the training set contains no Lebanese reviews, while approximately 20% of the test set is Lebanese. Adding additional Lebanese reviews from OCLAR partially reduces this gap, but does not eliminate it. The error analysis also shows that misclassifications are concentrated in the neutral class and in reviews that express mixed feelings, often with high confidence. These findings highlight the challenges of cross-dialect sentiment classification under unseen-dialect conditions.

paper.title: NAMAA Community at DialectSentEval 2026 Subtask 1: Dialect-Aware Arabic Sentiment Classification with Pretrained Transformer Models
paper.abstract: Arabic dialect sentiment analysis is challenging because regional varieties show considerable lexical, morphological, syntactical, and orthographic variation. This paper presents a transformer-based system developed for DialectSentEval 2026 Subtask 1, a three-class sentiment classification task covering Moroccan, Egyptian, Jordanian, and Saudi Arabic. The system independently fine-tunes three pretrained Arabic language models: AraBERTv2, MARBERTv2, and CAMeLBERT, using a common training protocol. The implementation uses an 80/20 stratified train-validation split, a maximum sequence length of 128, a batch size of 16, a learning rate of 2 \times 10^{-5}, and focal loss with \gamma=2=2. Model selection was conducted based on validation macro F1. Using the published labeled test set, MARBERTv2 achieves the strongest independent result with 94.07% macro F1, followed by CAMeLBERT at 81.96% and AraBERTv2 at 79.77%. The results demonstrate the importance of Arabic pretraining and dialect-oriented representations and establish MARBERTv2 as the strongest standalone backbone in the current system.

paper.title: NAMAA at DialectSentEval 2026 Subtask 2: From Reranked Sampling to Cross-Backbone Ensembling for Arabic Dialectal Sentiment Swap
paper.abstract: Arabic sentiment swap aims to reverse the polarity of a dialectal sentence while preserving its underlying meaning. We present NAMAA’s system for DialectSentEval 2026 Subtask 2. Fine-tuning AraT5v2 achieves 79.56 development sentiment-style accuracy, while reranked sampling over eight candidates, using sentiment agreement and content-overlap signals, raises this to 93.57. Cross-backbone ensembling further reaches a development score of 96.78. On the hidden test set, however, this ordering does not transfer: a widened rerank pool with a re-tuned content weight achieves our best official score of 0.7597, whereas the most complex all-source ensemble scores 0.7343. We identify two likely contributors to this development-to-test mismatch: the absence of gold source-polarity labels at test time, which requires classifier-based polarity inference, and train–development sentence duplication that may inflate development performance. These results show that additional generation and ensemble complexity can improve development metrics substantially without guaranteeing better generalization under shifted evaluation conditions.

paper.title: faisalm93 at DialectSentEval 2026: A Five-Fold MARBERTv2 Ensemble for Arabic Dialect Sentiment Analysis

author.affiliation: Maryam Abacha American University of Nigeria

paper.abstract: We describe our submission to DialectSentEval 2026 Subtask 1, a three-class sentiment task covering Moroccan, Egyptian, Lebanese, Jordanian, and Saudi Arabic. Our system fine-tunes MARBERTv2 in five stratified folds and averages their test probabilities. Using raw text without explicit dialect conditioning or external task-specific data, the official submission obtained 0.7939 macro-F1, 0.8152 accuracy, 0.7917 macro precision, and 0.7987 macro recall, ranking eighth among twelve systems in the supplied snapshot. Separately, a post-submission character 3-5-gram diagnostic falls from 0.9157 OOF macro-F1 with row-stratified folds to 0.7520 when repeated ID-label groups and normalized duplicates are kept together. This result establishes dataset-level split sensitivity; it does not quantify the effect on MARBERTv2. We document the submitted configuration, a group-aware diagnostic protocol, and the experiments still needed to isolate the effects of strict splitting and ensembling on the transformer system.

paper.title: Lahja at DialectSentEval Shared Task Subtask-1: Seed-Ensembled MARBERT for Multi-Dialect Arabic Sentiment Analysis with Zero-Shot Lebanese Transfer

author.affiliation: University of Aberdeen and Al-Imam Mohamed Ibn Saud Islamic University

paper.abstract: Arabic sentiment analysis must cope with dialects that differ in vocabulary, morphology and spelling. Subtask 1 of the DialectSentEval 2026 shared task poses this problem directly: systems label hotel review sentences from five Arabic dialects as positive, negative or neutral, and one dialect (Lebanese) appears only in the test set. In this paper, we describe the Lahja submission. Since the training corpus is small (1,731 sentences) and consists of parallel translations, we treat unreliable measurement (i.e. leaky validation splits and single training runs) rather than model capacity as the main risk. We fine-tune MARBERTv2 under three random seeds, average their softmax outputs, and validate on a split grouped by review identifier so that all dialect versions of a review stay on the same side. The ensemble reached 0.790 macro-F1 on the official test set, ranking 10th of 12 teams, and lost only about two points from validation to test despite the unseen dialect. Our ablations show that the variation between seeds (about 1.5 points) exceeds the effect of orthographic normalisation or class weighting, and that the normalised ensemble, although best on validation, generalised worst on test. We therefore recommend grouped validation and seed-spread reporting as standard practice for small-data shared tasks.

paper.title: NU-SentEval at DialectSentEval Shared Task Subtask-2: Fine-Tuning AraT5 for Arabic Dialect Sentiment Swap
paper.abstract: We present NU-SentEval’s system for DialectSentEval 2026 Subtask 2 (Arabic Dialect Sentiment Swap), which rewrites Arabic dialectal sentences into the opposite sentiment polarity while preserving their core content. Our approach fine-tunes AraT5v2-base-1024, a pretrained Arabic sequence-to-sequence model, directly on the shared task’s source-target sentence pairs, and generates outputs using standard beam search decoding. On the official Final Evaluation test leaderboard, our system achieves 54.63 BLEU, 72.61 chrF, and 68.98% sentiment preservation. Our manual error analysis shows the model reliably inverts sentiment for short, single-clause inputs, often matching the human reference exactly, though it occasionally fails to propagate the sentiment flip to secondary cues such as emojis, resulting in mixed-signal outputs.

paper.title: NU-SentEval at DialectSentEval Shared Task Subtask-1: Stacking Pre-trained Language Models with Focal Loss for Arabic Dialect Sentiment Analysis
paper.abstract: This paper presents the system developed by the NU-SentEval team for Subtask 1 (Sentiment Analysis in Dialectal Arabic) of the DialectSentEval 2026 Shared Task. Arabic dialect sentiment classification is challenging due to morphological complexity, orthographic variation across regional dialects, and class imbalances in user reviews. To address these challenges, we propose an ensembled architecture leveraging five diverse Pre-trained Language Models (PLMs): MARBERTv2, MARBERT, CAMeLBERT-DA, AraBERTv0.2-Twitter, and Twitter-XLM-RoBERTa. All models were fine-tuned using a customized Focal Loss objective combined with Label Smoothing to mitigate majority class bias and prevent overconfidence. Out-of-fold probability representations from individual models were aggregated through a Logistic Regression stacking meta-classifier (stacking_c1). On the official test set, our system achieved a Macro F1-score of 0.8141 and an Accuracy of 0.8343, demonstrating the effectiveness of combining specialized dialectal representations with loss regularization and meta-learning.

paper.title: ALEXIS at DialectSentEval Subtask 1 Adversarial Training and Iterative Self-Training for Zero-Shot Dialect Sentiment Analysis
paper.abstract: Dialect sentiment analysis asks for the polarity of a sentence written in a regional Arabic variety rather than Modern Standard Arabic. We present a system for Subtask 1 of DialectSentEval built on two observations about the data. First, the task is one of zero-shot transfer rather than classification: the test set introduces Lebanese, a dialect with no labeled training data and the highest out-of-vocabulary rate in the task (52.0% of word types, against 19.5–41.0% for the seen dialects). Second, k-fold cross-validation cannot see this, since it measures generalization to unseen sentences and never to an unseen dialect. We therefore validate with a leave-one-dialect-out diagnostic and score every component on the official leaderboard. Three dialectally diverse encoders (MARBERTv2, CAMeLBERT-DA, AraBERTv2) are trained with Fast Gradient Method adversarial training, then refined by confidence-filtered self-training on the unlabeled test set and character-level noise augmentation. Adversarial training contributes +0.040 Macro F1 over a gold-only ensemble, self-training a further +0.027, and per-class pseudo-label filtering +0.018. The final system reaches 0.8667 Macro F1, ranking 1st of 12 submissions, 4.6 points above the runner-up.

paper.title: ALEXIS at DialectSentEval Subtask 2 Retrieval-Augmented, Preference-Tuned Generation for Arabic Sentiment Swap
paper.abstract: Sentiment swap is the task of rewriting a sentence so that it carries the opposite polarity while its topic stays the same. We present a system for Arabic sentiment swap built on two observations about the data. First, the swap is a local edit rather than a paraphrase: 91% of reference rewrites stay within two words of their source. Second, the polarity to swap away from has to be predicted, because the test data does not provide it. We therefore fine-tune mT5 and refine it with Direct Preference Optimization under a reward that balances target-polarity probability against content preservation. At inference we pool candidates from four generators, one of them a minimal-edit tagger, together with a retrieval index, rerank them with the same balance, and repair them with polarity-flip lexicons mined from the training set. Source polarity is supplied by a dedicated classifier that reaches 97.3% accuracy, against 74.3% for the off-the-shelf sentiment model that the evaluation itself uses. Every component was scored on the official leaderboard: generation-side work contributes +0.044 Sentiment Style Accuracy, and the dedicated polarity classifier a further +0.155. The final system reaches 0.9581 Sentiment Style Accuracy, 56.91 BLEU and 72.18 chrF, ranking 1st of 15 submissions.

paper.title: ArA-DF 2026: Findings of the First Shared Task on Arabic Speech Deepfake Detection

author.affiliation: Saudi Data and AI Authority, Saudi Data and AI Authority

paper.abstract: We present ArA-DF 2026, the first shared task for Arabic speech deepfake detection, held at ArabicNLP-2026. Unlike existing benchmarks that conflate all distribution shift into a single evaluation set, ArA-DF 2026 separates dialect generalization (Track 1: unseen Arabic dialects and speakers) from acoustic robustness (Track 2: codec compression, noise, reverberation, re-encoding). We release 43,500 labeled training utterances spanning MSA and regional dialects, plus blind evaluation sets of 144,210 (Track 1) and 127,746 (Track 2) utterances, ranking systems by EER. Fourteen teams competed on Track 1 and twelve on Track 2, with eight system description papers submitted. The best submissions cut EER from 14.54% to 0.87% (Track 1) and from 27.11% to 0.66% (Track 2). Across independent submissions, three findings recur: augmentation and data curation move performance far more than architecture; simpler pooling heads often outperform graph-attention back-ends once augmentation is applied; and external synthetic Arabic speech with mismatched generation artifacts hurts rather than helps. Residual errors concentrate on short utterances and on spoofed audio misclassified as bona fide.

paper.title: SparkShield at ArA-DF 2026: Robust Arabic Speech Deepfake Detection via Realistic Audio Augmentation and Multi-Scale XLS-R Score Fusion

author.affiliation: Anhui Laboratory for Safe Artificial Intelligence in the Yangtze River Delta and IFLYTEK CO.LTD.

paper.abstract: This paper presents the SparkShield system submitted to ArA-DF 2026 Track 2, which focuses on robust Arabic speech deepfake detection under realistic acoustic degradations. To improve robustness, we apply a comprehensive augmentation pipeline involving background noise, reverberation, codec compression, reencoding, and volume perturbation. Our system consists of three parallel subsystems using XLS-R models with 300M, 1B, and 2B parameters as front-end feature extractors. Each subsystem employs learnable layer-wise feature fusion, followed by a Multi-kernel gated Convolution (MultiConv) module and Multi-Head Attention Pooling (MHAP) for utterance-level spoof detection. The output logits of the three independently trained subsystems are finally fused. The proposed system achieves an EER of 0.6575% on the evaluation set and ranks first in ArA-DF 2026 Track 2.

paper.title: PogranichnyZashchitnik at ArA-DF 2026: WavLM Large with LoRA and One-Class Softmax for Arabic Speech Deepfake Detection

author.affiliation: University of Information Technology, Vietnam National University

paper.abstract: This paper describes the system submitted by team PogranichnyZashchitnik to the ArA-DF 2026 shared task on Arabic Audio Deepfake Detection. We build on WavLM Large as a self-supervised feature extractor, fine-tuned with Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) so that only a small fraction of parameters need updating. Representations from all 25 hidden layers are blended via a learnable weighted sum, pooled into utterance-level embeddings with Attentive Statistics Pooling, and classified by an OC-Softmax head that treats bonafide speech as the target class. Combined with an augmentation pipeline of codec compression, additive noise, and reverberation, this single system achieves 12.54% EER on Track 1 (Dialect Generalization, 14th/15) and 5.66% EER on Track 2 (Acoustic Robustness, 8th/14), outperforming the organizer baseline on both tracks. Post-evaluation analysis shows that utterances shorter than two seconds are disproportionately difficult, and that a non-trivial fraction of spoofed samples are scored as confidently bonafide under dialect mismatch.

paper.title: R_A at ArA-DF 2026: Fine-Tuned Self-Supervised Encoders with Acoustic Degradation For Robust Arabic Deepfake Detection

author.affiliation: Higher Institute for Applied Sciences and Technology

paper.abstract: We describe our submission to ArA-DF 2026, the ArabicNLP shared task on Arabic speech deepfake detection, in which systems classify audio as real or deepfake. We participated in both tracks: Track 1 (Dialect Generalization) and Track 2 (Acoustic Robustness). Our systems investigated finetuning three large self-supervised speech encoders — WavLM, wav2vec2-XLS-R, and HuBERT — with a learnable attentive-pooling head. We evaluated each encoder separately and further combined encoders through a logistic-regression meta-classifier. In addition to improve robustness we apply an acoustic degradation pipeline (additive noise, lossy codec re-encoding, band-limiting, and gain) to 50% of the training data. For track one the best achieved result is, a fully fine-tuned WavLM with attentive pooling and augmentation, which scored 2.19% EER test set, and a deepfake-pretrained XLS-R achieves 7.80% EER on Track2 which out performed the official baseline. Our ablation study shows that augmentation and backbone choice are the primary factors, while adding correlated ensemble members yields no gain.

paper.title: SaAr-DF at ArA-DF 2026: When More Data Hurts — Diversity-Driven Ensembling for Arabic Speech Deepfake Detection
paper.abstract: We describe our system for Track 1 (dialectgeneralization) of the ArA-DF-2026 Arabic speech deepfake detection shared task. Starting from the organizers’ XLS-R+AASIST baseline (14.65% EER on the development test set), we show that (i) raw-waveform augmentation (RawBoost) roughly halves the error rate, (ii) replacing the AASIST back-end with a simple mean-pooling head over a posttrained self-supervised frontend removes a hard performance ceiling that persists even after full convergence, and (iii) a large, architecturally diverse ensemble is the only lever that keeps improving once single-model performance saturates. Our final system, a 13-member weighted ensemble spanning three frontend sizes, two back-ends, and four training-data recipes, reaches 2.34% EER on the development-test leaderboard and 2.42% EER on the official held-out blind evaluation set (144,210 utterances, 9× larger than the development test). We also report two negative results of practical value: injecting a large (54k-clip) multi-system Arabic text-to-speech corpus and a vocoder-copy-synthesis pseudospoof corpus both degrade accuracy, indicating that indiscriminately adding synthetic speech is harmful when its generation artifacts do not match the target domain. Our code is publicly available at https://github.com/Body123/aradf-2026-saar-df.

paper.title: Thakaa at ArA-DF 2026: Fusing Self-Supervised and Signal-Processing Detectors for Arabic Speech Deepfake Detection

author.affiliation: Thakaa, Advanced Company for Information Technology
Thakaa, Advanced Company for Information Technology

paper.abstract: ArA-DF 2026 is a shared task on binary Arabic speech deepfake detection, with two tracks: dialect generalisation and acoustic robustness. For both we submit rank-normalised score fusions of complementary detectors. Track 1 fuses five components in two stages: three fine-tuned XLS-R-300M networks and two ResNet-18 classifiers over linear-prediction residual and group-delay representations. Track 2 fuses two XLS-R-300M detectors differing in augmentation strategy. We reach 2.8961 EER on Track 1 and 2.7626 on Track 2, against baselines of 14.54 and 27.11. Our analysis on the released test labels shows individual EER to be a poor guide to fusion contribution, which depends on error independence: both fusions improve on their best member by over 40%, and components far weaker in isolation than any we submitted improve them further.

paper.title: Raid AI at ArA-DF 2026: Data, Scale and Inference-Time Augmentation for Arabic Speech Deepfake Detection
paper.abstract: We describe Raid AI’s entry to Track 1 (Dialect Generalization) of the ArA-DF 2026 shared task on Arabic speech deepfake detection, which placed 1st of 15 teams at 0.8719% Equal Error Rate against a 14.54% official baseline. The configuration of the submitted system is proprietary and is not disclosed. We instead report the ablation behind it, re-scored on the official 144,210-clip evaluation partition against the labels released after the challenge, with bootstrap confidence intervals and paired tests throughout. On development-test, corpus and augmentation alone move a fixed architecture from 13.13% to 1.37% EER. Encoder scale is not monotonic: a 1B encoder beats a 2B under a recipe matched on corpus, augmentation, learning rate, class weights and effective batch size, though the gap is inside the run-to-run spread we measure from three seeds. Three-crop test-time augmentation improves all ten models tested, by 17.4% relative on average, and is the only effect immune to seed variance because it is measured within a checkpoint; a per-crop decomposition shows the gain comes from averaging rather than from choosing a better window.

paper.title: UZH-CL at ArA-DF 2026: Prompt-Tuned Foundation Models and Track-Adaptive Score Fusion for Arabic Speech Deepfake Detection

author.affiliation: Idiap Research Institute and Faculty of Information Technology, Brno University of Technology

paper.abstract: Detecting synthetic and voice-converted speech remains difficult for low-resource languages with dialectal diversity, where systems must generalize across regional dialects and unseen acoustic channels. We present the UZH-CL submission to the ArA-DF 2026 Shared Task on Arabic speech deepfake detection, covering Track 1 (dialect generalization) and Track 2 (acoustic robustness). We freeze a W2V-BERT-2.0 backbone and adapt it with Wavelet Prompt Tuning, updating under 1% of parameters, and aggregate multi-layer representations with cross-layer attention and a general attentive-statistics pooling head rather than a specialized graph backend. Complementary detectors are obtained by varying adaptation strategy, training data, augmentation, and encoder family. We find that the two shift types require different fusion regimes: a broad multi-window ensemble for dialect generalization, and a compact, channel-matched, center-crop ensemble for acoustic robustness. Official evaluation yields 1.96% EER on Track 1 (6th place) and 1.04% EER on Track 2 (3rd place), corresponding to 87% and 96% relative reductions over the XLS-R+AASIST baselines.

paper.title: pi-labs.ai at ArA-DF 2026: Score-Level Fusion of Self-Supervised Speech Encoders with an AASIST Back-End for Arabic Audio Deepfake Detection
paper.abstract: This paper presents our submission to the ArADF 2026 Shared Task on Arabic Audio Deepfake Detection, focusing on Track 1, which evaluates robustness to previously unseen Arabic dialects. Our proposed system combines two complementary self-supervised speech encoders, XLS-R-300M and WavLM-Large, each integrated with an AASIST graph-attention back-end for spoofing detection. The final prediction is obtained through score-level fusion of the two independently trained models, enabling the system to leverage the complementary representations learned by each encoder. To improve robustness to domain shift, we introduce two complementary adaptation strategies: telephony channel augmentation to reduce the mismatch between the training and evaluation domains, and an iterative pseudolabel self-training framework that exploits highconfidence predictions on unlabeled evaluation data for progressive model refinement. On the official ArA-DF 2026 Track 1 evaluation set, our system achieved an Equal Error Rate (EER) of 0.9265%, ranking 4th on the official leaderboard. These results demonstrate that combining complementary self-supervised speech representations with domain-aware adaptation techniques provides an effective and robust solution for cross-dialect Arabic audio deepfake detection.

paper.title: AISA-ArabicFC: The First Shared Task on Arabic Function Calling for Agentic AI Systems
paper.abstract: Function calling connects language models to external tools, but Arabic structured tool use remains insufficiently evaluated. We present , a shared task at ArabicNLP 2026 built around 12{,}220 Arabic requests spanning five dialect groups and eight service domains. Each request has four candidate schemas drawn from a registry of 27 tools, including seven tools that never occur as gold calls; 223 requests require abstention. Systems decide whether to call, select a function, and extract its arguments. Two ranked tracks evaluate core calling and reasoning-trace compliance, with a third diagnostic examining dialect robustness. Twenty-two teams submitted to the blind phase, and 21 produced valid predictions on 1{,}125 test requests. We analyze 73 submissions and 13 system descriptions. A LoRA-adapted 4B model ranks first on both competition tracks, with scores of 0.9279 and 0.9400, while argument exact match peaks at 0.8816. However, a deterministic rule combining candidate order and released metadata matches the best observed function-name accuracy of 0.9973, limiting what this metric establishes about language understanding. Exact argument extraction provides most of the competitive separation. Maghrebi has the lowest score for every system, although its small test subset and differences in example composition limit interpretation. We provide public task data, a baseline checkpoint, the scorer, and final rankings, and document evaluation shortcuts and remaining reproducibility limitations.[<https://huggingface.co/spaces/TuwaiqAcademy/AISA-ArabicFC-Shared-Task>]

paper.title: Saudi Legal FC at AISA-ArabicFC: Disciplined Fine-Tuning and Gold-Free Post-Processing for Arabic Function Calling
paper.abstract: We describe the Saudi Legal FC submission to the AISA-ArabicFC shared task on Arabic function calling. Our system is a parameter-efficient fine-tune of Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct with LoRA, trained with completion-only loss masking. Beyond the model, our central contribution is methodological: we use written, falsifiable score predictions and a validated local scorer to gate submissions, with a post-processing safety net that uses no gold at inference. On the public development set our best configuration reaches Argument Exact-Match (ArgEM) 0.828 and function-name accuracy 1.0 (Overall-B 0.914) under the official v1.3 evaluator. Its weights were then lost; the blind submission comes from a reconstruction selected against that model’s frozen predictions, and ranks 12th on Track B with Overall-B 0.8946. We also report two negative findings—one retraining run, one rejected hypothesis—and an artifact-identity failure our behavioral checks caught before submission.

paper.title: Durham-Jazan at AISA-ArabicFC: A Field-Wise QLoRA Ensemble and the Sensitivity of Exact-Match Scoring

author.affiliation: University of Waikato and University of Alberta

paper.abstract: We describe the Durham-Jazan submission to AISA-ArabicFC 2026, an Arabic function-calling task in which a system selects one tool from four candidates and fills its arguments, scored on tool choice (FnAcc) and on strict exact match of the whole argument dictionary (ArgEM). Across six QLoRA fine-tunes of ALLaM-7B and Qwen2.5-7B, trained on the provided data, negatives derived from it and 68 hand-written no-tool utterances, and run on one 16 GB GPU, we vote on each argument separately, then apply two deterministic rules estimated from training statistics. The system reaches ArgEM 0.824 on development under the final evaluator and 0.826 on the blind test, placing 9th of 17 in Track A, 8th of 17 in Track B and 11th of 21 in Track C. Our main findings concern the benchmark. The reference tool is listed first on every training and development row that calls one, in every data release. Shuffling the candidates at inference costs the voted system 0.202 FnAcc and 0.190 ArgEM, and retraining one adapter per base on permuted candidates removes the dependence with no loss of ArgEM. One post-processing rule contributes 0.028 ArgEM and is the only component whose gain separates from zero, the other targets a convention the final data release removed and is inert, and the largest effect we can measure comes from the benchmark’s construction rather than from our modelling.

paper.title: Wajeh at AISA-ArabicFC: A Non-LLM Classical ML and Retrieval Pipeline for Arabic Function Calling
paper.abstract: We describe NABIQ, the system submitted by team Wajeh (واجه) to Tracks A and B of the AISA-ArabicFC shared task on Arabic function calling. NABIQ contains no large language model, no neural network of any kind, no external API and no GPU. It is a CPU-based pipeline of classical ML, retrieval and rule-based repair: a TF-IDF router, a per-tool nearest-argument retriever over train, span extractors with train-mined gazetteers, and a no-call detector. Its core mechanism is an evidence gate: a candidate value may replace a prediction only if it is a normalised substring of the utterance, a member of a closed canonical map, or a date whose tokens occur in the text. On the blind test the frozen system scored Overall A 0.7904 (rank 16) and Overall B 0.8282 (rank 15) at ThinkRate 1.0000. We keep five evaluation levels distinct because the submitted system drops 0.21 ArgEM from development to test. A rehearsal on 545 held-out training rows, run before the blind release, tracked our official Overall A far better than the tuned development estimate (composite error 0.0033 against 0.1724, cancelling larger FnAcc and ArgEM errors); that contrast, not the components, is our result.

paper.title: PuDyDG at AISA-ArabicFC: Decomposed Fine-Tuning with Function-Centric Few-Shot Augmentation for Arabic Function Calling

author.affiliation: University of Information Technology, Vietnam National University

paper.abstract: Tool calling has become increasingly important for agentic systems, but remains challenging in multilingual settings, particularly for Arabic. We present our system for the AISA-ArabicFC shared task at ArabicNLP 2026. Our approach combines decomposed multi-task fine-tuning, function-centric few-shot augmentation, and hybrid schema-aware inference. On the development set, our system achieves a function-name accuracy of 1.000 and a normalized argument exact match of 0.858. On the blind test set, the released baseline re-scored with the final scorer obtains a Track A score of 0.8000, compared with 0.9111 for our submission. Our system achieves a function-name accuracy of 0.9973 and an argument exact match score of 0.8536 on this set, ranking seventh in Track A. Our solution is released in the GitHub repository[<https://github.com/phud774/PuDyDG-AISA-ArabicNLP>].

paper.title: QMUL_AK at AISA-ArabicFC: Schema-Constrained Function Calling with ALLaM
paper.abstract: We describe the QMUL_AK submission to AISA-ArabicFC 2026. The system adapts the Arabic-English ALLaM-7B-Instruct model to function calling with low-rank adaptation (LoRA). It combines an Arabic schema-aware prompt, dialect and no-call resampling, a token-weighted training objective, and deterministic validation of generated calls against the candidate tool schema. The same output supports Track A function calling and Track B reasoning-augmented calling. Training uses only the official task data. On the development set, the system achieves 0.9982 function accuracy and 0.8920 argument exact match, corresponding to overall A and B scores of 0.9345 and 0.9454. On the blind test set, the system reaches overall A and B scores of 0.9253 and 0.9380, ranking 3rd on both submission tracks and 1st of 21 teams on the Track C dialect-robustness diagnostic with a macro-averaged score of 0.9075 and the smallest dialect gap in the shared task (0.077). The results show that function selection is nearly saturated, while argument extraction remains the main source of error.

paper.title: Abjad at AISA-ArabicFC: Error Analysis and Prompt Engineering for Arabic Function Calling
paper.abstract: We describe Abjad’s submission to the AISA-ArabicFC shared task (Track B), which targets Arabic function calling with explicit natural-language reasoning prior to the structured call. Rather than fine-tuning, our system builds a robust inference and evaluation pipeline around the organizers’ baseline model, AISA-AR-FunctionCall-Think, diagnosing and fixing two pipeline-level bugs that were silently depressing scores. On the 545-example development set, our system reaches a function-name accuracy of 96.15% but an argument exact-match of only 40.6%, yielding an official Track B score (overall_b) of 0.6665, below the organizer-reported baseline of 0.739. We present a fine-grained error analysis showing that failures concentrate almost entirely in argument value formatting, including currency codes, ISO language codes, and transliteration, rather than in tool selection or task comprehension. These findings suggest that targeted fine-tuning or post-processing for structured-value normalization is a promising direction for improving Arabic function-calling performance. abjad aisa arabicfc.pdf

paper.title: Siraj at AISA-ArabicFC: Selective Argument Repair and the Limits of Post-Editing in Arabic Function Calling

author.affiliation: King Abdullah University of Science and Technology
King Abdulaziz city for science and technology

paper.abstract: We describe Siraj’s Track B submission to AISA-ArabicFC. A QLoRA-tuned ALLaM-7B is followed by a separately trained argument repairer whose edits pass a type-restricted acceptance filter, then by one deterministic year rule. On the blind test set (1,125 rows) it scores 0.8245 ArgEM and 0.9101 Track B, 10th of 17 systems; the post-editing stage is worth about one example on test against four on development. Every rule that error inspection suggested was adjudicated on out-of-fold training predictions, scored with the task’s own published matcher, before it could touch development predictions; all five were rejected, one of them breaking 168 more rows than it fixed. Two development-time conclusions did not survive: the top three systems finished 5.5 to 5.7 ArgEM points ahead, so our error rate was not a task-level ceiling, and a later dataset revision lowers our development ArgEM from 0.850 to 0.8080 and neutralises our strongest rule. Post-editing rules fitted to gold conventions can inherit changes in those conventions.

paper.title: ArgTune at AISA-ArabicFC: A Modular Pipeline for Arabic Function Calling
paper.abstract: We present ArgTune, a modular pipeline for Arabic function calling developed for the AISA-ArabicFC shared task. ArgTune separates tool selection from argument extraction using three LoRA-fine-tuned AISA-AR-FunctionCall-Think (270M) models: a tool-selection model, a general argument model, and a specialist model for seven challenging tools, allowing each model to focus on a more specific task. Targeted augmentation, data balancing, and query-grounded post-processing further address difficult argument cases. On the official test set, ArgTune achieved 0.9964 FnAcc, 0.8506 ArgEM, and an overall score of 0.9089, ranking 8th. The results highlight the remaining difficulty of exact argument extraction despite highly accurate tool selection.

paper.title: Optimal at AISA-ArabicFC: A Hybrid Approach to Arabic Function Calling with PEFT Large Language Models and Deterministic Post-Processing
paper.abstract: Arabic function calling requires models to identify appropriate tools and reproduce arguments in the exact representation expected by evaluators. This is challenging due to dialectal variation, lexical alternatives, and surface-form normalization. We present a hybrid system based on Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct adapted with 4-bit QLoRA, followed by conservative deterministic post-processing. The neural model generates flexible tool calls, while a lightweight deterministic layer parses, validates, and casts the output to improve compliance with the exact-match evaluation format. On the official blind evaluation, our system obtains 93.24% Function Accuracy and 58.38% Argument Exact Match (Track A: 72.32%, Track B: 71.37%). Error analysis indicates that many remaining failures arise from argument-surface mismatches rather than function-selection errors, supporting a design where generative modeling handles semantics while deterministic processing controls exact realization.

paper.title: Yalla at AISA-ArabicFC: Argument-Focused Fine-Tuning and Per-Argument Ensembling for Arabic Function Calling
paper.abstract: We describe the Team Yalla submission to the AISA-ArabicFC shared task on Arabic function calling, which ranked second in both tracks (0.9273 Track A, 0.9395 Track B), within 0.0006 of the winning system. The headline metric, exact argument match (ArgEM), is unforgiving: a single wrong surface form loses the whole example. The provided targets bury the scored object inside a rationale: the tool name and argument dictionary are only 30.3% of the target characters. We trained on the 30.3%, which is our largest single gain (+0.020 ArgEM in a matched comparison). A matched follow-up shows that reasoning need not be removed entirely: emitting it after the arguments trails the JSON-only target by only 0.008 ArgEM. We add a reinforcement-learning stage that uses the official scorer as the reward, and combine three deliberately diverse fine-tunes with a per-argument majority vote, which repairs individual argument slots rather than choosing whole predictions. Every member is a LoRA fine-tune of a public 4B or 7B Qwen model trained on the official split alone, with no distillation and no external data. We note that two of the three voting members emit no rationale, so our Track B think field is attached after prediction from a separate reasoning-trained model whose predicted call for that row is identical: it is a post-hoc explanation, not the computation that produced the arguments. We report the experiments that failed alongside those that worked.

paper.title: Ṣaqr at AISA-ArabicFC: What Actually Influences Arabic Function Calling?
paper.abstract: We describe Ṣaqr, ranked first on both scored tracks of the AISA-ArabicFC shared task on Arabic function calling, scoring 0.9279 on Track A and 0.9400 on Track B over a 1,125- instance blind test set. The system is deliber- ately plain: one Qwen3-4B model with LoRA, two epochs, provided data only. Our contri- bution is not the system but an accounting of where score comes from. We find that scale helped only up to a point in our single-run, cross-family comparison, and that the remain- ing gains came instead from inference-time de- cisions worth +0.0063 Overall A and +0.0223 Overall B (Appendix A) with no retraining. prefilling the reasoning trace so the model can- not skip it, and parsing arguments against the declared schema . We also report two proper- ties of the data that bound any system’s score: abstention is decidable from prompt structure without reading the query, and the gold anno- tation is self-inconsistent on precisely the slots that separate strong systems.

paper.abstract: Argument exact-match (ArgEM) dominates the AISA-ArabicFC score. Under one prompt, a base gemma-4-12B-it reaches 0.9853 FnAcc but only 0.6940 ArgEM on dev, suggesting that argument convention rather than tool selection is the binding constraint. Fine-tuning on the provided train split raises ArgEM to 0.8880 while FnAcc increases only from 0.9853 to 0.9945, yet the model still fails 8.4% of the 10,500 positive training rows. Across rules, retrieval, prompting, selection, reranking, and fusion, dev-selected gains did not consistently transfer beyond development; smaller gains from other tested interventions remain unresolved. Explicit convention cards add 7.5 ArgEM points on a dev-selected 228-row subset for an unconfigured model, but give no measurable gain to the already configured pipeline. A scorer-equivalent gold answer occurs in a 20-sample pool for 34/56 (60.7%) rows missed by the raw fine-tune, but our selectors cannot exploit it. Our official prompt-only gemma-4-31B-it submission placed 6th of 17 on Track A, 5th of 17 on Track B, and 4th of 21 on Track C. The 12B fine-tune used for analysis was developed first but inadvertently omitted from the blind-test submission, so it has no official test score.

paper.title: Makeen at AISA-ArabicFC: Grounding LLM via Extracted Spans and Generalization Trade-off in Arabic Function Calling
paper.abstract: Reliable function calling is challenging for Arabic due to dialectal variation and limited task-specific resources. We present Makeen, a data-centric approach for the AISA-ArabicFC shared-task, and extend it with span extraction and confidence-gated routing. The best post-submission variant achieves 83.20% argument exact match and 91.11% Track B on development data under held-out (cross-validated) routing, while the submitted model achieves 82.65% argument exact match and 91.06% Track B on the blind test set, ranking 9th in Task B. We also release two Arabic tool-use datasets and show that external-tool augmentation improves unseen-tool argument exact match from 44.49% to 66.53%. These results highlight the importance of data quality, argument grounding, and tool-level generalization for Arabic function calling.

paper.title: Arabic Function Forge at AISA-ArabicFC: Copy, Don’t Interpret — Training-Free Arabic Function Calling
paper.abstract: Arabic Function Forge is our submission to AISA-ArabicFC 2026. Our system is training-free: it uses a single off-the-shelf open-weights model, prompted once per request, with no parameter updates. It placed fifth on Track A, fourth on Track B, and sixth on Track C. Our central observation is that function selection is nearly saturated on this benchmark while argument extraction is not: we reach 0.9893 function accuracy but only 0.8686 argument exact match, so 94.9% of the remaining headroom lies in arguments. The dominant failure is not misunderstanding but over-interpretation: the model translates values, converts dates to ISO form, and adds fields the user never provided. Our system is designed to suppress this behaviour by preserving argument values as written. We further find that the dialect penalty is concentrated rather than graded, with most of the drop occurring on Maghrebi.
